01_Magnets_and_magnetic_fields.json.title: Magnets and magnetic fields
01_Magnets_and_magnetic_fields.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe pole interactions (like poles repel, unlike poles attract), classify materials as magnetic or non-magnetic, and distinguish temporary magnets from permanent magnets and from electromagnets.
Define the direction of a magnetic field at a point as the direction of the force on a free north pole placed there, and explain induced magnetism in a nearby magnetic material.

prerequisites.statement: A force is a push or a pull that has both a size and a direction.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A magnetic field is defined by the direction of the force it would produce on a test pole, so you need to already treat force as something with a direction, not just a size.

prerequisites.statement: A force can act on an object without anything touching it (a non-contact force).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Magnetic attraction and repulsion happen across a gap with no contact; if you expect every force to need touching, a field explanation will feel like it is missing a mechanism.

diagnostic_items.question: Two trolleys sit on a smooth track without touching. A magnet is fixed to one trolley. With nothing touching either trolley, one of them suddenly accelerates toward the other. Can a force be acting on it even though nothing is in contact with it?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Yes. A non-contact force (here, a magnetic force) can act across a gap with nothing touching; the trolley accelerates because of that force alone.

common_wrong_answers.answer: No — a force always needs something to be touching the object.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has only met contact forces so far and rules out any force that acts across a gap, which will block a field-based explanation before it starts.

common_wrong_answers.answer: There must be a hidden string, draught of air, or someone pushing it.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner searches for a disguised contact mechanism instead of accepting that a field can act through empty space.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner already accepts non-contact forces, which every field-based explanation in this lesson depends on.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Revisit a non-contact force already met, such as gravity acting on a dropped object with nothing touching it, before introducing the magnetic case.

theory_blocks.title: A force that reaches across a gap
theory_blocks.body:
Hold two magnets apart, not touching, and move one near the other: it pulls or pushes, with nothing in between. This is a non-contact force, the same broad family as gravity, and it raises an obvious question: how strong is that push or pull, and which way does it act, *before* you actually bring a second magnet close enough to find out?

A [[blue:**magnetic field**]] is the answer: it is a map, drawn around a magnet, of the force that a magnetic pole would feel at every point nearby. Instead of testing every position by trial and error, you read the direction and strength of the force straight off the map. The rest of this lesson builds that map up from simple pole rules to a full field-line picture.

theory_blocks.title: Poles, materials, and three kinds of magnet
theory_blocks.body:
Every magnet has two **poles**, conventionally called north (N) and south (S). Bringing two poles together gives one of two outcomes: **like poles repel** (N near N, or S near S) and **unlike poles attract** (N near S). This rule alone predicts the outcome of any pole-facing-pole situation without needing to measure anything.

Only a small group of materials respond to a magnet at all: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are **magnetic materials**; most other materials, including copper, aluminium, wood, glass and plastic, are **non-magnetic** and are not attracted to a magnet in either orientation.

Magnets themselves come in three practical kinds. A **permanent magnet** (commonly made of steel) keeps its magnetism once magnetised, with no ongoing current needed. A **temporary magnet** (commonly made of soft iron) becomes strongly magnetic only while inside another magnetic field, and loses almost all of that magnetism once removed from it — useful whenever magnetism needs to be switched off. An **electromagnet** uses a current-carrying coil wrapped around a soft-iron core: its magnetism can be switched on and off, and its strength can be varied, simply by controlling the current, which neither a permanent nor an ordinary temporary magnet can do.

theory_blocks.title: Defining the direction of a magnetic field
theory_blocks.body:
To turn the pole rule into a full map, picture a small **test north pole**: a north pole so small that it does not disturb the field it is measuring. At any point near a magnet, the **direction of the magnetic field** at that point is defined as the direction of the force that test north pole would feel there.

Near the magnet's own north pole, a test north pole is repelled, so the field points *away* from the north pole. Near the magnet's south pole, a test north pole is attracted, so the field points *into* the south pole. Joining these directions point to point produces **field lines**: by convention they leave the north pole, loop around outside the magnet, and enter the south pole. Field lines never cross (the field only has one direction at any point), and where they are drawn closer together the field is stronger — most obviously right next to each pole.

assets.caption: Field lines of a bar magnet leave the north pole, loop round outside the magnet, and enter the south pole. A test north pole placed to the right of the N pole is repelled straight away from it, matching the field-line direction at that point.
assets.purpose: Make the force-on-a-test-pole definition of field direction concrete, and show that the field-line pattern around a bar magnet follows directly from it.

theory_blocks.title: Induced magnetism: borrowing magnetism without touching
theory_blocks.body:
A magnetic material placed inside another magnet's field can become magnetised itself, even without being touched or stroked — this is **induced magnetism**. An unmagnetised steel paperclip held near a magnet's pole becomes a magnet itself while it is in the field, which is exactly why it is then attracted (not repelled) regardless of which pole of the original magnet it is near: the field always induces the nearer face of the paperclip to become the *opposite* pole, so the two always attract.

This is also why a chain of paperclips can sometimes hang from a magnet, each one inducing magnetism in the next, and why a single unmagnetised iron nail does not by itself attract other objects: induced magnetism needs a field to switch it on.

theory_blocks.title: A field line is a force direction, not a travel path
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to read a field-line diagram the way you might read a map of roads, as if something travels along each line. It does not. A field line only shows [[blue:the direction of the force a free north pole would feel if it were placed at that exact point]]; a different point on the same diagram has its own field line showing the force direction there. Nothing is 'moving along' any of these lines unless you deliberately place something at a point and let the force act on it.

This also explains why field lines are always drawn pointing *away* from a north pole and *into* a south pole: that is simply the direction of the force on a test north pole at each location, following the same like-repels, unlike-attracts rule used for two full-sized poles.

keywords.definition: The region around a magnet in which a magnetic pole experiences a force.
One of the two ends of a magnet (north or south) where the magnetic effect is strongest.
A material, such as iron, steel, nickel or cobalt, that can be magnetised or attracted by a magnet.
A magnet, typically made of steel, that keeps its magnetism without needing to stay inside another field.
A magnet, typically made of soft iron, that is strongly magnetic mainly while inside another magnetic field.
A magnet made from a current-carrying coil around a soft-iron core, whose strength is controlled by the current.
Magnetism produced in a magnetic material by being placed inside another magnet's field, without contact or stroking.
A line showing the direction of the force on a free north pole at each point of a magnetic field; closer lines mean a stronger field.

worked_examples.statement: **Four pole combinations.** State whether each pair of poles, held facing each other, attracts or repels: (a) N facing N, (b) S facing S, (c) N facing S, (d) S facing N.
reasoning: Compare the two facing poles in each pair: if they are the same letter, the rule is repel; if they are different letters, the rule is attract.
worked_examples.solution: (a) N-N: repel. (b) S-S: repel. (c) N-S: attract. (d) S-N: attract.
worked_examples.interpretation: Every outcome follows from one rule (like repels, unlike attracts) applied to whichever two poles actually face each other — there is no separate rule to memorise for each case.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming any two magnets must attract, without checking which poles are actually facing each other.

worked_examples.statement: **Sorting materials and magnets.** A box contains a copper pipe, a steel paperclip, a soft-iron nail that is magnetic only while inside a magnet's field, and a battery-powered coil wound on a soft-iron core whose strength changes with the current through it. Classify each as magnetic or non-magnetic, and name the magnet type for each magnetic item.
knowns: magnetic materials: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt
permanent magnet keeps its magnetism unaided
temporary magnet is magnetic mainly while in a field
electromagnet's strength is controlled by a current
reasoning: Copper is not one of the magnetic materials, so the pipe is non-magnetic.
Steel keeps magnetism on its own, matching a permanent magnet once magnetised.
Soft iron that is magnetic mainly while inside a field matches a temporary magnet.
A current-controlled coil on a soft-iron core, with strength set by the current, matches an electromagnet.
worked_examples.solution: Copper pipe: non-magnetic. Steel paperclip: magnetic, permanent-magnet behaviour once magnetised. Soft-iron nail: magnetic, temporary-magnet behaviour. Coil on soft-iron core: magnetic, electromagnet.
worked_examples.interpretation: Each classification follows from a distinct, checkable property (does it respond to a magnet at all; does it keep its magnetism unaided; can its strength be switched by a current), not from guessing by appearance.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calling the copper pipe magnetic simply because it is a metal.

worked_examples.statement: **Field direction from the test-pole rule.** A small test north pole is placed directly to the right of a bar magnet's north pole (outside the magnet). State the direction of the force on it, and hence the direction of the field line at that point.
knowns: the point is outside the magnet, next to its north pole
field direction = direction of the force on a test north pole placed there
unknowns: direction of the force on the test pole
direction of the field line at that point
reasoning: The test pole is itself a north pole, and it is next to the magnet's north pole, so like poles are facing each other.
Like poles repel, so the force on the test pole points away from the magnet's north pole, i.e. further to the right.
The field line at that point follows the force direction, so it also points away from the north pole.
worked_examples.solution: The force on the test pole points away from the magnet, to the right; the field line at that point points in the same direction.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is exactly why every field-line diagram shows lines leaving a north pole: at any point just outside it, a test north pole is always repelled straight away from it.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating the field line as pointing toward the magnet, as if field lines always point 'into' the object that created them.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining an induced-magnetism observation.** An unmagnetised steel pin is brought close to the south pole of a bar magnet, without touching it, and is pulled toward the magnet. (a) Explain, in terms of induced magnetism, why the pin is attracted even though it was not magnetised beforehand. (b) State what you would expect to observe if the pin were instead brought close to the magnet's north pole.
knowns: the pin is steel (a magnetic material) and starts unmagnetised
the pin is brought near, not touching, the magnet's south pole
unknowns: the outcome near the north pole
reasoning: Steel is a magnetic material, so it can be magnetised by the field it sits in, even without being touched.
Induced magnetism always makes the face nearer the external pole become the opposite pole, so the pin's nearer face becomes a north pole facing the magnet's south pole.
Unlike poles attract, so the induced pin is pulled toward the magnet.
The same induction rule applies regardless of which pole of the magnet the pin approaches, since the induced face always becomes whichever pole is attracted to that external pole.
worked_examples.solution: (a) The field around the magnet's south pole induces magnetism in the steel pin, making the pin's nearer face a north pole; since a north pole and the magnet's south pole are unlike poles, they attract. (b) Bringing the pin near the north pole instead would again induce the pin's nearer face to become the opposite pole (south), so the pin would still be attracted.
worked_examples.interpretation: Induced magnetism is the reason an unmagnetised magnetic object is always attracted to either pole of a magnet, never repelled, which is a useful way to tell 'not yet magnetised' from 'already magnetised the wrong way round'.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Expecting the pin to be repelled from one of the two poles, as if it already had a fixed polarity of its own before being brought close.

guided_exercises.statement: You are given four unlabelled samples: an aluminium can, an iron nail, a steel screw and a wooden peg. Which of these would be attracted to a magnet, and which would not?
hints: List which of the four materials (aluminium, iron, steel, wood) are among the magnetic materials.
A sample is attracted to a magnet only if it is made from a magnetic material.
guided_exercises.answer: The iron nail and the steel screw would be attracted; the aluminium can and the wooden peg would not, since aluminium and wood are not magnetic materials.
common_errors: Assuming the aluminium can is attracted because it is a metal, rather than checking it against the specific list of magnetic materials.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** List which of the four materials (aluminium, iron, steel, wood) are among the magnetic materials.

**Step 2 — Method:** A sample is attracted to a magnet only if it is made from a magnetic material.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The iron nail and the steel screw would be attracted; the aluminium can and the wooden peg would not, since aluminium and wood are not magnetic materials.

guided_exercises.statement: A test north pole is placed directly to the left of a bar magnet's south pole (outside the magnet). State the direction of the force on the test pole and the direction of the field line at that point.
hints: Decide whether the test pole (a north pole) and the magnet's south pole are like or unlike poles.
Apply the like-repels, unlike-attracts rule to find the direction of the force.
The field line at that point points the same way as the force on the test pole.
guided_exercises.answer: The test pole (north) and the magnet's south pole are unlike poles, so they attract: the force on the test pole points toward the magnet, to the right. The field line at that point points in the same direction, into the south pole.
common_errors: Concluding the force points away from the magnet, by confusing the rule for a south pole with the rule already learned for a north pole.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Decide whether the test pole (a north pole) and the magnet's south pole are like or unlike poles.

**Step 2 — Method:** Apply the like-repels, unlike-attracts rule to find the direction of the force.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The test pole (north) and the magnet's south pole are unlike poles, so they attract: the force on the test pole points toward the magnet, to the right. The field line at that point points in the same direction, into the south pole.

**Step 4 — Check:** The field line at that point points the same way as the force on the test pole.

exercises.statement: State whether each pair of poles attracts or repels: (a) S facing N, (b) N facing N, (c) S facing S.
exercises.answer: (a) attract. (b) repel. (c) repel.
exercises.full_solution: Unlike poles (S facing N) attract; like poles (N-N or S-S) repel.

exercises.statement: A student has a bar magnet and four unlabelled rods: copper, nickel, steel and plastic. Using only the magnet, describe a simple test that would sort these into magnetic and non-magnetic groups, and state the expected result for each rod.
exercises.answer: Hold the magnet near each rod in turn: a rod that is pulled toward the magnet is magnetic; a rod with no effect at all is non-magnetic. Expected result: copper — no effect (non-magnetic); nickel — attracted (magnetic); steel — attracted (magnetic); plastic — no effect (non-magnetic).
exercises.full_solution: Copper and plastic are not among the magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt), so neither is attracted; nickel and steel are both magnetic materials, so both are attracted.

exercises.statement: A bar magnet stands vertically with its north pole at the top. A test north pole is placed directly above the north pole (outside the magnet, not touching it). State the direction of the force on the test pole.
exercises.answer: Directly upward, away from the magnet's north pole.
exercises.full_solution: The test pole is itself a north pole, so it faces like poles with the magnet's north pole; like poles repel, pushing the test pole directly away, which here is straight up.

exercises.statement: A crane in a scrapyard uses a large electromagnet to lift scrap steel from a pile and then drop it precisely into a separate container. Explain why an electromagnet, rather than a permanent magnet, is the better choice for this job.
exercises.answer: An electromagnet's magnetism can be switched off by switching off the current, releasing the scrap steel exactly over the container; a permanent magnet stays magnetic all the time and cannot be switched off to release its load on command.
exercises.full_solution: The job needs magnetism that can be turned on to pick the load up and turned off to let it go at a chosen moment; only an electromagnet's current-controlled strength allows that, which is the same property (current-controlled magnetism) introduced for electromagnets in this lesson.

exam_questions.statement: (a) State the rule that predicts whether two magnetic poles attract or repel. (b) A bar magnet is held with its north pole pointing toward the south pole of a second bar magnet. State and explain what happens. (c) The second bar magnet is now turned around so that its north pole faces the first magnet's north pole instead. State what happens now.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. (b) The two magnets attract each other, because a north pole is facing a south pole, which are unlike poles. (c) The two magnets now repel each other, because two north poles are facing each other, which are like poles.
exam_questions.full_solution: Each part applies the same single rule to a different pair of facing poles: N facing S gives attraction; N facing N gives repulsion.
mark_scheme: States the rule: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
States that the magnets in (b) attract.
Explains (b) by identifying the facing poles as unlike (N and S).
States that the magnets in (c) repel, because N now faces N.
common_errors: Giving the correct outcome in (b) or (c) without naming which two poles are actually facing each other, which loses the explanation mark.

exam_questions.statement: An unmagnetised steel washer is held near, but not touching, the north pole of a strong bar magnet. (a) State what is observed. (b) Explain this observation in terms of induced magnetism. (c) State one feature that would be different if the washer were made of copper instead of steel.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The washer is attracted toward the magnet. (b) The magnet's field induces magnetism in the washer, making the washer's nearer face a south pole; a south pole facing the magnet's north pole are unlike poles, so they attract. (c) A copper washer would show no attraction at all, because copper is not a magnetic material and cannot be magnetised by the field.
exam_questions.full_solution: Parts (a) and (b) use the induced-magnetism idea: a magnetic material can be magnetised by a field without contact, and the induced pole is always the one that gets attracted to the inducing pole. Part (c) checks that this entire effect depends on the washer being made of a magnetic material in the first place.
mark_scheme: States that the steel washer is attracted to the magnet.
States that the magnet's field induces magnetism in the washer.
Identifies the washer's induced nearer face as a south pole (opposite to the magnet's north pole).
Explains the attraction using the unlike-poles-attract rule on the induced pole.
States that a copper washer would show no attraction, because copper is non-magnetic.
common_errors: Describing the washer as already having a fixed pole of its own before it was brought near the magnet, instead of explaining that the pole is induced by the field.

mcq.stem: A bar magnet's south pole is held facing the south pole of a second bar magnet. What happens?

options.text: They repel, because like poles repel.
They attract, because opposite ends of two different magnets always pull together.
options.why_wrong: treats attraction as a general property of 'two magnets' rather than depending on which poles actually face each other.

options.text: Nothing happens, because both poles are the same type.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes matching poles produce no force at all, rather than a repulsive one.

options.text: They attract, because south poles are weaker than north poles.
options.why_wrong: invents a size difference between pole types that has nothing to do with the like/unlike rule.

mcq.explanation: S facing S is a like-pole pairing, and like poles repel.

mcq.stem: Which pair of materials are both magnetic (both would be attracted to a strong magnet)?

options.text: Copper and aluminium
options.why_wrong: neither copper nor aluminium is a magnetic material; both would show no attraction.

options.text: Steel and nickel
Gold and plastic
options.why_wrong: neither gold nor plastic is magnetic.

options.text: Aluminium and steel
options.why_wrong: aluminium is not magnetic, even though steel is; the pair is not both magnetic.

mcq.explanation: Steel and nickel are both among the small group of magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt).

mcq.stem: What does a magnetic field line actually represent at a chosen point?

options.text: The path a magnet would travel if released at that point.
options.why_wrong: confuses the field line with a trajectory; nothing travels along it.

options.text: The speed at which magnetism moves outward from the magnet.
options.why_wrong: invents a 'speed of magnetism' that field lines do not represent.

options.text: The direction of the force on a free north pole placed at that point.
The boundary of the region where the magnet has any effect at all.
options.why_wrong: treats a single field line as a boundary rather than one of many direction indicators throughout the field.

mcq.explanation: A field line shows the direction of the force a test north pole would feel at that point; its spacing separately shows field strength.

mcq.stem: Which property distinguishes an electromagnet from both a permanent magnet and a temporary magnet?

options.text: It is the only one of the three that is attracted to steel.
options.why_wrong: wrongly suggests permanent and temporary magnets do not attract steel; both do.

options.text: It is the only one of the three made from a magnetic material.
options.why_wrong: all three rely on a magnetic material (such as steel or soft iron); that is not the distinguishing feature.

options.text: It cannot attract or repel anything unless it is first magnetised by another magnet.
options.why_wrong: describes induced magnetism, not what makes an electromagnet distinct from a permanent or temporary magnet.

options.text: Its strength can be switched on, off, or varied by changing a current.

mcq.explanation: An electromagnet's defining feature is that its magnetic strength is controlled directly by the current through its coil, unlike a permanent or temporary magnet.

flashcards.front: What is the rule for whether two magnetic poles attract or repel?
flashcards.back: Like poles (N-N or S-S) repel; unlike poles (N-S) attract.

flashcards.front: What is the direction of a magnetic field at a point?
flashcards.back: The direction of the force that a free north pole would feel if placed at that point.

flashcards.front: How do a permanent magnet, a temporary magnet and an electromagnet differ?
flashcards.back: A permanent magnet (e.g. steel) keeps its magnetism unaided; a temporary magnet (e.g. soft iron) is magnetic mainly while inside another field; an electromagnet's strength is switched on, off or varied by a current.

flashcards.front: If an unmagnetised steel pin is attracted to a magnet's south pole, does that mean the pin was already magnetised beforehand?
flashcards.back: No — the magnet's field induces magnetism in the pin without any contact, making the pin's nearer face a north pole that is then attracted to the magnet's south pole.

flashcards.front: Why is an electromagnet, not a permanent magnet, used in a scrapyard crane that lifts and then releases steel?
flashcards.back: Its magnetism can be switched off by switching off the current, releasing the load on command, which a permanent magnet cannot do.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A north pole attracts any other north pole, the same way two different magnets always pull toward each other.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners often expect magnets to behave like a single general 'stickiness' that pulls other magnets in, rather than following a rule that depends on which poles face each other.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts attraction when shown two labelled north poles facing each other, or repulsion when shown a north pole facing a south pole.
misconceptions.correct_model: Like poles (north-north or south-south) repel; unlike poles (north-south) attract. The outcome depends on which two poles are facing each other, not on magnets being generally attractive.
misconceptions.remediation: Work through all four pole-facing combinations (N-N, S-S, N-S, S-N) explicitly and name the outcome of each one before moving on.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any metal is magnetic and will be attracted to a magnet.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Iron and steel objects are common and visibly stick to magnets, so it is easy to generalise 'metal' to mean 'magnetic' without separating magnetic metals from non-magnetic ones.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that a copper, aluminium or gold object will be attracted to a magnet.
misconceptions.correct_model: Only a small group of materials, including iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, are magnetic. Most metals, such as copper, aluminium and gold, are not attracted to a magnet at all.
misconceptions.remediation: Sort a short list of named materials into 'magnetic' and 'non-magnetic' before answering any interaction question, instead of assuming from the word 'metal'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Magnetic field lines are the paths that moving particles follow through the field.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Field-line diagrams look similar to trajectory diagrams used elsewhere in physics, so it is tempting to read them the same way.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a field line as 'the route a particle would travel' rather than as the direction of the force at each point.
misconceptions.correct_model: A field line shows the direction of the force a free north pole would feel if placed at that point; its spacing shows how strong the field is there (closer lines mean a stronger field). It is not a path that anything travels along.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what force (not velocity) a test north pole would feel at a chosen point on the diagram, and show that the field line at that point is simply that force's direction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming two magnets always attract, without checking which poles are facing each other.
common_mistakes.why: Everyday experience of magnets 'sticking' makes attraction feel like the default outcome.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always name the two facing poles first, then apply like-repels, unlike-attracts.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating every metal as magnetic.
common_mistakes.why: Iron and steel are common, visibly magnetic metals, so 'metal' and 'magnetic' get blurred together.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the material against the short list of magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) rather than its appearance.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a field-line diagram as a travel path.
common_mistakes.why: Field-line diagrams resemble route maps used elsewhere in physics.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask what force a test north pole would feel at a specific point, and treat the field line there as just that force's direction.

exam_notes: When asked why two magnets attract or repel, always name the two facing poles explicitly before stating the outcome.

Distinguish 'magnetic material' (can be magnetised or attracted) from 'magnet' (already magnetised): an unmagnetised magnetic object is always attracted to either pole of a magnet, never repelled, because of induced magnetism.
When describing a field-line diagram, state that lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole, and that closer lines mean a stronger field — do not describe lines as paths of travel.

summary.big_idea: A magnetic field maps the force a pole would feel at every point around a magnet, letting you predict attraction, repulsion and field direction without testing each position directly.
key_points: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
Only a small group of materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) are magnetic; most materials are not.
Permanent, temporary and electromagnets differ in how their magnetism is kept or controlled.
Field direction at a point is the direction of the force on a free north pole placed there; field lines leave N and enter S.
A magnetic material can be magnetised by a nearby field alone (induced magnetism), always becoming attracted, never repelled, to the inducing pole.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract — and a field line is just the direction of the force a test north pole would feel at that point, leaving N and entering S.

02_Charge_and_electric_fields.json.title: Charge and electric fields
02_Charge_and_electric_fields.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Predict whether two charged objects attract or repel, describe frictional charging as a transfer of electrons between solids, and classify materials as conductors or insulators.
State that charge is measured in coulombs, and define the direction of an electric field at a point as the direction of the force on a positive test charge placed there.

prerequisites.statement: A magnetic field is a region where a pole experiences a force, and its direction is defined by the force on a test pole placed in it.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The electric field in this lesson is defined the same way, except the test object is a positive charge instead of a north pole; recognising the pattern makes the new definition much easier to accept.

prerequisites.statement: Matter is made of atoms, and an atom has a central nucleus (containing protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Frictional charging only makes sense once you know which particle (the electron) is free to move between touching surfaces, while the nucleus and its protons stay put.

diagnostic_items.question: Think about a single atom of any element. Name the particles that are found inside its central nucleus, and name the particle that is found outside the nucleus.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Electrons are found outside the nucleus, surrounding it.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The nucleus contains protons and electrons, and the neutrons are outside it.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has swapped two of the three particles, so the one particle that can actually be rubbed off a surface, the outer electron, is in the wrong place in their picture of the atom.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Everything is inside the nucleus; the atom is just one solid lump.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has no internal structure to move anything between, so frictional charging will have to be taken on trust rather than explained.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Frictional charging in this lesson is explained as electrons being transferred while protons stay put, so the learner must already place electrons on the outside and protons locked in the nucleus.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch and label a simple atom, nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around the outside, and say which of the three is the easiest to pull away, before starting the lesson.

theory_blocks.title: Rub, then watch it pull or push
theory_blocks.body:
Rub a balloon on a jumper and hold it near your hair: strands of hair are pulled toward it. Rub two balloons the same way and bring them close together: they push apart. Something about rubbing leaves an object able to exert a force on other objects without touching them, and that something behaves in two opposite ways, since one pair of rubbed objects attracts while another pair repels.

That 'something' is **electric charge**. Just as with magnetic poles, there are two kinds, conventionally called positive and negative, and the pattern is the same shape of rule: [[blue:**like charges repel, unlike charges attract**]]. The rest of this lesson explains where the charge comes from, what carries it, and how to map the force it produces at a distance.

theory_blocks.title: Frictional charging: electrons move, charge is conserved
theory_blocks.body:
An atom has a nucleus, containing positively charged protons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons. The protons are locked inside the nucleus; the outer electrons are far more loosely held and can be transferred to another surface by rubbing. When two different insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons move from one surface to the other — never protons.

Whichever material **gains** electrons ends up with more negative charge than positive charge overall, so it becomes **negatively charged**. The material that **loses** those electrons is left with more positive charge than negative, so it becomes **positively charged**, by exactly the same amount. Because the electrons simply move from one object to the other, rather than being created or destroyed, the two charges produced are always equal in size and opposite in sign: the total charge of the pair, taken together, stays at zero, exactly as it was before rubbing. This is the **conservation of charge**.

assets.caption: While a cloth and a rod are rubbed together, electrons move from the cloth to the rod. After separating, the rod has gained a negative charge and the cloth is left with an equal, opposite positive charge; the two always sum to zero.
assets.purpose: Make the electron-transfer mechanism and the resulting conservation of charge visible side by side, as a single cause-and-effect picture.

theory_blocks.title: Conductors and insulators
theory_blocks.body: Whether a material can be charged by rubbing, and whether that charge stays put or spreads away, depends on how freely charge can move through it. In a **conductor** (metals such as copper and aluminium, and also graphite), charge can move easily through the material; rubbing a conductor you are holding tends not to leave it charged, because any charge produced flows away through your body to the ground almost as fast as it is produced. In an **insulator** (such as polythene, acetate, rubber, glass or dry cloth), charge cannot move freely through the material, so charge produced at the rubbed surface stays exactly where it was put, which is why frictional charging experiments use insulators, not bare metal conductors.

theory_blocks.title: Why an uncharged object can still be attracted
theory_blocks.body: A charged rod can attract small pieces of uncharged paper, even though the paper starts with zero total charge. Suppose the rod is positive. Its field pulls the paper's electrons very slightly toward the near side, leaving the far side slightly positive — the paper's total charge is still zero, but its charge is no longer evenly spread. (A negative rod pushes the electrons slightly toward the far side instead.) The near side of the paper (opposite in sign to the rod) is then slightly closer to the rod than the far side (same sign as the rod), and since electric force weakens with distance, the attraction to the near side wins overall. The paper is still attracted, not repelled, whichever sign the rod's own charge happens to be.

theory_blocks.title: Is it really charged? Simple tests
theory_blocks.body:
Making a charge is one thing; checking that an object actually carries one is another. There are three simple tests, in order of how much they prove.

**Small pieces of paper, or a thin stream of water.** Hold the object just above some small pieces of tissue paper. Two uncharged objects do not pull on each other, so if the pieces jump up to it, the object must be carrying charge. The same test works with a thin trickle of water from a tap: a charged object held beside the stream bends the stream toward itself. Neither version tells you which sign the charge is.

**A known charge, hanging freely.** Charge a polythene rod by rubbing (it becomes negative) and hang it in a paper stirrup so that it can swing, then bring the object being tested near one end. If the suspended rod [[blue:swings away]], the two must carry like charges: the object is definitely charged, and negative like the rod. If the suspended rod swings toward it instead, you have learnt much less, because a charged rod attracts an uncharged object as well, for the reason given in the block above. That is why [[red:repulsion is the only conclusive test for charge]] — attraction on its own never proves it.

A **gold-leaf electroscope** does the same job more sensitively. Hold a charged object near its metal cap and the thin gold leaf lifts away from the metal stem, because charge inside the metal is pushed so that the stem and the leaf are left with the same sign of charge and repel each other.

assets.caption: Testing an object for charge with a known charged rod hanging in a stirrup. The suspended rod swings away from the rod being tested, so the two carry like charges and the tested rod is definitely charged. A swing toward it would not have proved this, because an uncharged rod is attracted too.
assets.purpose: Show the repulsion test, the only conclusive test for charge, and make clear that it is the suspended known charge that moves.

theory_blocks.title: Defining the direction of an electric field
theory_blocks.body:
Charge is measured in **coulombs (C)**. One coulomb is a very large charge, so the charges produced by rubbing are tiny, usually a few nanocoulombs ($1\,\mathrm{nC} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{C}$), as in the examples in this lesson. An **electric field** is a region in which an electric charge experiences a force. To map the force a charge can exert at a distance, picture a small **positive test charge**: a positive charge so small that it does not disturb the field it is measuring. The **direction of the electric field** at a point is defined as the direction of the force that positive test charge would feel there.

Near a positive charge, a positive test charge is repelled, so the field points *away* from a positive charge, outward in every direction. Near a negative charge, a positive test charge is attracted, so the field points *into* a negative charge. This is exactly the same style of definition used for a magnetic field's direction, with a positive test charge standing in for the test north pole.

assets.caption: Field lines around an isolated positive charge $+Q$ point directly outward in every direction. A positive test charge placed on one of these lines is repelled straight away from $+Q$, matching the field-line direction at that point.
assets.purpose: Make the force-on-a-positive-test-charge definition of electric field direction concrete, directly mirroring the magnetic field definition from the previous lesson.

theory_blocks.title: Field direction is about a positive test charge, not an electron
theory_blocks.body: It is tempting to picture the field as the direction an electron would move, since electrons are the charge carriers you will meet throughout the rest of this unit. Resist that: the convention is fixed to a [[blue:**positive**]] test charge. [[red:An electron, being negative, is pushed the opposite way to the field line at every point]] — toward a positive charge, and away from a negative charge — exactly reversed from how the field itself is drawn.

keywords.definition: A property of matter, positive or negative, that causes a force between charged objects; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
Charging an insulator by rubbing it against another insulator, which transfers electrons between the two surfaces.
The principle that charge is never created or destroyed, only moved; the total charge of an isolated system stays constant.
A material through which electric charge can move freely.
A material through which electric charge cannot move freely, so charge stays where it is produced.
The SI unit of electric charge.
The region around a charged object in which another charge experiences a force; its direction at a point is the direction of the force on a positive test charge there.

worked_examples.statement: **What actually moves?** A polythene rod becomes negatively charged after being rubbed with a dry cloth. State which particle moved, and in which direction, to produce this charge.
knowns: the rod ends up negatively charged
only electrons, not protons, transfer between rubbed solids
unknowns: which particle moved and which way
reasoning: A negatively charged object has more electrons than protons overall, so it must have gained electrons.
Electrons can transfer between touching solids by rubbing; protons cannot, since they are locked inside each atom's nucleus.
worked_examples.solution: Electrons moved from the cloth onto the rod.
worked_examples.interpretation: The rod did not 'create' negative charge: it simply ended up with extra electrons that used to belong to the cloth.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying that protons moved onto the rod to make it negative, instead of identifying that electrons (not protons) are the particles that transfer.

worked_examples.statement: **Using conservation of charge.** After rubbing an acetate rod with a duster, the rod is found to carry a charge of $+5.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. State the charge on the duster, explaining your reasoning.
knowns: the pair started with zero total charge
charge is conserved: the two charges produced are equal in size and opposite in sign
reasoning: Before rubbing, the total charge of the rod and duster together was zero.
Conservation of charge means the total stays zero after rubbing too, so the duster's charge must be the exact negative of the rod's.
worked_examples.solution: $-5.0\,\mathrm{nC}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $(+5.0\,\mathrm{nC}) + (-5.0\,\mathrm{nC}) = 0$, matching the zero total charge the pair started with.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Guessing the duster's charge independently (e.g. assuming it must also be positive), instead of using conservation of charge to calculate it directly from the rod's charge.

worked_examples.statement: **Field direction near a negative charge.** A positive test charge is placed directly above an isolated negative charge $-Q$. State the direction of the force on the test charge, and hence the field direction at that point.
knowns: the charge producing the field is negative
field direction = direction of the force on a positive test charge placed there
unknowns: direction of the force on the test charge
reasoning: The test charge is positive and the source charge is negative, so unlike charges are involved.
Unlike charges attract, so the force on the test charge points toward $-Q$, i.e. straight down.
The field direction at that point is the same as the force direction on the test charge, so it also points straight down, into $-Q$.
worked_examples.solution: The force on the test charge points downward, toward $-Q$; the field line at that point points in the same direction, into the negative charge.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is exactly why field lines are always drawn pointing into a negative charge: a positive test charge placed anywhere near it is always attracted straight toward it.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Drawing the field pointing away from the negative charge, by applying the 'outward from a charge' pattern learned for a positive charge without checking the sign first.

worked_examples.statement: **A full charging-and-field explanation.** Two strips made from different insulating materials, A and B, are rubbed together. Strip A ends up with a charge of $-8.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. (a) State the charge on strip B, explaining your reasoning. (b) The two strips are then held apart, not touching. State whether they attract or repel, and why. (c) A positive test charge is placed at the midpoint between them. Explain why the forces from A and B on the test charge do not simply cancel to zero, even though the two strips carry equal and opposite charge.
knowns: charge is conserved between the two strips
unknowns: attraction or repulsion between A and B
why the field at the midpoint is not zero
reasoning: Conservation of charge gives strip B a charge equal in size and opposite in sign to strip A.
A is negative and B is positive, so the two strips carry unlike charges.
Unlike charges attract, giving the answer to (b).

At the midpoint, the force from A (pulling the positive test charge toward A) and the force from B (pushing the test charge away from B) both point the same way, toward A, so they add rather than cancel.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $+8.0\,\mathrm{nC}$, since $(-8.0\,\mathrm{nC}) + (+8.0\,\mathrm{nC}) = 0$ matches conservation of charge. (b) They attract, because A is negative and B is positive, and unlike charges attract. (c) The test charge is repelled by positive B (pushed toward A) and attracted by negative A (pulled toward A); both forces act in the same direction, so they add together instead of cancelling, and the field at the midpoint is not zero.
worked_examples.interpretation: Equal and opposite charges only cancel each other's *field* at points where the two individual forces point in opposite directions; at the midpoint between unlike charges, they point the same way instead.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming that because the two charges are equal and opposite, their effects everywhere must cancel to zero, without actually working out the direction of each individual force at the chosen point.

guided_exercises.statement: A polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth and found to carry a charge of $-2.4\,\mathrm{nC}$. State the charge on the cloth.
hints: The rod and cloth together started with zero total charge.
Conservation of charge means the total is still zero after rubbing.
The cloth's charge must be the exact negative of the rod's charge.
guided_exercises.answer: $+2.4\,\mathrm{nC}$, since $(-2.4\,\mathrm{nC})+(+2.4\,\mathrm{nC})=0$.
common_errors: Stating the cloth's charge as also $-2.4\,\mathrm{nC}$, by assuming both objects end up the same sign.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** The rod and cloth together started with zero total charge.

**Step 2 — Method:** Conservation of charge means the total is still zero after rubbing.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $+2.4\,\mathrm{nC}$, since $(-2.4\,\mathrm{nC})+(+2.4\,\mathrm{nC})=0$.

**Step 4 — Check:** The cloth's charge must be the exact negative of the rod's charge.

guided_exercises.statement: A positive test charge is placed directly to the left of an isolated positive charge $+Q$. State the direction of the force on the test charge and the field direction at that point.
hints: Decide whether the test charge and $+Q$ are like or unlike charges.
Apply like-repels, unlike-attracts to find the force direction.
The field direction matches the force direction on the test charge.
guided_exercises.answer: Both charges are positive, so they repel: the force on the test charge points away from $+Q$, to the left. The field direction at that point is the same, pointing left, away from $+Q$.
common_errors: Concluding the force points toward $+Q$, by confusing this case with the attraction case near a negative charge.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Decide whether the test charge and $+Q$ are like or unlike charges.

**Step 2 — Method:** Apply like-repels, unlike-attracts to find the force direction.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Both charges are positive, so they repel: the force on the test charge points away from $+Q$, to the left. The field direction at that point is the same, pointing left, away from $+Q$.

**Step 4 — Check:** The field direction matches the force direction on the test charge.

exercises.statement: State whether each pair of charges attracts or repels: (a) positive and positive, (b) negative and negative, (c) positive and negative.
exercises.answer: (a) repel. (b) repel. (c) attract.
exercises.full_solution: Like charges (both positive, or both negative) repel; unlike charges (one positive, one negative) attract.

exercises.statement: A student holds a polythene rod in one hand and rubs it with a dry cloth: the rod becomes charged. The student then holds a metal rod in the same way and rubs it with the same cloth: the metal rod does not stay charged. Explain this difference in terms of conductors and insulators.
exercises.answer: Polythene is an insulator, so the charge produced on its rubbed surface cannot move through the rod and stays where it was produced. Metal is a conductor, and the student's hand and body also conduct, so any charge produced on the metal rod flows through the rod and the student to the ground as fast as it is produced, and no charge builds up.
exercises.full_solution: Electrons are transferred by rubbing in both cases; what differs is whether the charge can then move away. In the insulator it cannot, so it stays; in the hand-held metal rod there is a conducting path through the rod, hand and body to earth, so it leaks away. (A metal rod held by an insulating handle could be charged, because that path to earth would be broken.)

exercises.statement: A positive test charge is placed directly below an isolated positive charge $+Q$. State the direction of the force on the test charge.
exercises.answer: Directly downward, away from $+Q$.
exercises.full_solution: The test charge and $+Q$ are both positive (like charges), so they repel, pushing the test charge directly away from $+Q$, which here is straight down.

exercises.statement: A photocopier works by using light to remove charge from parts of a charged drum, leaving a charge pattern that matches the page being copied; charged toner powder is then attracted only to the still-charged parts of the drum. Explain, using the ideas from this lesson, why toner powder sticks only to the charged regions and not to the regions where the charge has been removed.
exercises.answer: The toner particles are charged, and the still-charged regions of the drum carry the opposite charge to the toner, so unlike charges attract the toner onto exactly those regions. The regions where charge has been removed by light are left with little or no charge, so there is little or no electric force to attract toner there.
exercises.full_solution: This is the same attract/repel rule used throughout the lesson, applied to a real device: toner sticks only where there is enough opposite charge on the drum to produce an attractive force, which is precisely the pattern of the original page.

exercises.statement: A charged rod is brought near a small ball hanging on a thread, and the ball swings toward the rod. A student concludes that the ball must be carrying the opposite charge to the rod. Explain why that conclusion is not safe, and state what the ball would have to do instead for the student to be certain the ball is charged.
exercises.answer: Attraction does not prove the ball is charged at all: a charged rod also attracts an uncharged ball, because its field separates the charge inside the ball and the nearer, opposite side is pulled more strongly than the far side is pushed. The student can only be certain if the ball is repelled, because repulsion happens only between two objects that are both charged, with charges of the same sign.
exercises.full_solution: There are two possible explanations for the attraction: the ball carries the opposite charge, or the ball carries no charge at all. One observation cannot separate them, so the conclusion does not follow. Repulsion has only one explanation, so it is the conclusive test.

exam_questions.statement: A plastic comb is rubbed through dry hair. (a) State which particle transfers between the comb and the hair during this process. (b) The comb is found afterwards to be negatively charged. State what this tells you about the number of electrons gained or lost by the comb. (c) State the charge on the hair compared with the charge on the comb.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Electrons. (b) The comb has gained electrons (more electrons than protons overall, since it is negatively charged). (c) The hair carries a charge equal in size to the comb's but opposite in sign (positive), since charge is conserved between the two.
exam_questions.full_solution: Each part follows from the same electron-transfer-and-conservation model: only electrons move, the comb's sign tells you whether it gained or lost them, and the hair's charge is fixed by conservation once the comb's charge is known.
mark_scheme: States that electrons are the particles that transfer.
States that the comb has gained electrons.
States that the hair's charge is equal in size to the comb's.
States that the hair's charge is opposite in sign (positive) to the comb's.
common_errors: Stating that protons transferred, or that the comb 'lost' electrons despite being told it is negatively charged.

exam_questions.statement: A small isolated charge $-Q$ sits on a bench. (a) State the direction of the electric field at a point directly to the right of $-Q$. (b) A positive test charge placed at that point is released from rest. State the direction it initially accelerates. (c) State what would be different about your answers to (a) and (b) if the charge were $+Q$ instead of $-Q$.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The field points to the left, directly into $-Q$. (b) The test charge accelerates to the left, toward $-Q$, because unlike charges attract and the field direction matches the force direction on a positive test charge. (c) With $+Q$ instead, both the field and the force on the test charge would point to the right, directly away from the charge, since the test charge and $+Q$ would then be like charges that repel.
exam_questions.full_solution: Parts (a) and (b) give the same direction because the field direction is defined to be the direction of the force on a positive test charge; part (c) checks that reversing the source charge's sign reverses both answers together.
mark_scheme: States that the field at the point points left, into $-Q$.
States that the test charge accelerates left, toward $-Q$.
Links this to unlike charges attracting.
States that with $+Q$ the field would point right, away from the charge.
States that the test charge would then accelerate right, matching like charges repelling.
common_errors: Giving opposite directions for (a) and (b), by forgetting that the field direction is defined to be exactly the force direction on a positive test charge, not something separate from it.

exam_questions.statement: A student has a plastic rod and wants to find out whether it is charged. A polythene rod that is known to be negatively charged hangs freely in a paper stirrup nearby. (a) Describe a test the student could carry out using small pieces of tissue paper, and state the result that would show the plastic rod is charged. (b) The student instead holds the plastic rod near one end of the suspended rod, and the suspended rod swings away. State what this tells the student about the plastic rod, and explain why repulsion gives a more certain answer than attraction would.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Hold the plastic rod just above some small pieces of tissue paper; if the pieces are attracted up to the rod, the rod is charged. (b) The plastic rod is charged, and its charge is negative, the same sign as the suspended rod, because the suspended rod is repelled. Repulsion is more certain because only two charged objects with the same sign of charge repel, whereas a charged rod attracts an uncharged object as well, so an attraction would not have shown that the plastic rod carried any charge.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Hold the plastic rod just above some small pieces of tissue paper; if the pieces are attracted up to the rod, the rod is charged. (b) The plastic rod is charged, and its charge is negative, the same sign as the suspended rod, because the suspended rod is repelled. Repulsion is more certain because only two charged objects with the same sign of charge repel, whereas a charged rod attracts an uncharged object as well, so an attraction would not have shown that the plastic rod carried any charge.
mark_scheme: Describes holding the rod close to (just above) small pieces of tissue paper.
States that the pieces being attracted to the rod shows the rod is charged.
States that the plastic rod is charged and carries a negative charge, the same sign as the suspended rod.
Explains that an attraction would also occur if the rod were uncharged, so only repulsion proves the rod is charged.
common_errors: Claiming that attraction of the suspended rod would equally prove the plastic rod is charged, forgetting that a charged rod attracts uncharged objects too.
Giving the sign as positive, by treating repulsion as the unlike-charges case.

mcq.stem: A plastic rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes positively charged. What has happened?

options.text: The rod lost electrons to the cloth.
The rod gained protons from the cloth.
options.why_wrong: protons are locked inside atomic nuclei and do not transfer between rubbed solids.

options.text: The rod gained electrons from the cloth.
options.why_wrong: gaining electrons would make the rod negative, not positive.

options.text: New positive charge was created on the rod's surface.
options.why_wrong: charge is conserved, not created; the rod's positive charge comes from losing electrons, not from new charge appearing.

mcq.explanation: Only electrons transfer between rubbed solids; a rod that ends up positive must have lost electrons to the cloth.

mcq.stem: After rubbing, a duster carries a charge of $+4.0\,\mathrm{nC}$. What is the charge on the rod it was rubbed with?

options.text: $+4.0\,\mathrm{nC}$
options.why_wrong: gives the duster's own charge again, rather than the rod's, and ignores that the two must be opposite in sign.

options.text: $-4.0\,\mathrm{nC}$
$0\,\mathrm{nC}$
options.why_wrong: would only be correct if the rod had somehow kept all its electrons, but rubbing has definitely transferred charge.

options.text: Cannot be determined from the information given.
options.why_wrong: conservation of charge is exactly enough information: the rod's charge must be the negative of the duster's.

mcq.explanation: Conservation of charge: the pair started neutral, so the rod's charge must be equal in size and opposite in sign to the duster's, $(+4.0)+(-4.0)=0$.

mcq.stem: What is the direction of the electric field at a point directly above an isolated positive charge?

options.text: Downward, into the charge.
options.why_wrong: would be correct for a negative charge, not a positive one; a positive test charge is repelled, not attracted.

options.text: Horizontal, at right angles to the line joining the point to the charge.
options.why_wrong: invents a direction unrelated to the force a test charge would actually feel, which must point directly along that line.

options.text: Upward, away from the charge.
There is no field directly above a positive charge.
options.why_wrong: a positive charge produces a field at every point around it, including directly above.

mcq.explanation: A positive test charge placed above a positive source charge is repelled upward, away from it, so the field points upward at that point.

mcq.stem: Which material would be the best choice for an insulating stand, used so that a charged sphere does not lose its charge to the bench?

options.text: A bare copper rod.
options.why_wrong: copper is a conductor and would let charge flow away from the sphere.

options.text: An aluminium rod.
options.why_wrong: aluminium is also a conductor, for the same reason copper is unsuitable.

options.text: A steel rod.
options.why_wrong: steel is a conductor as well, so it would also let the charge leak away.

options.text: A polythene rod.

mcq.explanation: Polythene is an insulator: charge cannot move freely through it, so it does not provide a path for the sphere's charge to drain away.

flashcards.front: What is the rule for whether two charges attract or repel?
flashcards.back: Like charges (both positive or both negative) repel; unlike charges (one positive, one negative) attract.

flashcards.front: What actually transfers between two solids when one becomes charged by rubbing?
flashcards.back: Electrons. Protons stay fixed inside each atom's nucleus; only the more loosely held outer electrons can move between surfaces.

flashcards.front: How do a conductor and an insulator differ in how they handle charge?
flashcards.back: In a conductor, charge can move freely through the material; in an insulator, charge cannot move freely and stays wherever it was produced.

flashcards.front: Does rubbing two solids together create new electric charge?
flashcards.back: No — electrons already present simply move from one solid to the other; the total charge of the pair stays at zero throughout, which is conservation of charge.

flashcards.front: How is the direction of an electric field at a point defined?
flashcards.back: As the direction of the force on a positive test charge placed at that point: field lines point away from a positive charge and into a negative charge.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Rubbing two solids transfers protons from one to the other.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners know that charge transfer explains the charging, and may not yet distinguish which particle is actually free to move in a solid.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a rubbed object becoming positive because it 'gained protons', or negative because it 'lost protons'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Protons are bound inside the nucleus of each atom and do not transfer between solids by rubbing. Only electrons, which orbit the nucleus more loosely, can be rubbed off one surface and onto the other.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which particle is on the outside of an atom, easiest to dislodge, before describing what moves during rubbing.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Rubbing creates new electric charge out of nothing.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both objects start apparently uncharged and end up charged, so it can look as though charge has simply appeared.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner cannot say where the charge 'came from', or claims the total charge increases after rubbing.
misconceptions.correct_model: No charge is created or destroyed. Electrons that were already part of one object move to the other, so one object ends up short of electrons (positive) and the other has extra electrons (negative) — the charges are equal in size and opposite in sign, and the total charge of the two objects together is unchanged.
misconceptions.remediation: After finding the charge on one object, require the charge on the other to be calculated from conservation (equal size, opposite sign), not re-observed separately.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An electric field points in the direction a free electron would move if placed at that point.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Electrons are the charge carriers learners meet first (in circuits, later in this unit), so it is tempting to define field direction around their motion rather than a positive test charge's.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws a field pointing toward a positive charge, matching where an electron would be pulled, instead of away from it.
misconceptions.correct_model: Electric field direction is defined by convention as the direction of the force on a *positive* test charge. Field lines point away from a positive charge and into a negative charge; an electron, being negative, would actually be pushed the opposite way to the field line at any point.
misconceptions.remediation: Always name the test charge as positive first, work out the force on it from the like/unlike charge rule, and only then read off the field direction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying protons move between rubbed solids.
common_mistakes.why: Learners know charge transfers, but have not yet separated 'which particle moves' from 'which object ends up which sign'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that only electrons are free to move between touching solids; protons never transfer by rubbing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the two charges produced by rubbing as independent, instead of using conservation of charge.
common_mistakes.why: It looks as though each object is separately 'becoming charged', so the link between the two charges is easy to miss.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Once one object's charge is known, calculate the other directly as equal in size and opposite in sign, rather than guessing or re-measuring it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading electric field direction as the way an electron would move.
common_mistakes.why: Electrons are the charge carrier met first in circuits later in this unit, so it is tempting to centre the definition on them.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always define field direction using a positive test charge; an electron moves the opposite way to the field line at every point.

exam_notes: When asked for the charge on the 'other' object after frictional charging, use conservation of charge (equal size, opposite sign) rather than describing it independently.
State explicitly that it is electrons, not protons, that transfer during frictional charging — examiners look for this distinction by name.
When describing electric field direction, say 'the direction of the force on a positive test charge', not just 'the direction a charge would move', to avoid ambiguity about sign.

summary.big_idea: Electric charge comes in two kinds that follow a like-repels, unlike-attracts rule; frictional charging only moves electrons between objects, so the charge produced is always conserved, and an electric field maps the force a positive test charge would feel at each point.
key_points: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
Frictional charging transfers electrons, never protons, between insulators; the two resulting charges are equal in size and opposite in sign.
Conductors let charge move freely; insulators do not, so insulators are used for charging experiments.
An uncharged object can still be attracted to a charged one, through induced charge separation, not through gaining a net charge.
Electric field direction at a point is the direction of the force on a positive test charge there: away from a positive charge, into a negative charge.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Only electrons move during frictional charging, the charge produced is always conserved (equal and opposite), and field direction is always defined using a positive test charge.

03_Current_is_charge_flow.json.title: Current is charge flow
03_Current_is_charge_flow.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Relate electric current to the rate at which charge passes a point, connect an ammeter correctly in series, and distinguish direct current (d.c.) from alternating current (a.c.).
Calculate current, charge or time using $I = Q/t$, and distinguish the conventional current direction from the direction of electron drift in a metal.

prerequisites.statement: Charge comes in two kinds, positive and negative, and free electrons in a solid carry negative charge.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Current only makes sense once you already know which charged particles are free to move through a metal, and that they are negatively charged.

prerequisites.statement: A rate is a quantity divided by the time taken, such as speed being distance per unit time.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Current is defined as a rate (charge per unit time), so reading it as anything other than a 'per time' quantity will misapply the formula.

diagnostic_items.question: A copper wire lies on the bench with nothing connected to it. Inside the metal some particles are free to move about while the rest are held in place. Which particles are the free ones, and what sign of charge does each of them carry?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The free particles are electrons, and each electron carries a negative charge. The positive charge in the metal is on the protons inside the fixed nuclei, which cannot move through the wire.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The free particles are protons, and they carry positive charge.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner expects the positive particles to be the ones that move, so the contrast this lesson draws between conventional current and electron flow will look like a contradiction rather than a convention.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The free electrons carry positive charge.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The carrier is right but its sign is not, which will reverse every later statement about which way electrons drift.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This lesson defines current as a flow of charge and then compares the direction of conventional current with the direction electrons actually drift, which only works if the carrier and its sign are already secure.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Go back over the picture of a metal from the previous lesson, fixed positive nuclei with free negative electrons between them, and state out loud which of the two can move through the wire.

diagnostic_items.question: A car travels 240 m in 12 s at a steady speed. Work out its speed, and say what the word 'per' in 'metres per second' tells you about how that number was obtained.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Speed = 240 ÷ 12 = 20 m/s. 'Per second' means the distance has been divided by the time taken, so the number is the distance covered in each one second. Any 'per' quantity is one quantity divided by another.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner reads the pairing of two quantities as a multiplication, so a rate will be built the wrong way round whatever the quantities are.
The learner divides in the wrong order and does not use the unit to check which quantity goes on top.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Current is defined in this lesson as charge per unit time, exactly the same structure as distance per unit time, so a learner who cannot build one rate reliably will misapply the other.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Do two or three short speed calculations, each time reading the unit aloud to decide which quantity is divided by which, before meeting charge per unit time.

theory_blocks.title: Current is a rate, like water flowing past a point
theory_blocks.body:
Picture water flowing steadily through a pipe. You could describe 'how much flow' there is by counting the volume of water passing a fixed point each second. **Electric current** is defined the same way, except what is flowing is charge, not water: [[blue:current is the rate at which charge passes a fixed point in a circuit]].

This picture also answers a question that trips a lot of people up: does the flow rate drop after the water passes through a narrow valve? No — in a single unbranched pipe, exactly the same volume of water passes every point per second, upstream or downstream of the valve, because the water itself is neither created nor destroyed along the way. Current behaves the same way in a simple, unbranched loop: nothing about passing through a component removes charge from the flow. In a metal wire, the charge that flows is carried by electrons.

theory_blocks.title: Where an ammeter goes, and why its reading doesn't drop
theory_blocks.body:
An **ammeter** measures current, in amperes (A). To measure the current actually flowing through a particular wire, the wire must be broken at that point and the ammeter inserted into the gap, so every charge passing that point of the circuit has no choice but to pass through the ammeter too. This is connecting the ammeter **in series**.

Because a simple, unbranched loop carries the same current at every point (nothing is used up along the way), an ammeter gives the same reading wherever it is placed in that loop — before a lamp, after it, or anywhere else on the same unbranched path. A different reading before and after a component would only happen if charge were somehow leaking out of the circuit between those two points, which does not happen in a closed loop.

In practice, an **analogue ammeter** has a needle moving over a marked scale (for example, a scale from 0 to 1 A marked every 0.1 A, read to about the nearest half-division); a **digital ammeter** displays the current directly as a number (for example to the nearest 0.01 A), which is faster to read and avoids needing to judge the needle's position between markings. Both types come with different **ranges** (for example 0–100 mA, 0–1 A or 0–10 A): choose the smallest range that is still larger than the current you expect, so the reading is as precise as possible without going off the scale.

assets.caption: A simple circuit loop with the ammeter connected in series on the lower wire. Conventional current flows from the battery's positive terminal, round the loop, to its negative terminal; electrons in the metal wire drift the opposite way, from negative to positive.
assets.purpose: Show correct series ammeter placement and contrast conventional current direction with electron drift direction in the same circuit.

theory_blocks.title: Direct current and alternating current
theory_blocks.body: A cell or battery drives current in one fixed direction around a circuit at all times: this is **direct current (d.c.)**. A mains electricity supply instead drives current that regularly reverses direction, first one way then the other, over and over: this is **alternating current (a.c.)**. Both are still current in the sense already defined — a rate of charge flow — but d.c. keeps that flow going the same way, while a.c. keeps swapping which way it goes.

theory_blocks.title: Calculating current: $I = Q/t$
theory_blocks.body:
Current is defined formally as $$I = \frac{Q}{t}$$ where $I$ is current in amperes (A), $Q$ is charge in coulombs (C), and $t$ is time in seconds (s). One ampere is defined as a flow rate of one coulomb per second: $1\,\mathrm{A} = 1\,\mathrm{C/s}$.

The same relationship rearranges to find charge, $Q = It$, when current and time are known, or time, $t = Q/I$, when charge and current are known. Whichever quantity is unknown, write down the two you do know first and pick the arrangement that isolates the missing one, rather than trying to memorise three separate formulas.

theory_blocks.title: Conventional current versus electron drift
theory_blocks.body:
[[blue:**Conventional current**]] is defined as flowing from the positive terminal of a source, around the external circuit, to the negative terminal. This convention was fixed in the 18th century, long before the electron was discovered, by assuming (as it turns out, incorrectly) that current was a flow of positive charge.

In a metal wire, the particles actually free to move are **delocalised (mobile) electrons**, which are not tied to any one atom and are negatively charged. They are repelled from the negative terminal and attracted toward the positive terminal, so [[orange:**electron drift** happens from negative to positive]] — the exact opposite direction to conventional current. Both descriptions are used side by side in this course: circuit diagrams and all current calculations use conventional current direction, while explanations of what is physically moving in a metal use electron drift direction.

keywords.definition: The rate at which electric charge passes a point in a circuit, measured in amperes (A).
The SI unit of current; a flow rate of one coulomb of charge per second.
An instrument for measuring current, connected in series in the circuit.
Current that flows in one fixed direction only, such as the current from a battery.
Current that regularly reverses direction, such as a mains electricity supply.
The defined direction of current flow in a circuit, from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the source.
The actual direction of motion of the electrons carrying charge in a metal, from negative to positive, opposite to conventional current.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding current from charge and time.** A charge of $12\,\mathrm{C}$ passes a point in a circuit in $4.0\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the current.
reasoning: Use $I = Q/t$ directly, since charge and time are both already known.
worked_examples.solution: $I = \dfrac{12\,\mathrm{C}}{4.0\,\mathrm{s}} = 3.0\,\mathrm{A}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by substituting back: $3.0\,\mathrm{A}\times 4.0\,\mathrm{s} = 12\,\mathrm{C}$, matching the original charge.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing time by charge instead of charge by time, giving $4.0/12 \approx 0.33$ with the wrong units.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding charge from current and time.** A kettle's heating element carries a current of $5.0\,\mathrm{A}$ for $180\,\mathrm{s}$ (3.0 minutes). Calculate the charge that passes through it.
reasoning: Rearrange $I = Q/t$ to make charge the subject: $Q = It$.
