(a) Draw a circuit diagram of the arrangement the student should use, showing clearly where the ammeter and the voltmeter are connected. (b) Describe how the readings should be taken, and how the resistance is calculated from them.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The battery, switch, variable resistor, ammeter and fixed resistor are all connected in series in a single loop; the voltmeter is connected in parallel, as a separate branch across the fixed resistor only. (b) Close the switch and record the ammeter reading (the current through the fixed resistor) and the voltmeter reading (the p.d. across it) at the same moment. Adjust the variable resistor to change the current and record several pairs of readings, switching off between them so that the resistor does not warm up. For each pair, calculate $R = V/I$, then take the mean of these values as the resistance of the fixed resistor.
exam_questions.full_solution: The method is exactly the definition $R=V/I$ turned into an experiment: the ammeter must carry the same current as the resistor, so it goes in series, and the voltmeter must compare the two ends of the resistor, so it goes in parallel. Taking several pairs of readings and averaging reduces the effect of random error in reading the two scales.
mark_scheme: Circuit diagram shows the battery, switch, variable resistor, ammeter and fixed resistor in series in one complete loop.
Circuit diagram shows the voltmeter connected in parallel across the fixed resistor only.
Close the switch and record the ammeter and voltmeter readings together (current through, and p.d. across, the resistor).
Use the variable resistor to obtain several pairs of readings (switching off between readings so the resistor does not heat up).
Calculate $R=V/I$ for each pair of readings and take the mean.
common_errors: Connecting the voltmeter in series with the resistor, or the ammeter in parallel across it, so that neither meter measures the quantity it is supposed to.
Taking only one pair of readings, so there is no mean and no check on the value obtained.

exam_questions.statement: Sketch the current-voltage graph of a resistor of constant resistance, with current on the vertical axis and voltage on the horizontal axis, and explain the shape of the graph you have drawn.
exam_questions.answer: The graph is a straight line passing through the origin (axes labelled: current $I$ vertical, voltage $V$ horizontal). The current is directly proportional to the voltage, so doubling the voltage doubles the current. This happens because the resistance does not change, provided the temperature of the resistor stays constant: $V/I$ therefore has the same value at every point on the line, and the line's gradient, $I/V = 1/R$, is constant.
exam_questions.full_solution: A constant resistance forces a constant ratio $V/I$, and a constant ratio between two quantities is exactly what a straight line through the origin shows. The line must pass through the origin because zero voltage across the resistor drives zero current through it.
mark_scheme: Sketches a straight line through the origin on labelled axes (current vertical, voltage horizontal).
States that the current is directly proportional to the voltage.
Explains that the resistance stays constant (at constant temperature), so $V/I$ is the same at every point and the gradient $1/R$ does not change.
common_errors: Drawing a line that does not pass through the origin, which would mean a current flowing with no p.d. across the resistor, or a p.d. with no current.
Describing the gradient as the resistance rather than as $1/R$.

mcq.stem: Resistor X ($5\,\Omega$) and resistor Y ($20\,\Omega$) are each connected, one at a time, to the same supply voltage. Which statement is correct?

options.text: X carries a larger current than Y, because $I=V/R$ gives a smaller current for a larger resistance.
Y carries a larger current than X, because a bigger resistance must mean more current.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes a bigger resistance causes a bigger current, rather than a smaller one for the same voltage.

options.text: X and Y carry the same current, because the supply voltage is the same for both.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the current depends on resistance too, not on the voltage alone.

options.text: It is impossible to tell without knowing the supply voltage.
options.why_wrong: the comparison between X and Y can be made without the exact voltage value, since the smaller resistance always gives the larger current for any shared, fixed voltage.

mcq.explanation: For the same voltage, $I=V/R$ gives a smaller current for the larger resistance (Y) and a larger current for the smaller resistance (X).

mcq.stem: An I-V graph (current vertical, voltage horizontal) for a resistor has a gradient of $0.20\,\mathrm{A/V}$. What is the resistor's resistance?

options.why_wrong: takes the gradient value directly as the resistance, instead of its reciprocal.
squares the gradient instead of taking its reciprocal.

options.text: Cannot be found without knowing a specific point on the line.
options.why_wrong: for a straight line through the origin, the gradient alone is enough to find the resistance; no extra point is needed.

mcq.explanation: On an $I$-against-$V$ graph, $R = 1/\text{gradient} = 1/0.20\,\mathrm{A/V} = 5.0\,\Omega$.

mcq.stem: Two wires are made of the same material and have the same length. Wire P has twice the cross-sectional area of wire Q. Which wire has the greater resistance?

options.text: Wire P, because it contains more material overall.
options.why_wrong: a larger cross-sectional area gives more parallel routes for charge, which lowers resistance, not raises it.

options.text: Both wires have the same resistance, because they are the same length.
options.why_wrong: length is equal, but cross-sectional area is not, and area also affects resistance.

options.text: Wire Q, because it has the smaller cross-sectional area.
It cannot be determined without knowing the exact material.
options.why_wrong: the direction of the comparison (smaller area means greater resistance) does not depend on which specific material it is, only on the two wires sharing the same material and length.

mcq.explanation: A smaller cross-sectional area gives fewer parallel routes for charge, so wire Q (half the area of P) has the greater resistance.

mcq.stem: Extension (beyond this course). Which I-V graph shape correctly describes a filament lamp, as voltage increases from zero?

options.text: A straight line through the origin, like a constant resistor.
options.why_wrong: describes an ohmic conductor, not the filament lamp, whose resistance changes as it heats up.

options.text: Zero current until a threshold voltage, then a sharp rise.
options.why_wrong: describes a diode's forward characteristic, not a filament lamp's.

options.text: A straight line with a negative gradient.
options.why_wrong: would mean current decreases as voltage increases, which does not happen for a filament lamp.

options.text: A curve that bends increasingly away from a straight line, with current rising less steeply as voltage increases.

mcq.explanation: A filament lamp's resistance increases as it heats up with increasing current, so its I-V graph curves away from the straight line a constant resistance would give.

flashcards.front: What is the formula for resistance, and what is one ohm equal to?
flashcards.back: $R = V/I$; one ohm is the resistance that needs one volt to drive one ampere, $1\,\Omega = 1\,\mathrm{V/A}$.

flashcards.front: How is resistance measured experimentally?
flashcards.back: An ammeter in series gives the current through the component; a voltmeter in parallel gives the p.d. across it; resistance is the voltmeter reading divided by the ammeter reading.

flashcards.front: On a graph of current against voltage, is the gradient equal to the resistance?
flashcards.back: No — the gradient equals $1/R$; the resistance is the reciprocal of the gradient, $R=1/\text{gradient}$.

flashcards.front: (Extension, beyond the 0654 syllabus.) How do a resistor's, a filament lamp's and a diode's I-V graphs differ in shape?
flashcards.back: A resistor gives a straight line through the origin (constant R); a filament lamp curves over as it heats up (R increases); a diode conducts almost nothing until a forward threshold, then rises sharply.

flashcards.front: Why does doubling a wire's cross-sectional area (same length, same material) halve its resistance?
flashcards.back: A larger cross-section gives more parallel routes for charge to flow through side by side, lowering the overall opposition to the flow.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A component with more resistance always has more current flowing through it.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 'More' of one electrical quantity can feel like it should mean 'more' of another, so a bigger resistance is assumed to mean a bigger current.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a larger ammeter reading for a larger-resistance component connected to the same supply voltage.
misconceptions.correct_model: For a fixed voltage, a larger resistance means a *smaller* current, not a larger one: $R=V/I$ rearranges to $I=V/R$, and dividing by a bigger number gives a smaller result. Resistance is a measure of opposition to current, not a cause of more of it.
misconceptions.remediation: Rearrange $R=V/I$ to $I=V/R$ before predicting a current from a resistance, and check the direction of the relationship (I gets smaller as R gets bigger) explicitly.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The gradient of an I-V graph is always equal to the resistance, whichever axis is which.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Gradient is usually introduced as 'the thing you read off a graph', without always checking which variable is on which axis first.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reads the gradient of a current-against-voltage graph and reports it directly as the resistance, instead of taking its reciprocal.
misconceptions.correct_model: On a graph of current ($I$, vertical axis) against voltage ($V$, horizontal axis), the gradient equals $I/V = 1/R$, so the resistance is the *reciprocal* of the gradient, $R = 1/\text{gradient}$. The gradient only equals $R$ directly if the axes are swapped, with voltage vertical and current horizontal.
misconceptions.remediation: Before reading resistance off any I-V graph, name which quantity is on which axis, and only then decide whether the gradient needs to be inverted.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A thicker wire always has a greater resistance than a thinner one.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 'Thicker' can sound like 'more material to push through', which is easy to associate with 'more resistance' rather than less.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a higher resistance for a wire with a larger cross-sectional area, other factors unchanged.
misconceptions.correct_model: A larger cross-sectional area gives *more* parallel routes for charge to flow through, which *lowers* resistance, not raises it; only a *longer* wire (more material along the direction of flow) increases resistance, for the same material and cross-section.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate the two geometric factors explicitly: longer (same thickness) increases R; thicker (same length) decreases R. Never let 'more material' alone decide the direction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a bigger resistance means a bigger current for the same voltage.
common_mistakes.why: 'More' of one electrical quantity can feel like it should mean 'more' of another.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Rearrange to $I=V/R$ first: a bigger $R$ divides the same $V$ into a smaller $I$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the gradient of an I-V graph directly as the resistance.
common_mistakes.why: Gradient is often treated as automatically equal to whatever quantity the question is about, without checking the axes.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Confirm current is vertical and voltage horizontal, then take the reciprocal of the gradient to get $R$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a thicker wire always has more resistance.
common_mistakes.why: 'Thicker' can sound like 'more material', which is easy to associate with more resistance rather than less.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Keep the two geometric effects separate: longer increases R; thicker (larger area) decreases R.

exam_notes: State units explicitly: resistance in ohms ($\Omega$), from a voltage in volts divided by a current in amperes.
On any I-V graph question, name which axis is which before calculating a gradient or a resistance from it.
When a question changes both the length and the cross-sectional area of a wire, work out each factor's effect separately before combining them — they do not always reinforce each other.

summary.big_idea: Resistance, $R=V/I$, measures how much voltage is needed to drive a given current through a component; a constant-resistance (ohmic) conductor gives a straight-line I-V graph through the origin whose gradient is $1/R$, and a wire's resistance also depends on its length (directly) and its cross-sectional area (inversely). The filament lamp and diode graphs met in this lesson are extension material, beyond the 0654 syllabus.
key_points: Resistance $R=V/I$, measured in ohms ($\Omega$); determined experimentally with a series ammeter and a parallel voltmeter.
For a fixed voltage, a bigger resistance means a smaller current, not a bigger one.
An ohmic conductor's I-V graph is a straight line through the origin; its gradient equals $1/R$, not $R$.
Extension (beyond the core syllabus): a filament lamp's I-V graph curves over as its resistance rises with current, and a diode conducts almost nothing until a forward threshold, then rises sharply.
A longer wire has greater resistance; a wire with a larger cross-sectional area has lower resistance; the two effects are independent.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Resistance is $R=V/I$; a bigger R means a smaller current for the same voltage; an I-V graph's gradient is $1/R$, not $R$; longer wires resist more, thicker wires resist less.

06_Electrical_power_energy_and_cost.json.title: Electrical power, energy and cost
06_Electrical_power_energy_and_cost.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Explain electrical power as the rate of energy transfer in a circuit, describe how a circuit transfers energy from the source to the components and then into the surroundings, and calculate power, energy, kilowatt-hours and cost using $P=IV$ and $E=IVt$, converting units correctly throughout. (The equivalent forms $P=I^2R$, which is Supplement content met again for transmission losses, and $P=V^2/R$, which is beyond the core syllabus, are included as extension.)

prerequisites.statement: Current is charge per unit time ($I=Q/t$) and voltage is energy per unit charge ($V=E/Q$), and resistance is $R=V/I$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Electrical power in this lesson is built directly by combining current and voltage, and its equivalent forms substitute resistance in using $V=IR$, so all three quantities need to already be secure.

prerequisites.statement: Power is the rate of energy transfer, $P=E/t$, measured in watts (W), where $1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson applies the general definition of power directly to electrical circuits; without it, $P=IV$ would be just a formula to memorise rather than a specific case of a rate already met elsewhere.

theory_blocks.title: Rate of charge times energy per charge gives rate of energy
theory_blocks.body:
Current tells you how much charge passes a point each second; voltage tells you how much energy each unit of that charge carries. Multiply them together and the charge cancels out, leaving energy per second — exactly what **power** means. [[blue:This is why electrical power is simply current multiplied by voltage]]: it is not a new idea, just two quantities you already have, combined.

It is worth being clear about where that energy goes. An electric circuit is an energy-transfer chain: [[blue:it transfers energy from a source of electrical energy — a cell, a battery or the mains supply — to the circuit components, and from the components into the surroundings]], by heating, and by light, sound or movement. Power is simply the rate at which that chain carries energy.

theory_blocks.title: Electrical power and energy: $P=IV$ and $E=IVt$
theory_blocks.body:
Electrical power is $$P = IV$$ where $P$ is power in watts (W), $I$ is current in amperes (A), and $V$ is voltage in volts (V). One watt is one joule of energy transferred per second: $1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}$.

Since power is energy transferred per unit time, $P=E/t$, combining this with $P=IV$ gives the energy transferred in a time $t$ (in seconds): $$E = IVt = Pt$$ with $E$ in joules (J) whenever $P$ is in watts and $t$ is in seconds.

theory_blocks.title: Keep your unit path consistent: seconds with watts, hours with kilowatts
theory_blocks.body:
$E=Pt$ only gives joules if $P$ is in watts *and* $t$ is in seconds. A time given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds first if you intend to keep power in watts; mixing a time in minutes with a power in watts gives a number with no correct unit at all.

There is a second, separate unit path used for household bills: [[blue:keep power in **kilowatts** and time in **hours**]], and the energy comes out directly in **kilowatt-hours (kW h)** without ever converting to seconds. The two paths below must not be mixed partway through a calculation:

| Starting units | Target | Formula path |
|---|---|---|
| $P$ in W, $t$ in s | $E$ in J | $E = P \times t$ |
| $P$ in kW, $t$ in h | $E$ in kW h | $E = P \times t$ |
| $t$ in minutes | $t$ in seconds | $t_{\mathrm{s}} = t_{\mathrm{min}} \times 60$ |
| $t$ in hours | $t$ in seconds | $t_{\mathrm{s}} = t_{\mathrm{h}} \times 3600$ |
| $E$ in kW h | $E$ in J | $E_{\mathrm{J}} = E_{\mathrm{kWh}} \times 3\,600\,000$ |

theory_blocks.title: The kilowatt-hour: a unit of energy, not power
theory_blocks.body: A **kilowatt-hour (kW h)** is the energy transferred by a $1\,\mathrm{kW}$ appliance running for $1$ hour: $$1\,\mathrm{kWh} = 1000\,\mathrm{W} \times 3600\,\mathrm{s} = 3\,600\,000\,\mathrm{J} = 3.6\,\mathrm{MJ}$$ Despite containing the word 'kilowatt', a kW h is an amount of energy, exactly like a joule, just a much larger and more practically-sized one for billing a household's electricity use: a joule is far too small a quantity to describe a day's energy use conveniently.

theory_blocks.title: Cost depends on energy used, not on current alone
theory_blocks.body: The cost of running an appliance is $$\text{cost} = (\text{energy in kW h}) \times (\text{price per kW h})$$ Energy in kW h depends on *both* power (in kW) and time (in h); current alone tells you neither of these on its own. A low-power appliance run for a long time can transfer exactly the same energy, and so cost exactly the same, as a high-power appliance run only briefly — current by itself never settles which appliance costs more.

assets.tikz: \nbbars{120}{20}{LED bulb/1.8, Fridge-freezer/108, Kettle/7.5, Electric shower/27}
assets.caption: Approximate daily running cost (pence, at £0.30 per kW h) for four household appliances. A fridge-freezer, left running continuously at low power, costs far more per day than a kettle used briefly at very high power — cost tracks total energy, not current or power alone.
assets.purpose: Give a concrete, numerically-verified comparison showing that running cost depends on energy (power times time), not on current or power in isolation.

theory_blocks.title: Extension: two more ways to write power, $P=I^2R$ and $P=V^2/R$
theory_blocks.body:
**Extension (beyond the Core syllabus).** In Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences GCSE, $P=I^2R$ is Supplement content, met only to explain why power losses in transmission cables are smaller when the voltage is greater (P4.5.6.6); $P=V^2/R$ is not in this course at all. Core power, energy and cost questions are all answered with $P=IV$ and $E=IVt$. The two forms below are shown because they follow directly from $P=IV$.

$P=IV$ is not the only way to calculate power. Using $V=IR$ (from the resistance lesson) to replace $V$ in $P=IV$ gives $$P = I^2R$$ and using $I=V/R$ to replace $I$ instead gives $$P = \frac{V^2}{R}$$ All three forms, $P=IV$, $P=I^2R$ and $P=V^2/R$, describe exactly the same power and must always agree for the same component; which one to use depends simply on which two quantities ($I$ and $V$; $I$ and $R$; or $V$ and $R$) a question actually gives you, so you can calculate power without first finding the third quantity separately.

keywords.definition: The rate of energy transfer in a circuit, $P=IV$, measured in watts (W).
The SI unit of power; one joule of energy transferred per second, $1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}$.
The total energy transferred, $E=Pt=IVt$, in joules when power is in watts and time is in seconds.
A unit of energy equal to the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour; $1\,\mathrm{kWh}=3\,600\,000\,\mathrm{J}$.
The cost of operating an appliance, calculated as energy transferred (in kW h) multiplied by the price per kW h.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding power from current and voltage.** A component has a current of $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ through it and a p.d. of $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ across it. Calculate its power.
reasoning: Use $P = IV$ directly, since current and voltage are both already known.
worked_examples.solution: $P = 2.0\,\mathrm{A} \times 6.0\,\mathrm{V} = 12\,\mathrm{W}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by substituting back: $12\,\mathrm{W}/6.0\,\mathrm{V} = 2.0\,\mathrm{A}$, recovering the original current.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Adding current and voltage instead of multiplying them.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding energy from power and time.** The component above ($P=12\,\mathrm{W}$) runs for $60\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the energy transferred.
reasoning: Use $E = Pt$, since power is already in watts and time is already in seconds, so no conversion is needed.
worked_examples.solution: $E = 12\,\mathrm{W} \times 60\,\mathrm{s} = 720\,\mathrm{J}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $720\,\mathrm{J}/60\,\mathrm{s} = 12\,\mathrm{W}$, recovering the original power.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting that this unit path needs seconds, and substituting a time given in minutes directly.

worked_examples.statement: **Extension (beyond the Core syllabus): checking the three power formulas agree.** A component has $V=6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ across it and $I=2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ through it. (a) Calculate its resistance. (b) Use $P=I^2R$ to calculate its power. (c) Use $P=V^2/R$ to calculate its power, and confirm all three methods (including $P=IV$ from the first worked example) agree.
reasoning: Find resistance first using $R=V/I$, since both are known.
Substitute $I$ and the calculated $R$ into $P=I^2R$.
Substitute $V$ and the calculated $R$ into $P=V^2/R$.
Compare all three calculated powers.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $R = 6.0\,\mathrm{V}/2.0\,\mathrm{A} = 3.0\,\Omega$. (b) $P = (2.0\,\mathrm{A})^2 \times 3.0\,\Omega = 12\,\mathrm{W}$. (c) $P = (6.0\,\mathrm{V})^2/3.0\,\Omega = 36/3.0 = 12\,\mathrm{W}$. All three methods ($IV$, $I^2R$, $V^2/R$) give exactly $12\,\mathrm{W}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: The three formulas are not three different facts to memorise separately: they are the same physical quantity, reached by three different, interchangeable routes depending on which two quantities you already know.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating $P=I^2R$ and $P=V^2/R$ as unrelated formulas to be memorised independently, rather than as $P=IV$ with $V$ or $I$ substituted out using $V=IR$.

worked_examples.statement: **Energy, kilowatt-hours and cost together.** A kettle is rated at $2000\,\mathrm{W}$ and is used for a total of $3.0$ hours over a week. Electricity costs $\pounds 0.30$ per kW h. (a) Calculate the energy transferred, in kW h. (b) Calculate the cost. (c) Explain why it would be wrong to describe the kettle's kW h figure from part (a) as its 'power usage'.
unknowns: why kW h is not power
reasoning: Use the kilowatt/hour unit path directly: $E = P \times t$ with $P$ in kW and $t$ in h.
Multiply the energy in kW h by the price per kW h to find the cost.

A kW h is a total amount of energy transferred over the stated time, not a rate; the kettle's instantaneous power rating ($2.0\,\mathrm{kW}$) is the rate, and stays fixed regardless of how long it runs.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $E = 2.0\,\mathrm{kW} \times 3.0\,\mathrm{h} = 6.0\,\mathrm{kWh}$. (b) Cost $= 6.0\,\mathrm{kWh} \times \pounds 0.30/\mathrm{kWh} = \pounds 1.80$. (c) The $6.0\,\mathrm{kWh}$ figure is a total energy transferred over the full $3.0\,\mathrm{h}$, which depends on how long the kettle was used; the kettle's actual power usage (rate of energy transfer) is fixed at $2.0\,\mathrm{kW}$ the whole time it is switched on, regardless of how long that turns out to be.
worked_examples.interpretation: This directly separates the rate (power, kW) from the total (energy, kW h): the rate did not change, but the total energy grew as the kettle ran for longer.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calling the $6.0\,\mathrm{kWh}$ figure the kettle's 'power', confusing a total amount of energy with a fixed rate.

guided_exercises.statement: A lamp rated $60\,\mathrm{W}$ is left on for $5.0$ hours. Electricity costs $\pounds 0.30$ per kW h. Calculate (a) the energy transferred in kW h, and (b) the cost.
hints: Convert the lamp's power to kilowatts first.
Use $E = P \times t$ with $P$ in kW and $t$ in hours.
Multiply the energy in kW h by the price per kW h.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) $E = 0.060\,\mathrm{kW} \times 5.0\,\mathrm{h} = 0.30\,\mathrm{kWh}$. (b) Cost $= 0.30\,\mathrm{kWh} \times \pounds 0.30/\mathrm{kWh} = \pounds 0.090$.
common_errors: Using $60$ (watts) directly as kilowatts, giving an energy 1000 times too large.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Convert the lamp's power to kilowatts first.

**Step 2 — Method:** Use $E = P \times t$ with $P$ in kW and $t$ in hours.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** (a) $E = 0.060\,\mathrm{kW} \times 5.0\,\mathrm{h} = 0.30\,\mathrm{kWh}$. (b) Cost $= 0.30\,\mathrm{kWh} \times \pounds 0.30/\mathrm{kWh} = \pounds 0.090$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Multiply the energy in kW h by the price per kW h.

guided_exercises.statement: A hairdryer rated $800\,\mathrm{W}$ is used for $15$ minutes. Calculate the energy transferred, in joules.
hints: This unit path needs time in seconds, since power is given in watts.
Convert $15$ minutes to seconds first.
Use $E = Pt$ with $P$ in watts and $t$ in seconds.
guided_exercises.answer: $t = 15 \times 60 = 900\,\mathrm{s}$. $E = 800\,\mathrm{W} \times 900\,\mathrm{s} = 720\,000\,\mathrm{J}$ ($720\,\mathrm{kJ}$).
common_errors: Substituting $t=15$ directly into $E=Pt$ with $P$ in watts, giving an energy 60 times too small.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** This unit path needs time in seconds, since power is given in watts.

**Step 2 — Method:** Convert $15$ minutes to seconds first.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $t = 15 \times 60 = 900\,\mathrm{s}$. $E = 800\,\mathrm{W} \times 900\,\mathrm{s} = 720\,000\,\mathrm{J}$ ($720\,\mathrm{kJ}$).

**Step 4 — Check:** Use $E = Pt$ with $P$ in watts and $t$ in seconds.

exercises.statement: A component has a current of $5.0\,\mathrm{A}$ through it and a p.d. of $12\,\mathrm{V}$ across it. Calculate its power.
exercises.answer: $P = IV = 5.0\,\mathrm{A} \times 12\,\mathrm{V} = 60\,\mathrm{W}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $60\,\mathrm{W}/12\,\mathrm{V} = 5.0\,\mathrm{A}$.

exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond the Core syllabus).** A $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor carries a current of $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$. (a) Calculate its power using $P=I^2R$. (b) Calculate the p.d. across it, and use $P=IV$ to confirm your answer to (a).
exercises.answer: (a) $P = (3.0\,\mathrm{A})^2 \times 4.0\,\Omega = 36\,\mathrm{W}$. (b) $V = IR = 3.0\,\mathrm{A} \times 4.0\,\Omega = 12\,\mathrm{V}$; $P = IV = 3.0\,\mathrm{A} \times 12\,\mathrm{V} = 36\,\mathrm{W}$, matching (a).
exercises.full_solution: Both routes to power start from the same current and resistance and must agree, since they describe the same physical power.

exercises.statement: An appliance transfers $2.4\,\mathrm{kWh}$ of energy over the course of a day. Electricity costs $\pounds 0.30$ per kW h. Calculate the cost for that day.
exercises.answer: Cost $= 2.4\,\mathrm{kWh} \times \pounds 0.30/\mathrm{kWh} = \pounds 0.72$.
exercises.full_solution: This uses the cost formula directly, since the energy is already given in kW h.

exercises.statement: Appliance A uses $100\,\mathrm{W}$ and is run for $10$ hours a day. Appliance B uses $2000\,\mathrm{W}$ and is run for only $0.50$ hours a day. Calculate the daily energy (in kW h) and cost (at $\pounds 0.30$ per kW h) for each appliance, and explain what this shows about judging cost from power (or current) alone.
exercises.answer: Appliance A: $E = 0.100\,\mathrm{kW} \times 10\,\mathrm{h} = 1.0\,\mathrm{kWh}$, cost $= \pounds 0.30$. Appliance B: $E = 2.0\,\mathrm{kW} \times 0.50\,\mathrm{h} = 1.0\,\mathrm{kWh}$, cost $= \pounds 0.30$. Both appliances cost exactly the same per day, despite appliance B having 20 times the power of appliance A, because B is used for much less time: cost depends on the combination of power and time (total energy), not on power or current alone.
exercises.full_solution: This is a direct numeric counterexample to judging cost from power or current in isolation: the much higher-power appliance does not cost more here, because it runs for proportionally less time.

exercises.statement: A torch is switched on. Describe the energy transfers that take place, naming where the energy comes from, what it is transferred to, and where it finally ends up.
exercises.answer: The cell (the source of electrical energy) transfers energy to the circuit components; the lamp is the main component here, and it transfers that energy into the surroundings, as light and by heating.
exercises.full_solution: Every circuit follows the same chain: source of electrical energy $\rightarrow$ circuit components $\rightarrow$ surroundings. The components do not store the energy or use it up; they pass it on to the surroundings, which is why a torch keeps transferring energy for as long as it is switched on.

exam_questions.statement: An electric heater is rated $2300\,\mathrm{W}$ and is connected to the $230\,\mathrm{V}$ mains supply. (a) Calculate the current through the heater. (b) Calculate the heater's resistance. (c) The heater runs for $30$ minutes. Calculate the energy transferred, in kW h. (d) Calculate the cost of this, at $\pounds 0.30$ per kW h.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $I = P/V = 2300\,\mathrm{W}/230\,\mathrm{V} = 10\,\mathrm{A}$. (b) $R = V/I = 230\,\mathrm{V}/10\,\mathrm{A} = 23\,\Omega$ (or equivalently $R=V^2/P=230^2/2300=23\,\Omega$). (c) $E = 2.3\,\mathrm{kW} \times 0.50\,\mathrm{h} = 1.15\,\mathrm{kWh}$. (d) Cost $= 1.15\,\mathrm{kWh} \times \pounds 0.30/\mathrm{kWh} = \pounds 0.345$.
exam_questions.full_solution: Check for (a)-(b): $I^2R = (10\,\mathrm{A})^2\times23\,\Omega=2300\,\mathrm{W}$, matching the rated power.
mark_scheme: Calculates current $I=10\,\mathrm{A}$.
Calculates resistance $R=23\,\Omega$ (by either valid method).
Converts $30$ minutes to $0.50$ hours.
Calculates energy $E=1.15\,\mathrm{kWh}$.
Calculates cost $=\pounds 0.345$.
Rearranges $P=IV$ correctly as $I=P/V$ in (a) (C1).
common_errors: Using $30$ (minutes) directly as hours in part (c), giving an energy 60 times too large.

exam_questions.statement: A student claims: 'A $3\,\mathrm{kW}$ kettle used for 5 minutes must cost more to run than a $100\,\mathrm{W}$ lamp left on for 3 hours, because the kettle draws a much bigger current.' (a) Calculate the energy, in kW h, transferred by the kettle. (b) Calculate the energy, in kW h, transferred by the lamp. (c) State whether the student's claim is correct, and explain why, referring to your answers.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $E_{\text{kettle}} = 3.0\,\mathrm{kW} \times (5/60)\,\mathrm{h} = 0.25\,\mathrm{kWh}$. (b) $E_{\text{lamp}} = 0.100\,\mathrm{kW} \times 3.0\,\mathrm{h} = 0.30\,\mathrm{kWh}$. (c) The claim is incorrect: the lamp actually transfers slightly more energy ($0.30\,\mathrm{kWh}$) than the kettle ($0.25\,\mathrm{kWh}$), and so costs slightly more, even though the kettle draws a much bigger current; current alone does not determine cost, because the lamp runs for far longer.
exam_questions.full_solution: This is a direct counter-example to the idea that current alone decides cost: the higher-current appliance is not automatically the more expensive one to run, once the very different running times are taken into account.
mark_scheme: Calculates kettle energy $=0.25\,\mathrm{kWh}$.
Calculates lamp energy $=0.30\,\mathrm{kWh}$.
States the claim is incorrect.

Explains that the lamp transfers more energy ($0.30\,\mathrm{kWh}>0.25\,\mathrm{kWh}$) and so costs (slightly) more, despite drawing much less current (1 mark), because cost depends on energy $=$ power $\times$ time, and the lamp runs for much longer (1 mark).
common_errors: Agreeing with the student's claim without calculating either energy, reasoning from current alone.

mcq.stem: Which statement about the kilowatt-hour (kW h) is correct?

options.text: It is a unit of energy, equal to the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour.
It is a unit of power, equal to 1000 watts sustained for an hour.
options.why_wrong: describes power sustained over time, which is actually energy, not a unit of power itself.

options.text: It is the same as a joule, just under a different name.
options.why_wrong: a kW h and a joule are both energy units, but they are not the same size: $1\,\mathrm{kWh}=3\,600\,000\,\mathrm{J}$, not $1\,\mathrm{J}$.

options.text: It measures how quickly an appliance uses energy.
options.why_wrong: describes power (a rate), not the kilowatt-hour, which measures a total amount of energy transferred.

mcq.explanation: A kilowatt-hour is an energy unit: $1\,\mathrm{kWh} = 1000\,\mathrm{W}\times3600\,\mathrm{s} = 3\,600\,000\,\mathrm{J}$.

mcq.stem: A $500\,\mathrm{W}$ heater runs for $2$ minutes. What is the correct first step to find the energy transferred in joules?

options.text: Substitute $t=2$ directly into $E=Pt$ with $P=500\,\mathrm{W}$.
options.why_wrong: uses minutes directly with a power in watts, which does not give an energy in joules.

options.text: Convert $2$ minutes to $120$ seconds, then use $E=Pt$.
Convert $500\,\mathrm{W}$ to $0.500\,\mathrm{kW}$, then multiply by $2$ (minutes).
options.why_wrong: mixes the kilowatt/hour unit path with a time still in minutes instead of hours.

options.text: Divide $500\,\mathrm{W}$ by $2$ minutes.
options.why_wrong: divides instead of multiplying, and does not use seconds.

mcq.explanation: With power in watts, time must be converted to seconds before using $E=Pt$ to get an energy in joules.

mcq.stem: Appliance X draws a much bigger current than appliance Y. Which statement is correct?

options.text: X must cost more to run than Y, because it draws more current.
options.why_wrong: assumes current alone decides cost, ignoring voltage, power and running time.

options.text: Cost cannot depend on time at all, only on the appliances themselves.
options.why_wrong: cost explicitly depends on running time, since energy (and so cost) is power multiplied by time.

options.text: X and Y could cost the same, or Y could even cost more, depending on their running times and power.
X must have a higher power rating than Y.
options.why_wrong: a bigger current alone does not guarantee a bigger power rating, since power also depends on voltage, which may differ between X and Y.

mcq.explanation: Cost depends on total energy transferred (power $\times$ time), not on current alone; a lower-current appliance run for longer can cost the same or more.

mcq.stem: Extension (beyond this course). A component has $V=10\,\mathrm{V}$ across it and $R=5.0\,\Omega$. What is its power?

options.text: $2.0\,\mathrm{W}$
options.why_wrong: divides $V$ by $R$ instead of using $P=V^2/R$, finding the current rather than the power.

options.text: $50\,\mathrm{W}$
options.why_wrong: uses $P=VR$ directly, multiplying voltage by resistance instead of using $P=V^2/R$.
inverts the correct formula, dividing $R$ by $V^2$ instead of $V^2$ by $R$.

options.text: $20\,\mathrm{W}$

flashcards.front: What are the three equivalent formulas for electrical power, and which of them does 0654 require?
flashcards.back: $P=IV$, $P=I^2R$ and $P=V^2/R$ all describe the same power; you choose the one that uses the two quantities you know. Only $P=IV$ is required for 0654: $P=I^2R$ is Supplement (used for transmission losses) and $P=V^2/R$ is beyond the syllabus.

flashcards.front: What is the formula for electrical energy, and what units must power and time be in for the answer to be in joules?
flashcards.back: $E=Pt$ (or $E=IVt$); power in watts and time in seconds give energy in joules.

flashcards.front: Is a kilowatt-hour a unit of power or energy?
flashcards.back: Energy — it is the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour, $1\,\mathrm{kWh}=3\,600\,000\,\mathrm{J}$.

flashcards.front: Does a higher-current appliance always cost more to run than a lower-current one?
flashcards.back: No — cost depends on total energy (power $\times$ time), not on current alone; a low-power appliance run for a long time can cost the same or more.

flashcards.front: How do you calculate the cost of running an appliance from its power rating and running time?
flashcards.back: Convert power to kW and time to hours, multiply to get energy in kW h, then multiply by the price per kW h.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The kilowatt-hour (kW h) is a unit of power.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A kilowatt-hour's name contains 'kilowatt', a power unit, so it is easy to assume the whole combination also measures power.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes an appliance's energy bill in kW h as its 'power usage', or tries to add a kW h value directly to a power rating in W.
misconceptions.correct_model: A kilowatt-hour measures energy, not power: it is the energy transferred by a $1\,\mathrm{kW}$ appliance running for $1$ hour. Power (in W or kW) tells you the *rate* of energy transfer; a kilowatt-hour tells you the *total amount* of energy transferred once a time is included.
misconceptions.remediation: Always ask 'is this a rate (power, W or kW) or a total amount (energy, J or kW h)?' before using a value from a bill or an appliance label.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Minutes can be used directly in $E=IVt$ (or $E=Pt$) alongside a power in watts, without converting to seconds first.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Minutes are the everyday unit for short durations, so it is easy to substitute the number of minutes straight into a formula that actually requires seconds.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner substitutes, for example, $t=15$ directly (meaning 15 minutes) into $E=Pt$ with $P$ in watts, instead of converting to $900\,\mathrm{s}$ first.
misconceptions.correct_model: When power is in watts, time must be in seconds to give energy in joules ($1\,\mathrm{W}\times1\,\mathrm{s}=1\,\mathrm{J}$); minutes or hours must be converted to seconds first. (The separate kilowatt-hour route keeps power in kW and time in hours instead — the two unit paths must not be mixed.)
misconceptions.remediation: Before substituting into $E=Pt$ or $E=IVt$ with power in watts, convert any given time into seconds explicitly as a first step, writing the conversion down.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The cost of running an appliance depends only on the current it draws.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Current is the electrical quantity learners have worked with longest in this unit, so it is tempting to assume it alone determines cost.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that a higher-current appliance must always cost more to run than a lower-current one, without considering voltage, power or running time.
misconceptions.correct_model: Cost depends on the total energy transferred (power $\times$ time), not on current alone. A low-power appliance run for a long time can transfer the same energy, and cost the same, as a high-power appliance run briefly.
misconceptions.remediation: Calculate the energy in kW h (power in kW $\times$ time in hours) before comparing or predicting any cost, rather than comparing currents directly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a kilowatt-hour figure as a power.
common_mistakes.why: The name 'kilowatt-hour' contains a power unit, which is easy to over-generalise.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember a kW h is a total energy (power $\times$ time already included), not a rate.

common_mistakes.mistake: Substituting a time in minutes directly into $E=Pt$ with power in watts.
common_mistakes.why: Minutes are the everyday unit for short times, so converting to seconds is easy to skip.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always convert minutes or hours to seconds first when power is in watts, before substituting into $E=Pt$.

common_mistakes.mistake: Judging an appliance's running cost from its current alone.
common_mistakes.why: Current is the most familiar electrical quantity from earlier in this unit.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate the energy in kW h (power $\times$ time) before comparing or predicting cost.

exam_notes: State which unit path you are using (watts-and-seconds-to-joules, or kilowatts-and-hours-to-kilowatt-hours) and keep it consistent throughout a calculation.

When a question gives you current and voltage, use $P=IV$ directly — it is the only power equation 0654 requires. The extension forms $P=I^2R$ and $P=V^2/R$ are shortcuts for when a question gives you a resistance instead.
A cost question always needs energy in kW h as an intermediate step; never multiply a power or a current directly by a price.

summary.big_idea: Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer, $P=IV$: a circuit carries energy from the source to the components and then into the surroundings. Energy is power multiplied by time, with the kilowatt-hour as a convenient large energy unit for billing, and the cost of running an appliance always depends on the total energy used, not on current or power alone.
key_points: Power $P=IV$, measured in watts (W); a circuit transfers energy from the source to the components and then into the surroundings. (Extension: $P=I^2R$ and $P=V^2/R$ describe the same power but are not required for Core GCSE.)
Energy $E=Pt=IVt$, in joules when power is in watts and time is in seconds.
A kilowatt-hour (kW h) is a unit of energy, not power: $1\,\mathrm{kWh}=3\,600\,000\,\mathrm{J}$.
For a household bill, keep power in kW and time in hours to get energy directly in kW h.
Cost $=$ energy in kW h $\times$ price per kW h; cost depends on energy (power $\times$ time), never on current alone.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Power is a rate ($P=IV$, in W); energy is power times time ($E=Pt$, in J with seconds, or in kW h with hours); a kW h is energy, not power; and cost always needs the full energy, never current alone.

07_Drawing_and_reading_circuits.json.title: Drawing and reading circuits
07_Drawing_and_reading_circuits.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Draw and interpret circuit diagrams using the required symbols for cells, batteries, switches, fixed and variable resistors, lamps, heaters, motors, ammeters, voltmeters and fuses, and identify whether a drawn circuit gives a complete conducting path.
Include generator and LED symbols in a circuit diagram and state that an LED conducts, and emits light, only when connected in its forward direction.

prerequisites.statement: State that an ammeter is connected in series in the loop it measures, and that a voltmeter is connected in parallel, across the component it measures.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Reading and drawing a diagram correctly depends on already knowing where each meter belongs; this lesson adds the remaining symbols to that habit, it does not teach meter placement from scratch.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise current, voltage and resistance as the three quantities a circuit diagram's components control or measure.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A symbol is only useful once you know what physical quantity or behaviour it represents; this lesson assumes those quantities are already meaningful.

theory_blocks.title: A circuit diagram is a map, not a photograph
theory_blocks.body:
A road map does not look like the road: it keeps only what matters for finding your way, drawn with standard symbols that anyone can read. A circuit diagram works the same way. It keeps only two things: [[blue:which components exist, and which pairs of points they connect to]]. It throws away everything else, including the physical size of each component, the length of the wires, and the shape the loop happens to be drawn in.

This is exactly why the same circuit can be drawn as a neat rectangle on one page and as an oddly shaped loop on another, and still be the same circuit. What never changes is the set of connections: which component sits between which two points, called **nodes**. Learning to read a diagram means learning to see the connections first and treat the drawn shape as irrelevant.

theory_blocks.title: Standard symbols for the required Core components
theory_blocks.body:
Every component in a circuit diagram is drawn with one fixed symbol, so that any two people drawing the same circuit produce diagrams that match exactly:

- **Cell**: a long thin line (positive terminal) next to a short thick line (negative terminal).
- **Battery**: two or more cells drawn end to end, alternating long-thin and short-thick lines.
- **Switch**: a break in the wire with a lever that can swing to touch a fixed contact point, closing the gap.
- **Fixed resistor**: a plain rectangle.
- **Variable resistor**: a rectangle with a diagonal arrow drawn across it, showing that its resistance can be adjusted.
- **Lamp**: a circle with a cross inside.
- **Heater**: a rectangle divided into sections by two short vertical lines, representing a heating element.
- **Ammeter**: a circle containing the letter A, always placed in series in the loop it measures.
- **Voltmeter**: a circle containing the letter V, always placed in parallel, across the component it measures.
- **Motor**: a circle containing the letter M.
- **Fuse**: a narrow rectangle through which the main wire passes, representing a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current through it is too large.

The figure below shows every one of these symbols drawn to the same convention used throughout this course.

assets.caption: The required circuit symbols. Cell and battery share one convention (long thin line = positive, short thick line = negative); the ammeter, voltmeter, motor and generator all use the circle-with-letter convention, but an ammeter is connected in series and a voltmeter in parallel. The generator and the LED, below the dashed line, are Supplement only.
assets.purpose: Give every required symbol one single, memorable, and directly comparable reference drawing, so a learner can check an unfamiliar symbol against this key rather than guessing.

theory_blocks.title: Reading a diagram: find the nodes, then trace the loop
theory_blocks.body:
To read any circuit diagram correctly, follow the same three steps every time:

1. **Mark every junction.** A junction exists only where a solid dot is drawn, or where the diagram makes an explicit three-way (or more) join. A crossing of two lines with no dot is not a junction: the wires simply pass over each other with no electrical contact.
2. **Trace each possible path** from one terminal of the supply back to the other, moving only along drawn wires and through components, never jumping across an unmarked crossing.
3. **Decide series or parallel from the nodes, not the shape.** Two components are in series if they share exactly one node with each other and no other component also connects to that shared node. Two components are in parallel if both of their nodes are the same pair of nodes.

For a circuit to conduct at all, there must be at least one complete path from one terminal of the supply to the other with every switch along that path closed; an open switch, or a lamp with a broken filament, breaks every path that runs through it.

theory_blocks.title: Going further: the generator symbol and the LED
theory_blocks.body:
Two further symbols appear once a circuit includes alternating-current sources or light-emitting diodes. A **generator** is drawn as a circle containing the letter **G** (it is usually an a.c. source, whose output reverses direction rather than staying one way like a cell). An **LED** (light-emitting diode) is drawn as a diode symbol, a filled triangle pointing into a bar, with two small arrows pointing away from it to show emitted light.

The LED's triangle points in the direction conventional current is allowed to flow; in the simple GCSE model, an LED conducts, and emits light, only when connected this way round (its **forward direction**). Connected the other way round, it simply does not conduct: no current flows and no light is emitted, and nothing is damaged at the voltages used in this course.

keywords.definition: A point in a circuit diagram where two or more components meet; the connections between nodes, not the drawn shape, define the circuit.
A node where three or more wires or components meet, marked by a solid dot in a correctly drawn diagram.
The direction, shown by the triangle in an LED's symbol, in which the LED conducts and emits light; connected the other way, it does not conduct at the voltages used here.
A circle containing the letter G; a generator is usually an a.c. source, whose output reverses direction rather than staying one way.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading a simple loop.** A diagram shows a cell, a switch and a lamp drawn one after another around a single loop, with no other branch. State whether the lamp lights when the switch is closed, and explain your reasoning.
knowns: one cell, one switch, one lamp, drawn around a single unbranched loop
unknowns: whether the lamp lights with the switch closed
reasoning: Trace the loop from one terminal of the cell, through the switch, through the lamp, and back to the other terminal of the cell.
With the switch closed, every point on this single path is connected, so the path is complete.
worked_examples.solution: Yes, the lamp lights, because closing the switch completes the only path around the loop, giving the cell a complete conducting path through the lamp.
worked_examples.interpretation: If the switch were open instead, the same trace would hit a gap at the switch, so no complete path would exist and the lamp would not light.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the lamp lights regardless of the switch's state, because a cell and a lamp are both present in the diagram.

worked_examples.statement: **The ammeter reads the same value anywhere on this loop.** A $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ cell drives current through two identical $4.0\,\Omega$ lamps connected one after another around a single unbranched loop. An ammeter is inserted in series at one point in the loop. Calculate the ammeter's reading, then state what it would read if moved to any other point on the same loop.
reasoning: The two lamps share only one node with each other and no branch exists, so their resistances add: $4.0\,\Omega+4.0\,\Omega=8.0\,\Omega$.
Use $I=V/R$ with the total resistance of the single loop.
worked_examples.solution: $I=6.0\,\mathrm{V}\div8.0\,\Omega=0.75\,\mathrm{A}$. Because every point on an unbranched loop carries the same current, the ammeter would read exactly $0.75\,\mathrm{A}$ at any other point on this same loop.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $0.75\,\mathrm{A}\times8.0\,\Omega=6.0\,\mathrm{V}$, which recovers the supply voltage.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Expecting a different ammeter reading depending on which lamp the ammeter is drawn next to, instead of recognising that every point on this one unbranched loop carries the same current.

worked_examples.statement: **Same circuit, different shape.** Two identical circuits each contain a cell and two lamps connected one after another with no branch. One is drawn as a tidy rectangle; the other is drawn as an L-shaped loop that turns two sharp corners. Explain why both diagrams describe the same series circuit.
knowns: both diagrams show a cell and two lamps joined one after another with no branch, drawn in two different physical shapes
unknowns: whether the arrangement is really the same in both diagrams
reasoning: Ignore the outline of each diagram and identify the nodes instead: in both diagrams, the cell connects to lamp 1 at one node, lamp 1 connects to lamp 2 at a second node, and lamp 2 connects back to the cell at a third node.
No dot or junction exists anywhere else in either diagram, so no branching is possible in either case.
worked_examples.solution: Both diagrams describe the identical series circuit, because the sequence of nodes and components connecting them is exactly the same in both; only the physical shape used to draw the loop is different, and shape has no effect on series or parallel arrangement.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the direct answer to the idea that 'the drawing determines series or parallel': the drawing's outline carries no electrical information at all, only the node connections do.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding that the L-shaped diagram must be a different, perhaps parallel, circuit simply because it looks different from the familiar rectangle.

assets.caption: The same cell and two lamps, connected one after another with no branch in both cases: a tidy rectangular loop (left) and an L-shaped loop turning two corners (right). Tracing the nodes shows both are the identical series circuit.
assets.purpose: Make the independence of series/parallel arrangement from physical drawing shape visible by showing one real circuit drawn two different ways, directly targeting the 'drawing shape decides series/parallel' misconception.

worked_examples.statement: **Spotting a wrongly connected voltmeter.** A learner wants to measure the potential difference across a lamp in a simple series circuit. They draw the voltmeter broken directly into the main loop, in series with the lamp, rather than as a separate branch. (a) State what is wrong with this diagram. (b) Explain, in terms of the complete conducting path, what would happen to the lamp as a result, given that a voltmeter has a very high resistance. (c) Redraw the connection correctly, in words.
knowns: voltmeter drawn in series, directly in the main loop, with the lamp
unknowns: the fault, its consequence, and the correct connection
reasoning: A voltmeter must always be a separate branch joining the two nodes of the component it measures, not a component inserted into the main loop itself.
A voltmeter's very high resistance means almost no current can pass through it if it is forced to carry the full loop current.
worked_examples.solution: (a) The voltmeter has been wired in series instead of in parallel. (b) Because the voltmeter's resistance is very high, almost no current can flow through the single path that now includes it, so the lamp would not light, or would light only extremely dimly. (c) The voltmeter should instead be connected as an extra branch joining the two nodes of the lamp directly, leaving the lamp itself still in the main loop unchanged.
worked_examples.interpretation: A voltmeter in parallel barely changes the current in the main loop, because almost none of the current takes the voltmeter's high-resistance branch; a voltmeter in series nearly stops the current completely, because now all of the current must pass through that high resistance.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming any meter connected 'into' the circuit, regardless of series or parallel, will give a sensible reading without affecting the rest of the circuit.

guided_exercises.statement: A circuit is described as follows: a battery, a closed switch, a fixed resistor and a lamp are all connected one after another with no branch, forming a single loop. List the symbols you would draw, in order, going around the loop, and state whether the lamp lights.
hints: Draw each described component using its one standard symbol.
Connect them in exactly the order given, with no branch anywhere.
Check whether every switch on the single path is closed before deciding if the lamp lights.
guided_exercises.answer: Battery symbol, then switch symbol (closed), then resistor rectangle, then lamp circle-with-cross, joined one after another around a single loop back to the battery. Because the switch is closed and no component is missing or broken, the path is complete and the lamp lights.
common_errors: Drawing the switch symbol in its open position by mistake, which would wrongly suggest the lamp does not light.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Draw each described component using its one standard symbol.

**Step 2 — Method:** Connect them in exactly the order given, with no branch anywhere.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Battery symbol, then switch symbol (closed), then resistor rectangle, then lamp circle-with-cross, joined one after another around a single loop back to the battery. Because the switch is closed and no component is missing or broken, the path is complete and the lamp lights.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check whether every switch on the single path is closed before deciding if the lamp lights.

guided_exercises.statement: A learner has drawn an ammeter as a separate branch connected across a resistor, in the same way a voltmeter would be connected. Explain what is wrong with this and how to fix it.
hints: Recall which instrument is drawn in series and which is drawn in parallel.
An ammeter needs to carry the same current as the component it measures, not sit on a separate branch.
Describe the fix in terms of breaking the main loop open at one point.
guided_exercises.answer: The ammeter has been connected as a parallel branch, which is how a voltmeter is connected, not an ammeter. The fix is to break the main loop open at one point and insert the ammeter into that gap, so the full current through the resistor is forced to pass through the ammeter as well.
common_errors: Leaving the resistor's own branch connected and simply adding the ammeter alongside it, which keeps the ammeter in parallel rather than moving it into the series path.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Recall which instrument is drawn in series and which is drawn in parallel.

**Step 2 — Method:** An ammeter needs to carry the same current as the component it measures, not sit on a separate branch.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The ammeter has been connected as a parallel branch, which is how a voltmeter is connected, not an ammeter. The fix is to break the main loop open at one point and insert the ammeter into that gap, so the full current through the resistor is forced to pass through the ammeter as well.

**Step 4 — Check:** Describe the fix in terms of breaking the main loop open at one point.

exercises.statement: Name the standard symbol you would draw for each of the following: (a) a component that opens and closes a conducting path, (b) a component whose resistance can be adjusted while the circuit is running, (c) a component that melts and breaks the circuit if the current becomes too large.
exercises.answer: (a) Switch (a break in the wire with a lever touching a fixed contact when closed). (b) Variable resistor (a rectangle with a diagonal arrow across it). (c) Fuse (a narrow rectangle through which the main wire passes).
exercises.full_solution: Each symbol is fixed by convention, so the same three symbols are used by every diagram in this course and in an examination.

exercises.statement: Two resistors are drawn in a diagram. Resistor 1 connects node A to node B. Resistor 2 also connects node A to node B. State whether the resistors are in series or in parallel, and justify your answer using the nodes alone.
exercises.answer: They are in parallel.
exercises.full_solution: Two components are in parallel precisely when both of their nodes are the same shared pair; here both resistors join the identical pair of nodes, A and B, so they are in parallel regardless of how the diagram happens to be drawn.

exercises.statement: A diagram shows two wires crossing on the page, with no dot drawn at the crossing point, in a circuit that also contains a cell, a lamp and a switch. State whether current can pass from one of the crossing wires to the other at that point, and explain why.
exercises.answer: No, current cannot pass between them at that point.
exercises.full_solution: A crossing with no dot means the two wires simply pass over each other with no electrical contact; only a drawn dot (or an explicit join) makes a crossing into a real junction.

exercises.statement: A string of decorative fairy lights is wired so that if one bulb fails, the whole string goes dark; a household's wall sockets are wired so that one socket failing does not affect the others. Using only the ideas of nodes and shared connections from this lesson, explain which of the two is more likely to be wired in series and which in parallel.
exercises.answer: The fairy lights are wired in series (so each bulb shares exactly one node with the next, and a broken bulb breaks the only path for every bulb after it); the household sockets are wired in parallel (so each socket's own branch shares its pair of nodes with the supply, and a fault in one branch leaves the others' complete paths untouched).
exercises.full_solution: The fairy lights are wired in series (so each bulb shares exactly one node with the next, and a broken bulb breaks the only path for every bulb after it); the household sockets are wired in parallel (so each socket's own branch shares its pair of nodes with the supply, and a fault in one branch leaves the others' complete paths untouched).

exam_questions.statement: A technician describes a circuit: 'a battery is connected to a lamp and a motor, which are connected one after another with no branch between them; a switch is included so the whole circuit can be turned off; an ammeter measures the current reaching the motor.' (a) Draw, in words, the order of symbols around the loop. (b) State where exactly the ammeter must be placed to measure the current reaching the motor.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Battery symbol, then switch symbol, then lamp symbol, then motor symbol, joined one after another around a single loop back to the battery, with the ammeter inserted in series directly next to the motor. (b) The ammeter must be placed in series, in the main loop, directly next to the motor, so the same current that reaches the motor also passes through the ammeter.
exam_questions.full_solution: Because every component here is joined one after another with no branch, every point on the loop (including wherever the ammeter sits) carries the same current, so 'in series, somewhere on this loop' is enough to guarantee the ammeter reads the current reaching the motor.
mark_scheme: States the correct order of symbols around the single loop.
Includes the switch in the loop so the circuit can be turned off.
States that the ammeter is connected in series, not in parallel.
Explains that, on this unbranched loop, the current is the same everywhere, so any series position gives the motor's current.
common_errors: Placing the ammeter in parallel across the motor instead of in series.

exam_questions.statement: A diagram shows an LED connected in a simple loop with a cell, a switch and a resistor, but the LED does not light when the switch is closed. Tracing the loop from the cell's positive terminal, the LED's triangle symbol points back the way you came, towards the positive terminal. (a) Explain why the LED does not light. (b) State the single change needed to make it light, without changing any other component.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The LED is connected in its reverse direction: conventional current, which flows from the positive terminal around the loop, is trying to flow against the direction the triangle points, so the LED does not conduct and does not light. (b) Reverse the LED's connection in the loop, so its triangle points in the same direction as the conventional current flowing from the cell's positive terminal.
exam_questions.full_solution: An LED only conducts in its forward direction, the direction its triangle points; reversing its connection, with every other component unchanged, restores a direction in which it can conduct and emit light.
mark_scheme: States that the LED is connected the wrong way round (reverse direction).
Links this correctly to conventional current direction from the cell's positive terminal.
States that an LED does not conduct in reverse at these voltages.
States the single fix: reverse the LED's connection, changing nothing else.
common_errors: Suggesting the resistor or cell is faulty, instead of identifying the LED's direction as the cause.

mcq.stem: A circuit diagram shows two wires crossing on the page, with no dot drawn where they cross. What does this crossing mean?

options.text: One wire passes over the other with no electrical connection between them.
The two wires are joined at that point, forming a junction.
options.why_wrong: a junction (an actual electrical join) is shown by drawing a dot at the crossing; without that dot, the wires are not connected.

options.text: The two wires are joined only if both carry the same current.
options.why_wrong: whether two wires are joined is a drawing convention (a dot or its absence), not something that depends on the size of the current flowing in each wire.

options.text: The crossing is only possible if a component is drawn at that point.
options.why_wrong: wires are allowed to cross with no connection and no component at that point; the crossing simply shows the wires occupy the same point on the page, not in the real circuit.

mcq.explanation: Without a dot or an explicit join marked at the crossing, the two wires simply cross with no electrical connection; a dot is always needed to show a real junction.

mcq.stem: The same cell and two lamps, joined one after another with no branch, are drawn first as a rectangle and then redrawn as an L-shaped loop with two corners. What has changed about the circuit's arrangement?

options.text: The circuit has become parallel, because the shape is no longer a simple rectangle.
options.why_wrong: confuses the physical outline of the drawing with the node connections, which decide series or parallel and have not changed here.

options.text: Nothing: the node connections are unchanged, so it is the identical series circuit.
The resistance of each lamp has increased because the wire is now longer.
options.why_wrong: assumes redrawing a diagram changes a physical property of a component, which it cannot do.

options.text: It cannot be decided without knowing the physical length of each wire.
options.why_wrong: wrongly treats wire length as relevant to series/parallel arrangement, when only the node connections matter.

mcq.explanation: Series or parallel is decided entirely by which nodes each component shares, never by the physical shape or size of the drawing; here the node sequence is identical in both diagrams.

mcq.stem: Where should a voltmeter be connected to measure the potential difference across a single resistor in a circuit?

options.text: In series, inserted directly into the main loop next to the resistor.
options.why_wrong: is how an ammeter is connected; a voltmeter connected this way would nearly stop the current in the whole loop, because of its very high resistance.

options.text: Anywhere in the circuit, since a voltmeter always reads the supply voltage.
options.why_wrong: ignores that a voltmeter reads the potential difference between the two points it is actually connected to, not a fixed value regardless of placement.

options.text: As a separate branch, joining the two nodes of the resistor.
In series, but only if the ammeter is removed from the loop first.
options.why_wrong: still places the voltmeter in series, which is the wrong connection regardless of whether an ammeter is also present.

mcq.explanation: A voltmeter is always a separate branch across the two nodes of the component it measures, leaving the main loop and the resistor itself unchanged.

mcq.stem: An LED in a simple loop with a working cell does not conduct and gives no light, but it conducts and lights as soon as the LED alone is turned round. What had happened?

options.text: The LED has been connected in parallel instead of in series.
options.why_wrong: describes a different kind of wiring fault; an LED in parallel with another component could still conduct in its forward direction.

options.text: The circuit has too high a resistance for any LED to light.
options.why_wrong: is not supported by the question, which gives no resistance value and specifically describes a direction-related failure to conduct.

options.text: The cell has been connected with its terminals reversed, which has no effect on an LED.
options.why_wrong: contradicts the fact that reversing the cell would also reverse the direction current tries to flow through the LED, which does matter.

options.text: The LED has been connected in its reverse direction, against the way its triangle points.

mcq.explanation: An LED conducts, and emits light, only in its forward direction, the direction its triangle symbol points; connected the other way round, no current flows and no light is emitted.

flashcards.front: What is the standard symbol for a fixed resistor, and how does the variable resistor symbol differ from it?
flashcards.back: A fixed resistor is a plain rectangle; a variable resistor is the same rectangle with a diagonal arrow drawn across it, showing its resistance can be adjusted.

flashcards.front: What decides whether two components are in series or in parallel in a circuit diagram?
flashcards.back: Only the nodes they connect to: series components share exactly one node with no other branch there; parallel components share the identical pair of nodes. The drawn shape of the diagram has no effect.

flashcards.front: Two wires cross on a diagram with no dot drawn at the crossing. Are they connected?
flashcards.back: No. Without a dot (or an explicit join), a crossing means the wires simply pass over each other with no electrical contact.

flashcards.front: How does an ammeter's connection differ from a voltmeter's connection, even though both are drawn as a circle with a letter inside?
flashcards.back: An ammeter is connected in series, inserted directly into the loop it measures; a voltmeter is connected in parallel, as a separate branch across the component it measures.

flashcards.front: An LED does not light when a switch is closed, although the cell, switch and resistor are all working. What is the most likely cause, and what single change fixes it?
flashcards.back: The LED is almost certainly connected in its reverse direction. Reversing the LED's own connection in the loop, with nothing else changed, should let it conduct and light.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Two wires that cross on the page are always electrically connected at that point.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: On paper, two lines crossing look like a single joined shape, so it is natural to read a crossing as a junction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner treats a circuit as branched wherever two drawn lines cross, even when no dot marks a connection there.
misconceptions.correct_model: Two crossing wires are connected only if a solid dot (or an explicit join) is drawn at the crossing point; without it, one wire simply passes over or under the other with no electrical contact.
misconceptions.remediation: Before tracing any circuit, circle every dot on the diagram first, then trace paths using only those dots as junctions, ignoring every crossing without one.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Whether two components are in series or in parallel depends on the shape the diagram is drawn in, such as a straight line versus a loop.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A series circuit is usually first seen drawn as a simple rectangle, so that physical shape gets mistaken for the defining feature instead of the connections themselves.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says a circuit's arrangement has changed because it was redrawn in a different shape, even though every wire and junction is identical.
misconceptions.correct_model: Series or parallel is decided only by which components share both of their connection nodes with each other, never by the physical shape, size or orientation of the drawing.
misconceptions.remediation: Redraw the same circuit in an unfamiliar shape and check that the node-by-node connections, not the outline, are unchanged.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A voltmeter can be inserted anywhere in a circuit, in the same way an ammeter is inserted into a loop.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both instruments are drawn as a circle with a letter inside, so it is easy to assume they are interchangeable in how they connect.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws a voltmeter broken into the main loop in series, which removes the very component the voltmeter was meant to measure.
misconceptions.correct_model: A voltmeter is always connected in parallel, directly across the two nodes of the single component being measured, leaving the main loop with the component still in place.
misconceptions.remediation: Before drawing a voltmeter, identify the two nodes of the component it measures, then draw the voltmeter as an extra branch joining exactly those two nodes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating every crossing of two wires on a diagram as a junction.
common_mistakes.why: A crossing looks visually like a joined point, even when no electrical connection is intended there.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Only trust a dot (or an explicit join) as a junction; a plain crossing with no dot is never a connection.

common_mistakes.mistake: Deciding series or parallel from the physical shape of the diagram rather than the node connections.
common_mistakes.why: A series circuit is usually first met drawn as a simple rectangle, so that shape gets mistaken for the defining feature.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Identify every node first, then decide series or parallel from which components share which nodes, ignoring the outline completely.

common_mistakes.mistake: Connecting a voltmeter in series, in the same way an ammeter is connected.
common_mistakes.why: Both instruments share the same circle-with-letter symbol style, which can suggest they connect the same way.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Identify the two nodes of the component you want to measure, then draw the voltmeter as a separate branch joining exactly those two nodes.

exam_notes: Use exactly the symbol shown in the syllabus and this course for each component; a near-miss symbol (for example, a triangle instead of a rectangle for a resistor) can cost marks even if the rest of the diagram is correct.
When asked to identify series or parallel, state the node argument explicitly (which components share which nodes), rather than describing the diagram's shape.
A question about an LED not lighting almost always expects a direction (forward/reverse) answer, not a resistance or voltage answer, unless resistance values are explicitly given.

summary.big_idea: A circuit diagram records only which components connect to which nodes, not the shape it is drawn in; every component is drawn with a standard symbol fixed by convention, so any two people reading it agree on what it means.
key_points: Every required component (cell, battery, switch, fixed/variable resistor, lamp, heater, ammeter, voltmeter, motor, fuse) has one fixed symbol, used consistently.
A crossing of two wires is a connection only if a dot is drawn there; without a dot, the wires simply pass over each other.
Series or parallel is decided entirely by shared nodes, never by the physical shape the loop is drawn in.
An ammeter is always in series in the loop it measures; a voltmeter is always in parallel, across the component it measures.
A generator symbol (circle containing G) and an LED's direction-sensitive diode symbol are Supplement additions to the Core symbol set.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Trace a circuit by its nodes, never by its drawn shape: a dot means a connection, no dot means none, and series/parallel follows only from which components share which nodes.

epistemic_overrides.note: Simplified/ideal model used for GCSE level

08_Series_and_parallel_networks.json.title: Series and parallel networks
08_Series_and_parallel_networks.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Construct and interpret series and parallel circuits, calculate the total resistance of resistors in series, and explain why lamps connected in parallel can work independently of one another.
State the current (junction) and potential-difference laws for series and parallel networks, and calculate the equivalent resistance of two resistors connected in parallel.

prerequisites.statement: Read a circuit diagram by its nodes, and distinguish a series connection (one shared node, no other branch there) from a parallel connection (both nodes shared).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every rule in this lesson depends on first telling series from parallel correctly; a wrong series/parallel call makes the resistance rule applied afterwards wrong as well.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate current, voltage and resistance for a single component using $I=V/R$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Series and parallel rules combine several single-component relationships into a whole network; without a secure $I=V/R$, a network calculation cannot be checked at any step.

theory_blocks.title: One road or several: series and parallel branches
theory_blocks.body:
Imagine charge flowing around a circuit the way traffic flows along roads. A [[blue:**series**]] arrangement is a single road with no junctions: every vehicle that enters must pass every point on that road, one after another, so the same flow rate is measured anywhere along it. A [[orange:**parallel**]] arrangement is a junction where the road splits into two or more separate roads that later rejoin: traffic leaving the junction divides between the roads, and whatever each road carries recombines once they meet again.

This single picture explains both of this lesson's rules at once. On an unbranched road (series), there is only one flow rate to measure, so it must be the same everywhere. At a junction (parallel), each road is a separate route between the same two places, so anything travelling along either road experiences the same change in height (p.d.) between those two places, even though the two roads might carry different amounts of traffic.

theory_blocks.title: Series networks: one current, added resistances
theory_blocks.body:
In a series circuit, every component lies on the same single unbranched path, so three facts follow directly:
