1. **The current is the same at every point** on the path, because there is nowhere else for charge to go.
2. **The individual potential differences add up to the supply p.d.**, because together they account for all the energy transferred per unit charge around the complete loop.
3. **The total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances**: $R_{\text{total}}=R_1+R_2+\cdots$, because each extra resistor in the one path makes it harder, overall, for the same current to be driven around that path.

For example, $3\,\Omega$ and $5\,\Omega$ in series give $R_{\text{total}}=3\,\Omega+5\,\Omega=8\,\Omega$. Driven by a $16\,\mathrm{V}$ supply, the current is $I=16\,\mathrm{V}\div8\,\Omega=2\,\mathrm{A}$, the same $2\,\mathrm{A}$ at every point on the loop.

theory_blocks.title: Same current does not mean same voltage
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to assume that, because the current is the same everywhere in series, the voltage must be too. It is not. Each component still obeys $V=IR$ on its own, so with the same current $I$ flowing through every component, [[blue:a component with a larger resistance gets a larger share of the p.d.]], and [[orange:a component with a smaller resistance gets a smaller share]].

For the $3\,\Omega$ and $5\,\Omega$ example above, both carry the same $2\,\mathrm{A}$, but the p.d.s are $2\,\mathrm{A}\times3\,\Omega=6\,\mathrm{V}$ and $2\,\mathrm{A}\times5\,\Omega=10\,\mathrm{V}$: different values that add to the $16\,\mathrm{V}$ source p.d., exactly as the series rule for voltage requires. The two series facts are not interchangeable: current is shared equally because there is only one path; voltage is shared in proportion to resistance, not equally, unless the resistances themselves happen to be equal.

theory_blocks.title: Parallel networks: shared p.d., independent branches
theory_blocks.body:
In a parallel arrangement, two or more branches connect the identical pair of nodes. Because both ends of every branch sit at the same two points, **every branch has the same p.d. across it**, equal to the p.d. between those two shared nodes, regardless of what resistance each branch has.

The current leaving the supply divides between the branches, with more current taking the branch of lower resistance, and the separate branch currents recombine once the branches rejoin. This has a direct practical consequence: because each branch is a separate complete path between the same two nodes, **one branch can be broken, or removed, without disturbing the p.d. across the other branches at all**. This is exactly why household lamps are wired in parallel: if one lamp's filament breaks, every other lamp still has the full supply p.d. across it and keeps working normally, whereas a single lamp failing in a series string would break the only path and switch every lamp off.

Extra branches also make the whole arrangement easier for the supply to drive current through, so **the combined resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than that of either resistor by itself** — always less, even than the smaller of the two. Expect this before you work anything out; the calculation that puts a number on it is in the next block.

assets.caption: Left: a series network, nodes A, B and C, with $R_1$ then $R_2$ on the single path; the same current flows at A, B and C. Right: a parallel network, both $R_1$ and $R_2$ share nodes A and B, so both see the same p.d.; the supply current divides between them.
assets.purpose: Make the node-sharing difference between series and parallel directly visible, labelling the shared nodes that the formal rules in this lesson depend on.

theory_blocks.title: Going further: the junction law and two resistors in parallel
theory_blocks.body:
The splitting and recombining of current described above is itself a law: at any junction, the total current arriving equals the total current leaving, so for two branches, $I_{\text{total}}=I_1+I_2$. Combined with $V=IR$ applied to each branch (both branches share the same p.d., call it $V$), this gives $I_1=V/R_1$ and $I_2=V/R_2$, so
$$\frac{V}{R_{\text{total}}}=\frac{V}{R_1}+\frac{V}{R_2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}}=\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}.$$
For two resistors this rearranges to $R_{\text{total}}=\dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}$.

For example, $6\,\Omega$ and $3\,\Omega$ in parallel give $\dfrac{1}{R_{\text{total}}}=\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $R_{\text{total}}=2\,\Omega$. Notice this is smaller than either branch alone ($2\,\Omega<3\,\Omega<6\,\Omega$): adding a second path can only make it easier, overall, for current to flow, never harder, so a parallel equivalent resistance is always less than the smallest individual branch resistance. Always predict this direction before calculating, and treat a result that is not smaller than the smallest branch as a sign of an arithmetic error.

keywords.definition: An arrangement in which components lie on a single unbranched path, so the same current flows through all of them and their p.d.s add to the supply p.d.
An arrangement in which two or more branches connect the identical pair of nodes, so every branch has the same p.d. across it and the supply current divides between the branches.
The total current arriving at a junction equals the total current leaving it; for two branches, $I_{\text{total}}=I_1+I_2$.
The single resistance that would draw the same total current, from the same supply p.d., as a whole network of resistors.

worked_examples.statement: **Two resistors in series.** A $3\,\Omega$ resistor and a $5\,\Omega$ resistor are connected in series across a $16\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Find the current in the circuit and the p.d. across each resistor.
reasoning: Add the series resistances: $R_{\text{total}}=3\,\Omega+5\,\Omega=8\,\Omega$.
Use $I=V/R$ on the whole loop, then $V=IR$ on each resistor separately, using the same current for both since they are in series.
worked_examples.solution: $I=16\,\mathrm{V}\div8\,\Omega=2\,\mathrm{A}$. Across the $3\,\Omega$ resistor, $V_1=2\,\mathrm{A}\times3\,\Omega=6\,\mathrm{V}$; across the $5\,\Omega$ resistor, $V_2=2\,\mathrm{A}\times5\,\Omega=10\,\mathrm{V}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $6\,\mathrm{V}+10\,\mathrm{V}=16\,\mathrm{V}$, the full supply p.d., even though the two individual p.d.s are different from each other.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the $16\,\mathrm{V}$ splits equally, giving $8\,\mathrm{V}$ across each resistor, instead of in proportion to each resistor's own resistance.

worked_examples.statement: **A parallel lamp fails.** Two identical $8.0\,\Omega$ lamps are connected in parallel across a $12\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. (a) Find the current in each lamp and the total current from the supply. (b) One lamp's filament breaks, leaving an open gap in that branch. State the p.d. across the remaining lamp and its current, and explain what happens to its brightness.
reasoning: Both lamps share the same pair of nodes, so both have the full $12\,\mathrm{V}$ across them.
Use $I=V/R$ on each lamp separately, then add the two branch currents for the total.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Each lamp carries $I=12\,\mathrm{V}\div8.0\,\Omega=1.5\,\mathrm{A}$; total current $=1.5\,\mathrm{A}+1.5\,\mathrm{A}=3.0\,\mathrm{A}$. (b) The remaining lamp's branch is unaffected: it still has the full $12\,\mathrm{V}$ across it, so it still carries $1.5\,\mathrm{A}$ and its brightness does not change; only the total current from the supply falls, to $1.5\,\mathrm{A}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the direct reason lamps are wired in parallel in a building: each branch's p.d. depends only on the shared nodes, not on whether another branch is still working.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the remaining lamp gets dimmer, or stops working, because 'half the circuit is broken', instead of checking that its own branch and its own p.d. are unaffected.

worked_examples.statement: **Predict, then calculate: two resistors in parallel.** A $6.0\,\Omega$ resistor and a $3.0\,\Omega$ resistor are connected in parallel. Before calculating, predict whether the equivalent resistance will be smaller or larger than $3.0\,\Omega$. Then calculate the equivalent resistance and check your prediction.
reasoning: Prediction: a second parallel path gives current an extra route, so the combined resistance must be smaller than the smaller branch, $3.0\,\Omega$.
Apply $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/R_1+1/R_2$.
worked_examples.solution: $\dfrac{1}{R_{\text{total}}}=\dfrac{1}{6.0}+\dfrac{1}{3.0}=\dfrac{1}{2.0}$, so $R_{\text{total}}=2.0\,\Omega$.
worked_examples.interpretation: $2.0\,\Omega$ is indeed smaller than both $3.0\,\Omega$ and $6.0\,\Omega$, confirming the prediction and giving a built-in check on the arithmetic.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Adding the two resistances directly to get $9.0\,\Omega$, a value larger than either branch, which the prediction step would have flagged as impossible.

worked_examples.statement: **A mixed network.** A $5.0\,\Omega$ resistor is connected in series with a parallel pair of two $4.0\,\Omega$ resistors. The combination is connected across a $14\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Find (a) the equivalent resistance of the parallel pair, (b) the total resistance of the whole network, (c) the total current from the supply, and (d) the current in each of the two parallel resistors.
reasoning: Combine the parallel pair first: $1/R_p=1/4.0+1/4.0=1/2.0$, so $R_p=2.0\,\Omega$.
Add this to the series resistor to get the total resistance of the whole network.
Use $I=V/R$ on the whole network for the total current, which is also the current through the $5.0\,\Omega$ resistor.
The p.d. across the parallel pair is the total current times $R_p$; divide this by $4.0\,\Omega$ for each branch, since the two parallel resistors are equal.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $R_p=2.0\,\Omega$. (b) $R_{\text{total}}=5.0\,\Omega+2.0\,\Omega=7.0\,\Omega$. (c) $I=14\,\mathrm{V}\div7.0\,\Omega=2.0\,\mathrm{A}$. (d) P.d. across the parallel pair $=2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times2.0\,\Omega=4.0\,\mathrm{V}$; each $4.0\,\Omega$ branch carries $4.0\,\mathrm{V}\div4.0\,\Omega=1.0\,\mathrm{A}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: the two branch currents, $1.0\,\mathrm{A}+1.0\,\mathrm{A}=2.0\,\mathrm{A}$, recombine to the full $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ that passed through the series resistor, exactly as the junction law requires.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Trying to add the $5.0\,\Omega$ series resistor directly to one of the $4.0\,\Omega$ parallel resistors, instead of first reducing the whole parallel pair to its single equivalent resistance.

guided_exercises.statement: A $2.0\,\Omega$ resistor and a $6.0\,\Omega$ resistor are connected in series across a $4.0\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Find the total resistance and the current in the circuit.
hints: Add the two series resistances to find the total resistance.
Apply $I=V/R$ to the whole loop using that total resistance.
Check by confirming that $I\times R_{\text{total}}$ recovers the $4.0\,\mathrm{V}$ supply.
guided_exercises.answer: $R_{\text{total}}=2.0\,\Omega+6.0\,\Omega=8.0\,\Omega$; $I=4.0\,\mathrm{V}\div8.0\,\Omega=0.50\,\mathrm{A}$.
common_errors: Forgetting to add both resistances and using only one of them in $I=V/R$.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Add the two series resistances to find the total resistance.

**Step 2 — Method:** Apply $I=V/R$ to the whole loop using that total resistance.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $R_{\text{total}}=2.0\,\Omega+6.0\,\Omega=8.0\,\Omega$; $I=4.0\,\mathrm{V}\div8.0\,\Omega=0.50\,\mathrm{A}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check by confirming that $I\times R_{\text{total}}$ recovers the $4.0\,\mathrm{V}$ supply.

guided_exercises.statement: Two identical $10\,\Omega$ resistors are connected in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance, and state how it compares with the resistance of a single $10\,\Omega$ resistor.
hints: Use $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/R_1+1/R_2$ with both resistances equal to $10\,\Omega$.
Predict, before calculating, that the answer should be smaller than $10\,\Omega$.
Compare your final value with $10\,\Omega$ directly.
guided_exercises.answer: $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/10+1/10=1/5$, so $R_{\text{total}}=5.0\,\Omega$: exactly half of a single $10\,\Omega$ resistor, since the two equal branches share the current equally.
common_errors: Adding the two $10\,\Omega$ resistances to get $20\,\Omega$, which is larger rather than smaller than a single branch.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Use $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/R_1+1/R_2$ with both resistances equal to $10\,\Omega$.

**Step 2 — Method:** Predict, before calculating, that the answer should be smaller than $10\,\Omega$.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/10+1/10=1/5$, so $R_{\text{total}}=5.0\,\Omega$: exactly half of a single $10\,\Omega$ resistor, since the two equal branches share the current equally.

**Step 4 — Check:** Compare your final value with $10\,\Omega$ directly.

exercises.statement: Two identical $2.0\,\Omega$ lamps are connected in series across a $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Find the total resistance and the current in the circuit.
exercises.answer: $R_{\text{total}}=2.0\,\Omega+2.0\,\Omega=4.0\,\Omega$; $I=6.0\,\mathrm{V}\div4.0\,\Omega=1.5\,\mathrm{A}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $1.5\,\mathrm{A}\times4.0\,\Omega=6.0\,\mathrm{V}$.

exercises.statement: A $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor and a $12\,\Omega$ resistor are connected in parallel across a $12\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Find (a) the equivalent resistance, (b) the current in each resistor, and (c) the total current from the supply.
exercises.answer: (a) $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/4.0+1/12=1/3.0$, so $R_{\text{total}}=3.0\,\Omega$. (b) $I_1=12\,\mathrm{V}\div4.0\,\Omega=3.0\,\mathrm{A}$; $I_2=12\,\mathrm{V}\div12\,\Omega=1.0\,\mathrm{A}$. (c) $I_{\text{total}}=3.0\,\mathrm{A}+1.0\,\mathrm{A}=4.0\,\mathrm{A}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $R_{\text{total}}=3.0\,\Omega$ is smaller than the smaller branch ($4.0\,\Omega$), as expected; and $12\,\mathrm{V}\div3.0\,\Omega=4.0\,\mathrm{A}$ matches the sum of the two branch currents.

exercises.statement: Without calculating a value, state whether connecting a second, different resistor in parallel with an existing $5.0\,\Omega$ resistor will make the combined resistance larger than $5.0\,\Omega$, smaller than $5.0\,\Omega$, or impossible to say without more information. Justify your answer.
exercises.answer: Smaller than $5.0\,\Omega$.
exercises.full_solution: Adding a second branch in parallel always gives current an extra path between the same two nodes, which can only make it easier overall for current to flow, so the equivalent resistance must fall below the smaller of the two branch resistances; since $5.0\,\Omega$ is one of the branches, the combined value must be below it, whatever the second resistance turns out to be.

exercises.statement: A simple torch can be built from two identical cells and two identical bulbs in two different ways: wiring the two bulbs in series, or wiring them in parallel, with the two cells always providing a fixed total e.m.f. Using only the series and parallel rules from this lesson, explain which wiring gives each bulb a bigger share of the available p.d., and which wiring keeps a bulb lit if the other bulb's filament breaks.
exercises.answer: Wiring the bulbs in parallel gives each bulb the full available p.d. (since both share the same two nodes), while wiring them in series splits the p.d. between the two bulbs, giving each one less than the full amount. Parallel wiring also keeps the working bulb lit if the other one's filament breaks, because its branch and its p.d. are unaffected; series wiring would switch both bulbs off, because the broken filament removes the only path for current.
exercises.full_solution: Wiring the bulbs in parallel gives each bulb the full available p.d. (since both share the same two nodes), while wiring them in series splits the p.d. between the two bulbs, giving each one less than the full amount. Parallel wiring also keeps the working bulb lit if the other one's filament breaks, because its branch and its p.d. are unaffected; series wiring would switch both bulbs off, because the broken filament removes the only path for current.

exam_questions.statement: A $2.0\,\Omega$, a $3.0\,\Omega$ and a $5.0\,\Omega$ resistor are connected in series across a $20\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. (a) Calculate the total resistance of the circuit. (b) Calculate the current in the circuit. (c) State the current through the $3.0\,\Omega$ resistor, giving a reason.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $R_{\text{total}}=2.0\,\Omega+3.0\,\Omega+5.0\,\Omega=10\,\Omega$. (b) $I=20\,\mathrm{V}\div10\,\Omega=2.0\,\mathrm{A}$. (c) $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$, the same as the circuit current, because all three resistors lie on the one unbranched path and so carry the same current.
exam_questions.full_solution: Check: $2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times10\,\Omega=20\,\mathrm{V}$, the full supply p.d.
mark_scheme: Adds the three series resistances correctly: $10\,\Omega$.
Applies $I=V/R$ correctly: $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$.
States the current through the $3.0\,\Omega$ resistor as $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$.
Gives the correct reason: series components share the same single path, so the same current.
common_errors: Calculating a separate, smaller current for the $3.0\,\Omega$ resistor using only its own resistance and the full $20\,\mathrm{V}$, instead of recognising it shares the one series current.

exam_questions.statement: A $6.0\,\Omega$ resistor and a $3.0\,\Omega$ resistor are connected in parallel across a $9.0\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. (a) Calculate the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination. (b) Calculate the current in each resistor. (c) Calculate the total current drawn from the supply, and show that it is consistent with your answer to (a).
exam_questions.answer: (a) $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/6.0+1/3.0=1/2.0$, so $R_{\text{total}}=2.0\,\Omega$. (b) $I_1=9.0\,\mathrm{V}\div6.0\,\Omega=1.5\,\mathrm{A}$; $I_2=9.0\,\mathrm{V}\div3.0\,\Omega=3.0\,\mathrm{A}$. (c) Total current $=1.5\,\mathrm{A}+3.0\,\mathrm{A}=4.5\,\mathrm{A}$, which matches $9.0\,\mathrm{V}\div2.0\,\Omega=4.5\,\mathrm{A}$ found directly from the equivalent resistance.
exam_questions.full_solution: This double route to the total current, once from adding the branch currents and once from the equivalent resistance, is exactly the consistency check the junction law guarantees.
mark_scheme: Equivalent resistance $=2.0\,\Omega$ (A1).
Current in the $6.0\,\Omega$ resistor $=9.0\,\mathrm{V}\div6.0\,\Omega=1.5\,\mathrm{A}$ (B1).
Current in the $3.0\,\Omega$ resistor $=9.0\,\mathrm{V}\div3.0\,\Omega=3.0\,\mathrm{A}$ (B1).
Total current $=1.5\,\mathrm{A}+3.0\,\mathrm{A}=4.5\,\mathrm{A}$ (B1).
Shows consistency: $9.0\,\mathrm{V}\div2.0\,\Omega=4.5\,\mathrm{A}$, the same total (B1).
common_errors: Adding $6.0\,\Omega$ and $3.0\,\Omega$ directly to get $9.0\,\Omega$ for part (a), which does not match the current calculated in part (c).

challenge_questions.statement: A $6.0\,\Omega$ resistor is connected in series with a parallel pair of a $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor and a $12\,\Omega$ resistor. The whole network is connected across an $18\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Find the current in each of the three resistors, and show that the two parallel branch currents are consistent with the current through the $6.0\,\Omega$ resistor.
hints: Reduce the $4.0\,\Omega$ and $12\,\Omega$ parallel pair to a single equivalent resistance first.
Add that equivalent resistance to the $6.0\,\Omega$ series resistor to find the total resistance, then find the total current.
Use the total current to find the p.d. across the parallel pair, then find each branch's current from that shared p.d.
challenge_questions.answer: Parallel pair: $1/R_p=1/4.0+1/12=1/3.0$, so $R_p=3.0\,\Omega$. Total resistance $=6.0\,\Omega+3.0\,\Omega=9.0\,\Omega$. Total current (through the $6.0\,\Omega$ resistor) $=18\,\mathrm{V}\div9.0\,\Omega=2.0\,\mathrm{A}$. P.d. across the parallel pair $=2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times3.0\,\Omega=6.0\,\mathrm{V}$. Current in the $4.0\,\Omega$ branch $=6.0\,\mathrm{V}\div4.0\,\Omega=1.5\,\mathrm{A}$; current in the $12\,\Omega$ branch $=6.0\,\mathrm{V}\div12\,\Omega=0.50\,\mathrm{A}$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Check: $1.5\,\mathrm{A}+0.50\,\mathrm{A}=2.0\,\mathrm{A}$, exactly the current through the $6.0\,\Omega$ series resistor, confirming the junction law across the whole network.

mcq.stem: Three lamps are connected one after another with no branch, forming a single series loop. An ammeter at one point reads $0.80\,\mathrm{A}$. What does an ammeter read if moved to a point further around the same loop?

options.text: $0.80\,\mathrm{A}$, the same reading.
Less than $0.80\,\mathrm{A}$, because some current has been used up by the lamps already passed.
options.why_wrong: treats current as a quantity that gets used up, when in fact the same current passes every point on an unbranched loop.

options.text: More than $0.80\,\mathrm{A}$, because more lamps add more current.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes extra series components add current, when in a single unbranched loop there is only one current value throughout.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing each lamp's resistance.
options.why_wrong: is unnecessary information here: the series rule that current is the same everywhere on one unbranched loop needs no resistance values at all.

mcq.explanation: On a single unbranched series loop, the same current passes every point, so the ammeter reads the identical $0.80\,\mathrm{A}$ wherever it is placed on that loop.

mcq.stem: A $2.0\,\Omega$ resistor and an $8.0\,\Omega$ resistor are connected in series. Which statement about the p.d. across each resistor is correct?

options.text: The p.d.s must be equal, because the current through both is equal.
options.why_wrong: over-generalises the series current rule to voltage; p.d. depends on each resistor's own resistance, not only on the shared current.

options.text: The p.d. across the $8.0\,\Omega$ resistor is larger than across the $2.0\,\Omega$ resistor.
The p.d. across the $2.0\,\Omega$ resistor is larger than across the $8.0\,\Omega$ resistor.
options.why_wrong: has the comparison backwards: with the same current, a larger resistance gives a larger p.d., by $V=IR$, not a smaller one.

options.text: Neither resistor has a p.d. across it, because the supply p.d. is used up entirely by the connecting wires.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the supply p.d. is shared between the two resistors themselves, not consumed by the wires, which are treated as having no resistance here.

mcq.explanation: Both resistors carry the same series current, so by $V=IR$ the resistor with the larger resistance ($8.0\,\Omega$) has the larger p.d. across it; the two p.d.s are not equal unless the resistances are equal.

mcq.stem: A $5.0\,\Omega$ resistor and a $20\,\Omega$ resistor are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?

options.text: $25\,\Omega$
options.why_wrong: adds the two resistances directly, as in series, which gives a value larger than either branch and cannot be correct for a parallel combination.
averages the two resistances instead of applying $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/R_1+1/R_2$; the correct result must be smaller than the smaller branch, $5.0\,\Omega$, and $12.5\,\Omega$ is not.
equals the smaller branch exactly, which would mean the second branch carries no current at all; a genuine second path must reduce the combined resistance below $5.0\,\Omega$.

mcq.explanation: $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/5.0+1/20=4/20+1/20=5/20=1/4.0$, so $R_{\text{total}}=4.0\,\Omega$, smaller than both branch resistances, as expected for a parallel combination.

mcq.stem: Two identical lamps are connected in parallel across a battery. One lamp's filament breaks. What happens to the other lamp?

options.text: It goes out too, because the circuit is now broken.
options.why_wrong: describes what would happen in series, not in parallel, where the remaining branch is a separate complete path.

options.text: It becomes dimmer, because it now has to share the battery's energy with the broken lamp.
options.why_wrong: misapplies a series-style sharing idea; the broken branch simply stops carrying current, it does not take a 'share' from the working branch.

options.text: It becomes brighter, because all the available current now flows through it.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes current is a fixed total that must all go somewhere; the remaining lamp's own p.d. and resistance set its own current, unchanged by the other branch failing.

options.text: It keeps working exactly as before, because its own branch and its own p.d. are unaffected.

mcq.explanation: Because both lamps share the same two nodes, the p.d. across the working lamp does not depend on whether the other branch is intact; it keeps the same current and the same brightness.

flashcards.front: In a series circuit, what stays the same at every point, and what is shared between components?
flashcards.back: The current stays the same at every point; the supply p.d. is shared between the components in proportion to each one's own resistance.

flashcards.front: How do you find the equivalent resistance of two resistors connected in parallel?
flashcards.back: $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/R_1+1/R_2$, which for two resistors rearranges to $R_{\text{total}}=R_1R_2/(R_1+R_2)$; the result is always smaller than the smaller of the two resistances.

flashcards.front: Does current 'divide up' and get used along a series loop, so a component further from the supply gets less of it?
flashcards.back: No. A series loop is a single unbranched path, so exactly the same current passes every point on it, however far from the supply.

flashcards.front: Compare how series and parallel arrangements respond when one component fails (breaks completely).
flashcards.back: In series, one broken component removes the only path, so every component on that loop stops working. In parallel, a broken branch leaves the other branches' p.d. and current unaffected, so they keep working normally.

flashcards.front: A $4.0\,\Omega$ resistor already has current flowing through it. A second resistor is added in parallel with it. Does the combined resistance rise or fall, and why?
flashcards.back: It falls, below $4.0\,\Omega$, because the second branch gives current an extra path between the same two nodes, which can only make it easier overall for current to flow.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: In a series circuit, the current divides between the components, so a component further from the supply receives less current.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Current is often pictured as a fixed quantity of 'stuff' leaving the supply that gets shared out, by analogy with a fixed amount of water or sweets handed around.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a lower ammeter reading at a point further around a series loop than at a point closer to the supply.
misconceptions.correct_model: In a series circuit there is only one path, so exactly the same current passes every point on that path; current is not a fixed quantity that gets shared out, it is a rate that stays constant all the way around an unbranched loop.
misconceptions.remediation: Place an ammeter at several different points on the same series loop (in explanation or in a real measurement) and confirm the reading does not change.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: In a series circuit, the potential difference is always the same across every component.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners over-generalise the true series rule for current (always the same) to voltage as well, without checking that voltage sharing instead depends on each component's resistance.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner assumes two different resistors in series must have equal p.d.s across them.
misconceptions.correct_model: In series, the current is the same everywhere, but the p.d. across each component depends on its own resistance ($V=IR$ for that component); the individual p.d.s add up to the supply p.d., and are equal only if the resistances happen to be equal.
misconceptions.remediation: Calculate the p.d. across two unequal series resistors carrying the same current and show the two values are different, even though they add to the supply p.d.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel is found by adding the two resistances together, the same way as in series.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Adding resistances works for series, so it feels natural to apply the same single operation to parallel without checking whether it still gives a sensible answer.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner adds two parallel resistances directly and does not notice that the result is larger than either branch alone, which cannot be correct for extra parallel paths.
misconceptions.correct_model: Adding a second parallel branch gives current an extra path, so the combined resistance to the supply must fall, not rise; for two resistors in parallel, $1/R=1/R_1+1/R_2$, and the result is always smaller than the smaller of the two branch resistances.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating, predict whether the equivalent resistance should be larger or smaller than the smallest branch, then calculate it and check the prediction holds.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating current as a quantity that gets shared out or used up along a series loop.
common_mistakes.why: Current is easy to picture as a fixed amount of 'stuff' handed around, like a fixed number of sweets.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember current is a rate, not a stored quantity: on one unbranched path, that rate is the same measured anywhere.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming p.d. is always shared equally between series components, the way current is always equal.
common_mistakes.why: The genuinely correct series rule for current gets over-generalised to voltage without checking it against $V=IR$.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate each component's p.d. separately from $V=IR$ using its own resistance, and only expect equal p.d.s if the resistances themselves are equal.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding two parallel resistances directly, the same way as in series.
common_mistakes.why: Series addition is the first resistance-combining rule learned, so it gets applied automatically to parallel as well.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Predict the direction first (parallel equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest branch), then use $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/R_1+1/R_2$, and check the result is smaller than expected.

exam_notes: When asked for current 'at a named point' in a series circuit, state clearly that it equals the one series current, with a one-line reason (single unbranched path), rather than recalculating from scratch.

For a parallel resistance question, always show the predicted direction (smaller than the smallest branch) as a check alongside the calculation; an examiner can award method marks even if the final arithmetic slips.
A mixed series-parallel network must be reduced step by step: combine the parallel section into one equivalent resistance first, then treat the network as a simple series circuit.

summary.big_idea: Series and parallel are two different ways branches can share nodes, and each sharing pattern fixes, by itself, what must stay the same (current in series, p.d. in parallel) and what must instead be calculated (p.d. in series, equivalent resistance in parallel).
key_points: Series: the same current flows everywhere on the one unbranched path; resistances add, $R_{\text{total}}=R_1+R_2+\cdots$; p.d.s add to the supply p.d. but are not generally equal.
Parallel: every branch shares the same p.d., because both ends of every branch are the same two nodes; the supply current divides between the branches and recombines.
A parallel equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest individual branch resistance; for two resistors, $1/R_{\text{total}}=1/R_1+1/R_2$.
A broken branch in parallel leaves the other branches unaffected; a broken component in series stops the whole loop.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Series shares current equally and voltage by resistance; parallel shares voltage equally and current by resistance; a parallel combination is always easier to flow through than its smallest single branch.

09_Electrical_safety.json.title: Electrical safety
09_Electrical_safety.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe how excess current heats a cable and name the mains hazards of damaged insulation, overheating, dampness and overloading; choose a suitable fuse or trip-switch rating for a stated appliance; and explain how earthing or double insulation protects a user from a fault in the case of an appliance.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate current from power and voltage using $I=P/V$.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Choosing a fuse rating starts with knowing the appliance's normal working current, which this lesson calculates from its power rating rather than measuring directly.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise circuit symbols for a switch and a fuse, and state that a switch or a broken fuse interrupts the one path it sits on.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A fuse or trip switch protects by breaking the circuit; that only makes sense once interrupting a path is already a familiar idea.

prerequisites.statement: State that branch currents add at a junction, so a fault current can take a path separate from the normal working current.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Earthing works by giving a fault current an extra, very low-resistance branch to follow; understanding that a junction can carry more than one current path is needed before that mechanism makes sense.

theory_blocks.title: Current always heats a cable; the question is how much
theory_blocks.body:
[[blue:Any current passing through a cable's resistance transfers some electrical energy into heat]], exactly as it does in the heating element of a toaster or a kettle, just normally by a far smaller, harmless amount. A mains hazard begins whenever something pushes that heating effect, or the risk of a live conductor being exposed, beyond what is safe: damaged insulation can expose a live conductor directly; a damp environment can let current pass somewhere it should not; and drawing more current than a cable or a plug is rated for (overloading, for example by plugging too many high-power appliances into one socket) makes that ordinary heating effect large enough to damage the cable or start a fire.

None of these hazards needs a dramatic fault to begin: a frayed cable, a kettle used in a wet kitchen, or one extension lead carrying several kettles and heaters at once are all everyday situations where the same current-heating and exposed-conductor effects become dangerous rather than negligible.

theory_blocks.title: Choosing a fuse: above normal current, below fault current
theory_blocks.body:
A fuse is a thin wire, placed in the live wire's path, that melts and breaks the circuit once the current through it is too large; a trip switch (circuit breaker) does the same job without needing to be replaced afterwards. Choosing the right rating is a balance: it must sit **above** the appliance's normal working current, so it does not blow during ordinary use, but **low enough** to interrupt the much larger current that a genuine fault would cause.

The normal working current is found from $I=P/V$ using the appliance's power rating. For example, an appliance rated at $2300\,\mathrm{W}$ on a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply draws $I=2300\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}=10\,\mathrm{A}$ normally. If the only ratings available are $5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$, the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would blow immediately during completely normal use, since $10\,\mathrm{A}>5\,\mathrm{A}$; the $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse is the only one of the two that both survives normal use and still interrupts a current large enough to be dangerous.

theory_blocks.title: Earthing and double insulation protect in different ways
theory_blocks.body:
Two different strategies protect a user from a fault inside an appliance's case:

- **Earthing** connects a metal case to the ground with a very low-resistance wire. If a fault connects the live wire to the case, this low-resistance path carries a very large fault current, far above the fuse's rating, which blows the fuse (or trips the breaker) almost immediately and disconnects the live supply before a person could be harmed by touching the case.
- **Double insulation** avoids the problem a different way: the appliance has no conducting case at all that a fault could reach; every part a user could touch is separated from any live conductor by non-conducting material, so there is nothing for a fault to make dangerous in the first place, and no earth wire is needed.

Both strategies are complete solutions on their own: an earthed metal-cased appliance and a correctly double-insulated plastic-cased appliance are both considered safe, but mixing the two ideas up, for example assuming a plastic-cased appliance also needs an earth wire, or that a metal case is safe without either protection, is a genuine safety error.

assets.caption: A live wire with damaged insulation touches an earthed metal case. The earth wire gives the resulting fault current a low-resistance path to the ground, and this large current blows the fuse in the live wire, disconnecting the supply.
assets.purpose: Make the complete fault-current path, from the point of damage through the case and earth wire back to the fuse, visible as a single traceable loop, directly supporting the earthing explanation in the theory and countering the related idea and the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: What a fuse does not do, and what the earth wire does not carry
theory_blocks.body:
[[blue:A fuse protects by breaking the live wire's path, nothing more]]: it has no direct effect on a case, and cannot prevent a fault from occurring, only remove the current that would make an existing fault dangerous. It also cannot protect at all if it is fitted in the neutral wire instead of the live wire, since a broken neutral alone would still leave the case connected to the live supply through the fault.

[[orange:The earth wire carries no current while an appliance works normally]]: its only job is to be ready, as a very low-resistance path, for the moment a fault connects a live conductor to the case. Treating it as just another working conductor, or assuming an unearthed metal case is safe simply because the appliance currently works, both ignore that the earth wire's entire purpose is to handle a fault that has not happened yet.

keywords.definition: A thin wire in the live wire's path that melts and breaks the circuit when the current through it exceeds its rating.
A switch that automatically opens the circuit when the current through it is too large, and can be reset afterwards without replacement.
Connecting a conducting case to the ground with a low-resistance wire, so a live-to-case fault drives a large current that blows the fuse quickly.
Protecting a user by ensuring no touchable part of an appliance can ever be connected to a live conductor, removing the need for an earth wire.

worked_examples.statement: **Sizing a fuse for a toaster.** A toaster is rated at $920\,\mathrm{W}$ on a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Available fuse ratings are $3\,\mathrm{A}$ and $5\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate the toaster's normal working current and state which fuse rating is suitable.
reasoning: Find the normal working current using $I=P/V$.
Choose the smallest available rating that is still above this current, so the fuse survives normal use.
worked_examples.solution: $I=920\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}=4.0\,\mathrm{A}$. The $3\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would blow during ordinary use, since $4.0\,\mathrm{A}>3\,\mathrm{A}$, so the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse is the suitable choice.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $5\,\mathrm{A}>4.0\,\mathrm{A}>3\,\mathrm{A}$, confirming the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse is the smallest rating that still survives normal operation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Choosing the larger rating 'to be safe' without checking that the smaller rating would already fail during normal use, which is a separate, necessary test.

worked_examples.statement: **Sizing a fuse for a heater.** An electric heater is rated at $2300\,\mathrm{W}$ on a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Available fuse ratings are $5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate the heater's normal working current, state which fuse is suitable, and explain what would happen if the other rating were fitted instead.
reasoning: Find the normal working current using $I=P/V$.
Compare this current with each available rating before choosing.
worked_examples.solution: $I=2300\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}=10\,\mathrm{A}$. The $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse is suitable, since $13\,\mathrm{A}>10\,\mathrm{A}$. Fitting the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse instead would blow it immediately during completely normal use, since the heater's own working current, $10\,\mathrm{A}$, already exceeds $5\,\mathrm{A}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: A fuse rated below the appliance's own normal current can never work at all: it would blow the instant the appliance is switched on, with no fault present.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming a lower-rated fuse is always 'more protective', without checking that it must first survive the appliance's genuinely normal operating current.

worked_examples.statement: **What is the earth wire doing right now?** A metal-cased, earthed kettle is plugged in, switched on, and boiling water completely normally. Explain what current, if any, is flowing in its earth wire at this moment, and explain when that would change.
knowns: kettle operating completely normally, metal case, earthed
unknowns: current in the earth wire during normal operation
reasoning: The earth wire is not part of the path that powers the heating element; current for normal operation flows only in the live and neutral wires.
The earth wire's only purpose is to provide a path if the case becomes connected to the live wire by a fault.
worked_examples.solution: No current flows in the earth wire while the kettle operates normally; it carries current only if a fault connects the live wire to the case, at which point a large fault current flows briefly through the earth wire until the fuse blows.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the direct answer to treating the earth wire as 'just another working wire': its entire job only begins at the moment something has already gone wrong.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the earth wire must be carrying some current whenever the appliance is switched on, because it is physically part of the same cable as the live and neutral wires.

worked_examples.statement: **An unearthed fault.** A metal-cased appliance has no earth wire and is not double insulated. A live wire inside works loose and touches the case. (a) State what happens to the case as a result. (b) Explain why the fuse in the live wire does not blow at this point. (c) Explain the danger this creates for a user who then touches the case while also touching something connected to the ground.
knowns: metal case, no earth wire, not double insulated
unknowns: why the fuse does not blow
reasoning: With no earth wire, there is no low-resistance path from the case to the ground for a fault current to take.
The fuse only blows if the current through the live wire becomes large; without an extra path, the fault alone may not draw a current large enough to do that.
worked_examples.solution: (a) The case becomes connected to the live wire, so the whole case becomes live (at mains potential), even though the appliance may appear to work normally. (b) With no earth wire providing a low-resistance path, the fault does not, by itself, draw a current large enough to exceed the fuse's rating, so the fuse stays intact and gives no warning. (c) A user touching the live case while also touching something connected to the ground (for example, a metal pipe, or simply standing on damp ground) completes a path for current through their own body, which can cause a dangerous electric shock.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is exactly the danger earthing exists to prevent: without it, the fault is silent (no blown fuse, no obvious sign) right up until a person's body completes the dangerous path instead of the earth wire.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the fuse must always blow whenever a fault occurs, regardless of whether a low-resistance earth path exists to drive a large enough fault current through it.

guided_exercises.statement: A bedside lamp is rated at $60\,\mathrm{W}$ on a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Available fuse ratings are $3\,\mathrm{A}$, $5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate the lamp's normal working current and state which fuse rating is the most suitable, giving a reason.
hints: Use $I=P/V$ to find the normal working current first.
Compare this current with the smallest available rating.
The most suitable fuse is the smallest rating that still survives normal use, since it interrupts a fault current soonest.
guided_exercises.answer: $I=60\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}\approx0.26\,\mathrm{A}$. Even the smallest available rating, $3\,\mathrm{A}$, is comfortably above this, so $3\,\mathrm{A}$ is the most suitable choice: it survives normal use and interrupts a fault at the lowest current of the three options.
common_errors: Choosing the largest rating available by default, without checking whether a smaller rating would already be more than enough.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Use $I=P/V$ to find the normal working current first.

**Step 2 — Method:** Compare this current with the smallest available rating.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $I=60\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}\approx0.26\,\mathrm{A}$. Even the smallest available rating, $3\,\mathrm{A}$, is comfortably above this, so $3\,\mathrm{A}$ is the most suitable choice: it survives normal use and interrupts a fault at the lowest current of the three options.

**Step 4 — Check:** The most suitable fuse is the smallest rating that still survives normal use, since it interrupts a fault current soonest.

guided_exercises.statement: A plastic-cased hairdryer has no earth pin on its plug; a metal-cased washing machine has a three-pin plug with a connected earth wire. Explain why each appliance is designed this way.
hints: Ask whether each appliance has a conducting case that a fault could reach.
Recall the two different protection strategies covered in this lesson.
State which strategy applies to each appliance and why the other would be unnecessary or insufficient for it.
guided_exercises.answer: The hairdryer is double insulated: its casing is non-conducting, so no fault inside it can make an outer surface live, and an earth wire would serve no purpose. The washing machine has a metal case, which a fault could make live, so it needs an earth wire to give any fault current a low-resistance path that blows the fuse quickly.
common_errors: Assuming every mains appliance needs an earth wire, rather than checking whether its case is conducting in the first place.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Ask whether each appliance has a conducting case that a fault could reach.

**Step 2 — Method:** Recall the two different protection strategies covered in this lesson.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The hairdryer is double insulated: its casing is non-conducting, so no fault inside it can make an outer surface live, and an earth wire would serve no purpose. The washing machine has a metal case, which a fault could make live, so it needs an earth wire to give any fault current a low-resistance path that blows the fuse quickly.

**Step 4 — Check:** State which strategy applies to each appliance and why the other would be unnecessary or insufficient for it.

exercises.statement: An iron is rated at $1150\,\mathrm{W}$ on a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Available fuse ratings are $3\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate the iron's normal working current and state which fuse rating is suitable.
exercises.answer: $I=1150\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}=5.0\,\mathrm{A}$. The $3\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would blow during normal use, since $5.0\,\mathrm{A}>3\,\mathrm{A}$, so the $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse is the suitable choice from the two offered.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $13\,\mathrm{A}>5.0\,\mathrm{A}>3\,\mathrm{A}$, so only the $13\,\mathrm{A}$ rating survives normal use.

exercises.statement: State two everyday causes, other than a sudden short circuit, that can make a mains cable or socket hazardous, and explain briefly how each one does so.
exercises.answer: Example answer: damaged or frayed insulation can expose a live conductor that a person might touch directly; a damp environment can let current pass through paths, including a person's body, that are normally too resistive to carry it.
exercises.full_solution: A third acceptable cause is overloading a socket or extension lead with too many high-power appliances, which draws more current than the cable is rated for and increases the heating effect in the cable itself.

exercises.statement: Explain, in terms of fault current, why an earthed metal case is safe to touch during a live-to-case fault, while an unearthed metal case is not.
exercises.answer: With earthing, the fault drives a very large current through the low-resistance earth path, which blows the fuse almost immediately and disconnects the live supply before the case stays dangerous for long. Without earthing, there is no such low-resistance path, so the fault current may never become large enough to blow the fuse, leaving the case live and dangerous indefinitely, with no warning.
exercises.full_solution: The key difference is not whether a fault can happen, which is possible either way, but whether a safe, automatic path exists to turn that fault into a fuse blowing rather than a person being shocked.

exercises.statement: A single extension lead, rated to carry a maximum of $13\,\mathrm{A}$ safely, has a kettle ($2300\,\mathrm{W}$), a heater ($2000\,\mathrm{W}$) and a toaster ($920\,\mathrm{W}$) all plugged into it and switched on at the same time, all on a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Using the current-heating idea from this lesson, explain why this is hazardous, even though each appliance has its own correctly rated fuse inside its own plug.
exercises.answer: The three appliances together draw $I=(2300+2000+920)\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}\approx22.7\,\mathrm{A}$ through the single extension lead, nearly double its $13\,\mathrm{A}$ rating. Even though each appliance's own plug fuse is correctly sized for that one appliance, none of them individually draws enough current to blow its own fuse, so nothing trips; it is the lead itself, carrying all three currents combined, that is overloaded and at risk of overheating.
exercises.full_solution: The three appliances together draw $I=(2300+2000+920)\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}\approx22.7\,\mathrm{A}$ through the single extension lead, nearly double its $13\,\mathrm{A}$ rating. Even though each appliance's own plug fuse is correctly sized for that one appliance, none of them individually draws enough current to blow its own fuse, so nothing trips; it is the lead itself, carrying all three currents combined, that is overloaded and at risk of overheating.

exercises.statement: A kitchen ring circuit runs from a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ mains supply. At its busiest a kettle ($2300\,\mathrm{W}$), a microwave oven ($1150\,\mathrm{W}$) and a dishwasher ($2070\,\mathrm{W}$) are all drawing current at the same time. The consumer unit can be fitted with a trip switch set to $6\,\mathrm{A}$, $16\,\mathrm{A}$ or $32\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate the largest current the circuit must carry in normal use, and state which trip-switch setting should be fitted, with a reason.
exercises.answer: Total power $=2300\,\mathrm{W}+1150\,\mathrm{W}+2070\,\mathrm{W}=5520\,\mathrm{W}$, so the current is $I=5520\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}=24\,\mathrm{A}$. The $6\,\mathrm{A}$ and $16\,\mathrm{A}$ settings would both trip during completely normal use, since $24\,\mathrm{A}>16\,\mathrm{A}>6\,\mathrm{A}$, so the $32\,\mathrm{A}$ setting is the one to fit: it is above the normal working current, but still low enough to cut off the much larger current a genuine fault would cause.
exercises.full_solution: A trip switch is chosen by exactly the same rule as a fuse — above the normal working current, below the fault current — and the normal working current of a whole circuit is found by adding the powers of everything that can be on at once before dividing by the supply p.d. The difference is only what happens afterwards: a trip switch is reset, while a blown fuse has to be replaced.

exercises.statement: In a correctly wired appliance, both the fuse and the on/off switch are placed in the live wire. Explain why fitting either of them in the neutral wire instead would leave the appliance dangerous, even though it would still switch on and off normally.
exercises.answer: Breaking the neutral wire does stop the current, so the appliance stops working, but the live wire is still joined to the inside of the appliance. Everything it reaches, including a metal case that a loose live wire is touching, stays at the live supply potential, so anyone touching it provides a path to earth and receives a shock. Only breaking the live wire disconnects the appliance from that potential, which is why the fuse and the switch both belong there.
exercises.full_solution: This is also why a fuse fitted in the neutral wire gives no real protection: it may well melt during a fault, but what it disconnects is the return path, not the dangerous one.

exam_questions.statement: A metal-cased washing machine is correctly earthed. A live wire inside works loose and touches the case. (a) Describe the path the resulting fault current takes. (b) Explain why this current is large. (c) Explain how this protects a user who touches the case shortly afterwards.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The fault current flows from the live wire, through the point of contact, into the case, along the earth wire, and down to the ground. (b) The earth wire has a very low resistance, so for a given p.d. this path allows a very large current to flow, far above the fuse's rated current. (c) This large current blows the fuse (or trips the breaker) almost immediately, disconnecting the live supply from the whole appliance before a user has time to be harmed by touching the case.
exam_questions.full_solution: The chain is: fault touches the case, earth wire gives it a low-resistance path, large current blows the fuse, supply is disconnected, case is no longer live.
mark_scheme: Describes the fault current path from live wire, through the case, along the earth wire, to the ground.
States that the earth wire's low resistance is why the fault current is large.
Links the large current to the fuse (or trip switch) correctly.
States that this disconnects the supply before the user is harmed.
States that the case is then no longer live (it is at earth potential), so a user touching it does not receive a shock.
common_errors: Describing the fuse as acting directly on the user's safety, rather than on the current through the live wire.

exam_questions.statement: A workshop heater is rated at $2530\,\mathrm{W}$ on a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Fuse ratings of $5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$ are available. (a) Calculate the heater's normal working current. (b) State which fuse rating should be fitted, with a reason. (c) Explain what would happen if the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse were fitted instead, and what would happen if a $30\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse were fitted instead.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $I=2530\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}=11\,\mathrm{A}$. (b) The $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse, because it is above the heater's normal working current of $11\,\mathrm{A}$ and so survives normal use, while still being low enough to interrupt a genuine fault current. (c) The $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would blow immediately during completely normal operation, since $11\,\mathrm{A}>5\,\mathrm{A}$; a $30\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would survive normal use but might not interrupt a fault quickly enough, since it allows a much larger, more dangerous current to keep flowing before it blows.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $I=2530\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}=11\,\mathrm{A}$. (b) The $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse, because it is above the heater's normal working current of $11\,\mathrm{A}$ and so survives normal use, while still being low enough to interrupt a genuine fault current. (c) The $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would blow immediately during completely normal operation, since $11\,\mathrm{A}>5\,\mathrm{A}$; a $30\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would survive normal use but might not interrupt a fault quickly enough, since it allows a much larger, more dangerous current to keep flowing before it blows.
mark_scheme: Uses $I=P/V$: $2530\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}$ (C1).
Selects the $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse with a reason referring to the normal current.
Explains that the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse would blow during normal operation.
Explains that a much higher rating would allow a larger, more dangerous fault current before interrupting it.
Normal working current $=11\,\mathrm{A}$ (A1).
common_errors: Choosing the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse because 'lower is always safer', without checking it against the calculated normal current first.

mcq.stem: What does a correctly rated fuse actually do when a fault causes a dangerously large current?

options.text: It melts and breaks the live wire's path, removing the supply from the appliance.
It senses that the casing has become dangerous and insulates the casing directly.
options.why_wrong: describes the fuse as acting on the casing itself, when a fuse only ever acts on the current through the live wire it sits in.

options.text: It reduces the current to a safe level without breaking the circuit.
options.why_wrong: misses that a fuse protects by breaking the circuit completely, not by limiting current while current continues to flow.

options.text: It redirects the dangerous current safely into the neutral wire.
options.why_wrong: invents a redirecting function a fuse does not have; a fuse interrupts its own path, it does not reroute current elsewhere.

mcq.explanation: A fuse is a thin wire in the live wire's path that melts and breaks that path once the current through it is too large, removing the supply from the whole appliance.

mcq.stem: An earthed, metal-cased appliance is switched on and working completely normally. What current is flowing in its earth wire at this moment?

options.text: The same current as in the live wire, since all three wires are part of one circuit.
options.why_wrong: wrongly treats the earth wire as carrying the same working current as the live and neutral wires, when it normally carries none at all.

options.text: None, because the earth wire is not part of the path that powers the appliance during normal operation.
A small, constant background current, lower than the live wire's current.
options.why_wrong: invents a background current with no physical basis; the earth wire carries current only if a fault occurs, not a reduced version of normal current.

options.text: It depends on the appliance's power rating.
options.why_wrong: wrongly links the earth wire's current to the appliance's power, when in normal operation the earth wire carries no current regardless of power rating.

mcq.explanation: The earth wire carries no current during normal operation; its only role is to provide a low-resistance path if a fault later connects the live wire to the case.

mcq.stem: A kettle is rated at $2000\,\mathrm{W}$ on a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Fuse ratings of $3\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$ are available. Which fuse should be fitted?

options.text: The $3\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse, because a lower rating is always safer.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the kettle's own normal current, about $8.7\,\mathrm{A}$, already exceeds $3\,\mathrm{A}$, so this fuse would blow during ordinary use.

options.text: Either fuse, since both will protect the kettle equally well.
options.why_wrong: overlooks that the $3\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse cannot even survive the kettle's normal operation, so it is not a working option at all.

options.text: The $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse, because it is above the kettle's normal working current.
Neither; a kettle needs a fuse rated below $1\,\mathrm{A}$ for proper protection.
options.why_wrong: proposes a rating far below the kettle's own normal current, which would make the kettle unable to run at all.

mcq.explanation: The kettle draws $I=2000\,\mathrm{W}\div230\,\mathrm{V}\approx8.7\,\mathrm{A}$ normally; only the $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse is above this value, so only it survives normal use while still protecting against a larger fault current.

mcq.stem: A hairdryer has a plastic casing with no metal parts a user could touch, and no earth pin on its plug. Why is this design safe?

options.text: Plastic conducts electricity poorly enough that a fault current is always small.
options.why_wrong: misdescribes the mechanism: the plastic casing is not a poor conductor carrying a small fault current, it is a non-conducting barrier that a fault cannot reach through to a touchable surface at all.

options.text: The missing earth pin automatically makes the appliance's internal voltage lower.
options.why_wrong: confuses the presence or absence of an earth pin with the appliance's operating voltage, which is unaffected by whether an earth wire is fitted.

options.text: A hairdryer draws too little current for any fault to be dangerous.
options.why_wrong: is not the real reason; double insulation protects regardless of the current a fault might otherwise draw, by preventing any touchable surface from becoming live.

options.text: The plastic casing means no fault inside can ever make an outer touchable surface live, so no earth path is needed.

mcq.explanation: Double insulation works by ensuring no touchable part is ever connected to a live conductor, even if an internal fault occurs, so there is no live case for an earth wire to protect against in the first place.

flashcards.front: Name four everyday causes of electrical hazard mentioned in this lesson.
flashcards.back: Damaged or frayed insulation; a damp environment; overheating; overloading a cable, socket or extension lead with too much current.

flashcards.front: What two conditions must a correctly chosen fuse rating satisfy?
flashcards.back: It must be above the appliance's normal working current, so it survives ordinary use, and low enough to interrupt a genuine fault current before it becomes dangerous.

flashcards.front: How much current flows in the earth wire of a correctly working, earthed appliance?
flashcards.back: None. The earth wire carries current only if a fault connects the live wire to the case; in normal operation it carries nothing at all.

flashcards.front: Compare how earthing and double insulation each protect a user from an internal fault.
flashcards.back: Earthing gives a fault current a low-resistance path that blows the fuse quickly, removing the live supply from a conducting case. Double insulation prevents any touchable surface from ever being connected to a live conductor, so no earth path is needed at all.

flashcards.front: An appliance's own normal working current is $9\,\mathrm{A}$. Fuse ratings of $5\,\mathrm{A}$ and $13\,\mathrm{A}$ are available. Which should be fitted, and why?
flashcards.back: The $13\,\mathrm{A}$ fuse, because $9\,\mathrm{A}$ already exceeds the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ rating, which would blow during completely normal use.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A fuse protects a user by somehow acting on the appliance's casing directly, wherever the user might touch it.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A fuse is only ever discussed in the context of safety, so it is easy to picture it as a general safety device rather than a specific component doing one specific job.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a fuse as 'stopping the case from being dangerous' rather than as a component that breaks the live wire's path when the current through it is too large.
misconceptions.correct_model: A fuse is a thin wire placed in the live wire's path; it protects only by melting and breaking that one path when the current through it exceeds its rating, which then removes the supply from the whole appliance. It has no effect on the casing directly: it only removes the current that could make the casing dangerous in the first place.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace the live wire's path through the fuse to the appliance and back, and show that melting the fuse breaks this path completely, so no current (and so no danger from current) can reach the appliance's internal fault at all.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The earth wire is a normal working conductor, carrying current during an appliance's ordinary operation, just like the live and neutral wires.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: All three wires in a mains cable look identical and are grouped together, so it is natural to assume they all do the same kind of job.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes the earth wire as part of the normal circuit that powers the appliance.
misconceptions.correct_model: In normal operation, no current flows in the earth wire at all; it carries current only if a fault connects the live wire to the case, and even then only briefly, until the resulting large fault current blows the fuse or trips the breaker.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the earth wire's role directly with the live and neutral wires: ask what each one is doing while the appliance works perfectly normally, and show the earth wire's honest answer is 'nothing, unless something has already gone wrong'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A metal-cased appliance with no earth connection is safe as long as it is working normally.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Nothing seems wrong while the appliance runs normally, so the absence of an earth wire does not feel like it is doing any harm.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner judges an appliance's safety purely by whether it currently works, rather than by what would happen if a fault occurred.
misconceptions.correct_model: An unearthed metal case is safe only until an internal fault connects the live wire to it; with no earth wire and no double insulation, that fault would leave the whole case live and dangerous, with nothing to interrupt the circuit until a person completes the path to the ground themselves.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would happen, not what is happening: trace the consequence of a single internal wire touching the case, with and without an earth wire present, and compare the two outcomes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a fuse as acting directly on an appliance's casing, rather than on the current in the live wire.
common_mistakes.why: A fuse is always discussed in the context of safety, so it is easy to picture it as a general safety device rather than one specific component doing one job.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Trace the live wire's actual path through the fuse and back, and describe the fuse's effect only in terms of breaking that one path.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the earth wire as a normal working conductor that carries current whenever the appliance is switched on.
common_mistakes.why: All three mains wires look identical and are grouped in one cable, so it is tempting to assume they all do the same kind of job.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask what current flows in the earth wire during completely normal operation first (none), before describing what it does during a fault.

common_mistakes.mistake: Judging an unearthed metal-cased appliance as safe simply because it currently works without any problem.
common_mistakes.why: Nothing seems wrong while an appliance runs normally, so a missing earth connection does not feel like it is doing any harm.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask what would happen if an internal fault occurred, not just what is happening now, before judging an appliance's safety.

exam_notes: A fuse-sizing answer needs both halves of the argument: the chosen rating must be above the normal working current (calculated from $I=P/V$) and still low enough to interrupt a fault; stating only one half typically loses a mark.
An earthing explanation should name the complete chain: fault touches the case, the low-resistance earth path carries a large current, the large current blows the fuse, the supply is disconnected.
Do not introduce a residual-current device or any other protective device not covered in this lesson; stay with fuses, trip switches, earthing and double insulation.

summary.big_idea: Electrical safety devices do not prevent a fault from happening; they make sure that when one does, the dangerous current is interrupted, or never reaches a touchable surface, before it can harm a person.
key_points: Current always heats a cable; damaged insulation, dampness and overloading all push this ordinary effect, or the risk of an exposed live conductor, into dangerous territory.
A fuse rating must be above the appliance's normal working current (found from $I=P/V$) but low enough to interrupt a genuine fault.
Earthing gives a fault current a low-resistance path that blows the fuse quickly; it carries no current during normal operation.
Double insulation protects by ensuring no touchable surface can ever become live, so no earth wire is needed.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A correct fuse rating sits above normal current and below a dangerous fault current; earthing and double insulation are two separate, complete ways to stop a fault reaching a person, not two halves of one solution.

10_Induction_and_the_ac_generator.json.title: Induction and the a.c. generator
10_Induction_and_the_ac_generator.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe how a changing magnetic field linking a conductor induces an e.m.f., and state the factors that affect the size of the induced e.m.f.
Describe the construction and action of a rotating-coil a.c. generator, including its slip rings and brushes, and sketch the e.m.f.-time graph it produces.

prerequisites.statement: Describe a magnetic field as a region where a pole experiences force, and sketch field direction around a bar magnet.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Induction is described entirely in terms of a conductor's exposure to a magnetic field changing; without a working picture of what a field is, 'changing field linkage' has nothing to refer to.

prerequisites.statement: State that e.m.f. is the energy supplied per unit charge by a source, measured in volts.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A generator is a new kind of source of e.m.f.; recognising e.m.f. as a quantity already measured in volts, rather than a new idea entirely, lets this lesson focus on how that e.m.f. is produced.

theory_blocks.title: Induction needs change, not just a field
theory_blocks.body:
A magnetic field sitting still around a stationary conductor does nothing electrically, no matter how strong it is. What induces an e.m.f. is [[blue:**change**]]: either the conductor moves relative to the field, so it continuously meets new field lines (described as 'cutting' field lines), or the field linking a stationary conductor itself grows or shrinks over time. Either way, it is the changing exposure of the conductor to the field, not the field's mere presence, that does the work.

This is exactly why pushing a magnet into a coil deflects a sensitive meter connected to the coil while the magnet is moving, but the deflection returns to zero the instant the magnet stops, even though the magnet (and its field) are still right there inside the coil.

theory_blocks.title: What makes an induced e.m.f. bigger
theory_blocks.body:
Three factors increase the size of an induced e.m.f., and all three work by increasing how quickly the conductor's exposure to the field is changing:

- **Faster relative motion** (or a more rapidly changing field): pushing a magnet into a coil quickly induces a larger e.m.f. than pushing it in slowly.
- **A stronger magnetic field**: a stronger magnet induces a larger e.m.f. for the same motion, because the field changes by more for the same change in position.
- **More turns on the coil**: each turn has an e.m.f. induced in it by the same changing field, and a coil's turns add their individual e.m.f.s together, so more turns means a larger total e.m.f. for the same motion and field.

None of these factors needs a numerical formula at this level: it is enough to predict, for a described change to speed, field strength or number of turns, whether the induced e.m.f. increases or decreases.

theory_blocks.title: The rotating-coil generator
theory_blocks.body:
A simple a.c. generator rotates a coil continuously inside a magnetic field (or, equivalently, rotates a magnet inside a fixed coil). As the coil turns, its orientation relative to the field is constantly changing, so an e.m.f. is induced continuously, exactly as the induction rule above predicts for continuous relative motion.

Because the coil itself is turning, its two ends cannot be wired directly to a fixed external circuit without the wires twisting up. Instead, each end of the coil is connected to its own **slip ring**, a separate conducting ring that turns with the coil, and a fixed **brush** presses against each ring to maintain electrical contact with the external circuit as the rings turn beneath it. The slip rings are two separate, continuous rings: they do not reverse any connection themselves, and should not be confused with the split-ring commutator used in a motor (covered in a later lesson), which exists specifically to reverse a connection every half turn.

assets.caption: A simple rotating-coil generator: the coil turns between the N and S poles, and each end of the coil is connected to its own slip ring on the axle. A fixed brush presses on each ring, carrying the output to the external lamp circuit without twisting the leads.
assets.purpose: Show every named part of the generator (coil, two separate slip rings, brushes, external circuit) and make clear that the coil's two ends reach the external circuit through separate rings.

theory_blocks.title: Why the output alternates, and the e.m.f.-time graph
theory_blocks.body:
As the coil turns at a steady rate, its motion relative to the field reverses every half turn: a side of the coil moving one way relative to the field during the first half turn is moving the opposite way during the second half turn. Since the induced e.m.f.'s direction depends on the direction of this relative motion, the e.m.f. itself reverses direction every half turn, which is exactly why the generator's output is **alternating current**, not direct current.

Over one complete turn, the e.m.f.-time graph rises from zero to a positive peak, falls back through zero to a negative trough, and returns to zero, ready to repeat. The induced e.m.f. is zero exactly when the coil's sides are moving parallel to the field (momentarily not cutting any new field lines) and at its peak size when the coil's sides are moving perpendicular to the field (cutting field lines fastest).

The **period**, $T$, is the time for one complete cycle, related to the rotation frequency $f$ by $T=1/f$. A coil rotating at $50$ complete turns per second ($50\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the UK mains frequency) has $T=1/50\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.02\,\mathrm{s}$ for each cycle. Doubling the rotation speed to $100$ turns per second halves the period to $T=1/100\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.01\,\mathrm{s}$, so the graph completes twice as many cycles in the same stretch of time. Because the coil's sides now also cut the field lines twice as fast, each peak and trough is also higher (about twice the size): faster rotation gives both a higher frequency and a larger peak e.m.f.

assets.caption: The e.m.f.-time graph for a coil rotating at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$: two complete cycles in $0.04\,\mathrm{s}$, each cycle alternating between a positive half and a negative half, crossing zero every $0.01\,\mathrm{s}$.
assets.purpose: Show the alternating shape and the period numerically correctly to scale, directly countering the related idea (the graph staying positive) and giving a concrete reference for the period-frequency relationship.

theory_blocks.title: Reading the graph: where the coil is at each point
theory_blocks.body:
The e.m.f.-time graph is much easier to sketch, and to read, once you can say where the coil is at each point on it. Taking $T$ as the period, one complete turn always follows the same pattern.

- **E.m.f. zero.** The coil's plane is perpendicular to the field, so both of its sides are moving along the field lines rather than across them. For that instant no field lines are being cut, and the induced e.m.f. is zero. These are the points where the curve crosses the time axis: at $0$, $T/2$ and $T$.
- **E.m.f. at a peak.** A quarter of a turn later the coil's plane is parallel to the field, so its sides are moving straight across the field lines and cut them as fast as they can. The induced e.m.f. is at its largest size here: these are the crest and the trough of the curve, at $T/4$ and $3T/4$.

The crest and the trough are the same size but opposite in sign, because after half a turn the two sides of the coil have swapped places and each is now moving the opposite way through the field.

[[blue:When you are asked to sketch the graph for a faster rotation, change two things, not one]]: the period becomes shorter, so the cycles are squeezed up along the time axis, **and** every peak becomes larger, because the sides now cut the field lines faster at every instant.

assets.caption: The coil after $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ of a turn, lined up with the e.m.f.-time graph below. The red line is the coil seen end-on, the green arrows show how its two sides are moving, and the coil turns anticlockwise in this view. The e.m.f. is zero where the sides move along the field and at a peak where they move across it.
assets.purpose: Link each point on the e.m.f.-time graph to a definite coil orientation, which is how P4.5.2.2 is usually examined.

keywords.definition: The production of an e.m.f. in a conductor caused by a change in the magnetic field linking it, whether from relative motion or from a changing field strength.
A continuous conducting ring, turning with a generator's coil, that a fixed brush presses against to maintain electrical contact with an external circuit.
The time for one complete cycle of a repeating graph, related to frequency by $T=1/f$.
A current (or e.m.f.) that repeatedly reverses direction, as produced by a rotating-coil generator.

worked_examples.statement: **Magnet in, magnet still, magnet out.** A bar magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a sensitive centre-reading meter, held still inside the coil for several seconds, and then pulled back out. Describe what the meter shows during each of these three stages.
knowns: magnet pushed in, held still, then pulled out, coil connected to a sensitive meter
reasoning: An e.m.f. (and so a meter deflection) is induced only while the magnet's exposure to the coil is changing.
While the magnet is held still, nothing about the field linking the coil is changing, however strong the field is.
