worked_examples.solution: While the magnet moves in, the meter deflects one way. While the magnet is held still, the meter reads zero, even though the magnet is still inside the coil. While the magnet moves out, the meter deflects the other way.
worked_examples.interpretation: The meter's reading tracks change, not presence: it is zero exactly when nothing about the magnet's position relative to the coil is changing.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Expecting the meter to keep deflecting, or to settle on some nonzero steady reading, for as long as the magnet remains inside the coil.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing two set-ups.** Set-up A pushes a magnet into a coil of $100$ turns at a certain speed. Set-up B pushes an identical magnet, at the same speed, into a coil of $300$ turns. State which set-up induces the larger e.m.f., and explain why, then state what would happen to set-up A's e.m.f. if the same magnet were instead pushed in twice as fast.
knowns: set-up A: 100 turns; set-up B: 300 turns; same magnet, same speed
unknowns: which set-up gives the larger e.m.f.
effect of doubling the speed in set-up A
reasoning: More turns on a coil means each turn's individually induced e.m.f. adds to a larger total, for the same magnet and the same speed.
A faster relative motion increases the rate of change the coil experiences, independently of the number of turns.
worked_examples.solution: Set-up B (300 turns) induces the larger e.m.f., because its extra turns each add their own induced e.m.f. to the total while the magnet's speed and strength are unchanged. If set-up A's magnet were instead pushed in twice as fast, set-up A's own induced e.m.f. would increase, because faster relative motion means a faster rate of change of the coil's exposure to the field.
worked_examples.interpretation: The turns factor and the speed factor act independently: increasing either one increases the induced e.m.f., whether or not the other factor also changes.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the two coils must induce the same e.m.f. because the magnet and its speed are identical in both cases, overlooking that the number of turns is itself one of the factors that changes the size of the induced e.m.f.

worked_examples.statement: **Doubling the rotation speed.** A generator's coil rotates at $50$ complete turns per second. (a) State the period of its e.m.f.-time graph. (b) The rotation speed is doubled to $100$ complete turns per second. State the new period, and explain what this means for the graph over a fixed time interval such as $0.04\,\mathrm{s}$.
reasoning: Use $T=1/f$ to convert each rotation frequency to a period.
Compare how many complete cycles fit into the same fixed time interval at each period.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $T=1/50\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.02\,\mathrm{s}$. (b) At $100\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $T=1/100\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.01\,\mathrm{s}$: half the previous period. Over a fixed $0.04\,\mathrm{s}$ interval, the original graph shows $0.04\,\mathrm{s}\div0.02\,\mathrm{s}=2$ complete cycles, while the faster graph shows $0.04\,\mathrm{s}\div0.01\,\mathrm{s}=4$ complete cycles: twice as many in the same time. The peaks are also higher, because the coil now cuts the field lines faster.
worked_examples.interpretation: Doubling the rotation frequency halves the period and doubles how many complete alternations fit into any fixed stretch of time; because the coil also moves through the field faster, the peak e.m.f. increases too, so each cycle is both shorter and taller.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the period doubles along with the rotation speed, instead of recognising that a faster rotation completes each cycle in less time, so the period falls.

worked_examples.statement: **Where does a generator's electrical energy come from?** A hand-cranked torch uses a small generator, turned by a hand crank, to light an LED. (a) Name the energy transformation taking place. (b) Explain why cranking the handle faster makes the LED brighter. (c) Explain why the LED cannot be made arbitrarily bright simply by using a generator with more turns, without also increasing the mechanical energy supplied by the hand crank.
unknowns: limit on brightness from turns alone
reasoning: A generator transforms the mechanical energy put into turning its coil into electrical energy; it does not create energy from nothing.
More turns increase the induced e.m.f. for a given motion, but the electrical energy delivered still has to come from the mechanical work done turning the coil.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Mechanical (kinetic) energy, from the hand turning the crank, is transformed into electrical energy. (b) Cranking faster increases the rate of change the coil experiences, which increases the induced e.m.f. and so the power delivered to the LED, making it brighter. (c) More turns alone increase the induced e.m.f. for the same mechanical input, but the total electrical energy produced still cannot exceed the mechanical energy supplied by the hand crank; without also cranking harder or faster, the energy available to light the LED is still limited by that same mechanical energy input.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the direct answer to picturing a generator as creating electricity 'from nothing': every joule of electrical energy it delivers has to be accounted for by a joule of mechanical energy put in, consistent with conservation of energy.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating 'more turns' as a way to get more electrical energy for free, without noticing that the mechanical energy input has not changed.

guided_exercises.statement: A magnet is held completely still, fully inside a coil connected to a sensitive meter. State the meter's reading, and explain your answer using the idea of change.
hints: Ask what, if anything, is changing about the magnet's position or the field linking the coil.
Recall that induction needs a change in the conductor's exposure to the field, not just the field's presence.
State the reading as a specific value, not just 'small'.
guided_exercises.answer: The meter reads zero. Nothing about the magnet's position relative to the coil is changing, so there is no changing field linkage to induce an e.m.f., however strong the magnet's field is.
common_errors: Expecting a small but nonzero steady reading, rather than exactly zero, because the magnet and its field are still present.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Ask what, if anything, is changing about the magnet's position or the field linking the coil.

**Step 2 — Method:** Recall that induction needs a change in the conductor's exposure to the field, not just the field's presence.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The meter reads zero. Nothing about the magnet's position relative to the coil is changing, so there is no changing field linkage to induce an e.m.f., however strong the magnet's field is.

**Step 4 — Check:** State the reading as a specific value, not just 'small'.

guided_exercises.statement: Two identical coils, each wired to its own identical sensitive meter, have the same magnet pushed into each at the same speed. Coil 1 uses an ordinary bar magnet; coil 2 uses a stronger magnet of the same size and shape. State which meter shows the larger deflection, and explain why.
hints: Identify which of the three factors affecting induced e.m.f. (speed, field strength, number of turns) differs between the two set-ups.
Recall that a stronger field changes by more for the same change in position.
State your answer in terms of that one differing factor only.
guided_exercises.answer: Coil 2's meter shows the larger deflection, because its stronger magnet produces a larger induced e.m.f. for the same speed and the same coil, since the field linking the coil changes by more for the same motion.
common_errors: Assuming the deflections must be equal because the speed and the coils themselves are identical, overlooking that field strength is itself one of the three factors.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify which of the three factors affecting induced e.m.f. (speed, field strength, number of turns) differs between the two set-ups.

**Step 2 — Method:** Recall that a stronger field changes by more for the same change in position.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Coil 2's meter shows the larger deflection, because its stronger magnet produces a larger induced e.m.f. for the same speed and the same coil, since the field linking the coil changes by more for the same motion.

**Step 4 — Check:** State your answer in terms of that one differing factor only.

exercises.statement: State two different ways to increase the e.m.f. induced in a coil by a moving magnet, without changing how fast the magnet moves.
exercises.answer: Use a stronger magnet, or use a coil with more turns.
exercises.full_solution: Both of these increase the induced e.m.f. independently of the magnet's speed, which is the third, separate factor covered in this lesson.

exercises.statement: A small generator's coil rotates at $60$ complete turns per second. Calculate the period of its e.m.f.-time graph.
exercises.answer: $T=1/60\,\mathrm{Hz}\approx0.017\,\mathrm{s}$ (2 s.f.).
exercises.full_solution: Check: $60\,\mathrm{Hz}\times0.017\,\mathrm{s}\approx1$, consistent with one complete cycle occurring in that time.

exercises.statement: Describe, in terms of the coil's orientation relative to the magnetic field, when during one rotation the induced e.m.f. is (a) at its largest size and (b) exactly zero.
exercises.answer: (a) The e.m.f. is largest when the coil's sides are moving perpendicular to the field, cutting field lines fastest. (b) The e.m.f. is zero when the coil's sides are momentarily moving parallel to the field, cutting no new field lines at that instant.
exercises.full_solution: These two orientations occur twice each per complete rotation, which is exactly why the e.m.f.-time graph has two zero-crossings and two peaks (one positive, one negative) in every cycle.

exercises.statement: A bicycle dynamo works by induction: as the bicycle wheel turns, it rotates a small magnet near a fixed coil connected to the bike's light. Using the factors covered in this lesson, explain why cycling faster makes the light noticeably brighter, and why the light goes out completely the moment the bicycle stops.
exercises.answer: Cycling faster rotates the magnet faster, increasing the rate of change the coil experiences, which increases the induced e.m.f. and so the power delivered to the light, making it brighter. When the bicycle stops, the magnet stops moving relative to the coil, so nothing about the coil's exposure to the field is changing any longer, and the induced e.m.f. falls to zero immediately.
exercises.full_solution: Cycling faster rotates the magnet faster, increasing the rate of change the coil experiences, which increases the induced e.m.f. and so the power delivered to the light, making it brighter. When the bicycle stops, the magnet stops moving relative to the coil, so nothing about the coil's exposure to the field is changing any longer, and the induced e.m.f. falls to zero immediately.

exam_questions.statement: State three factors that affect the size of the e.m.f. induced in a coil, and explain, for each one, why increasing it increases the induced e.m.f.
exam_questions.answer: Speed of relative motion (or rate of change of the field): a faster change means the coil's exposure to the field changes more quickly. Strength of the magnetic field: a stronger field changes by more for the same change in position. Number of turns on the coil: each turn's own induced e.m.f. adds to the total, so more turns give a larger combined e.m.f. for the same motion and field.
exam_questions.full_solution: All three factors work through the same underlying idea: each one increases how quickly, or by how much, the coil's exposure to the field is changing.
mark_scheme: States speed of relative motion (or rate of field change) as a factor, with a correct reason.
States field strength as a factor, with a correct reason.
States number of turns as a factor, with a correct reason.
Links all three factors back to the general idea of a greater or faster change in exposure to the field.
common_errors: Listing a factor (for example, the coil's resistance) that does not actually affect the size of the induced e.m.f. itself.

exam_questions.statement: A student sketches a generator's e.m.f.-time graph as a curve that rises from zero to a peak and falls back to zero, staying at or above zero for the whole sketch. (a) Explain what is wrong with this sketch. (b) Describe the correct shape of the graph over one complete rotation. (c) Explain, in terms of the coil's motion, why the e.m.f. must become negative during part of each rotation.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The sketch is missing the negative half of the cycle: a generator's output genuinely reverses direction, it does not simply return to zero and repeat the same positive shape. (b) The correct graph rises from zero to a positive peak, falls back through zero to a negative trough, and returns to zero, repeating this full pattern every rotation. (c) The coil's motion relative to the field reverses every half turn, and since the induced e.m.f.'s direction depends on the direction of this relative motion, the e.m.f. itself must reverse sign during the second half of each rotation.
exam_questions.full_solution: The negative half of the graph is not an optional detail: it is the direct graphical signature of the coil's motion genuinely reversing every half turn, which is also exactly why the output is called alternating current.
mark_scheme: Identifies that the sketch wrongly omits the negative half of the cycle.
Describes the correct shape: positive peak, zero crossing, negative trough, zero crossing, repeating.
Links the sign change to the coil's motion relative to the field reversing every half turn.
States that the induced e.m.f. (and so the current) reverses direction, so the output is alternating (a.c.).
States that the positive peak and negative trough are equal in size and occur half a rotation apart (e.m.f. zero when the coil sides move parallel to the field).
common_errors: Describing the negative half as the e.m.f. 'decreasing' rather than genuinely reversing direction.

exam_questions.statement: A simple a.c. generator has a coil rotating at $25$ complete turns per second, and its e.m.f.-time graph has a peak e.m.f. of $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$. The coil is then driven so that it rotates at $50$ complete turns per second instead. (a) Calculate the period of the e.m.f.-time graph before and after the change. (b) State and explain two ways in which the new graph differs from the original.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Before: $T=1/f=1/25\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.04\,\mathrm{s}$. After: $T=1/50\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.02\,\mathrm{s}$, exactly half the original period. (b) First, each cycle now takes half as long, so the new graph fits twice as many complete cycles into the same stretch of time. Second, the peaks and troughs are about twice as large, roughly $12\,\mathrm{V}$ instead of $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$, because the coil's sides cut the field lines twice as fast, which increases the e.m.f. induced at every instant.
exam_questions.full_solution: The common slip is to squeeze the cycles up along the time axis but leave the peaks at $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$. Rotating faster changes both the period and the size of the induced e.m.f., because the rate at which field lines are cut is exactly what sets the e.m.f.
mark_scheme: Original period $T=1/25\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.04\,\mathrm{s}$.
New period $T=1/50\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.02\,\mathrm{s}$, half the original.
States that each cycle takes half as long, so twice as many complete cycles fit into the same time interval.
States that the peak e.m.f. is about twice as large, roughly $12\,\mathrm{V}$.
Explains the larger peak by the coil's sides cutting field lines faster, so a larger e.m.f. is induced at every instant.
common_errors: Changing only the period and drawing the new peaks at the same height as the original ones.

challenge_questions.statement: A generator's coil rotates at $50$ complete turns per second. (a) Calculate how many complete e.m.f. cycles occur in $0.20\,\mathrm{s}$. (b) The rotation speed is increased so that the period halves. Calculate how many complete cycles now occur in the same $0.20\,\mathrm{s}$, and state the new rotation frequency.
hints: Find the period at $50$ turns per second first, then divide the total time by that period.
Halving the period means doubling the frequency; use $T=1/f$ in reverse to find the new frequency.
Repeat the same division with the new, smaller period.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) $T=1/50\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.02\,\mathrm{s}$; number of cycles $=0.20\,\mathrm{s}\div0.02\,\mathrm{s}=10$. (b) New period $=0.01\,\mathrm{s}$, so new frequency $=1/0.01\,\mathrm{s}=100\,\mathrm{Hz}$; number of cycles $=0.20\,\mathrm{s}\div0.01\,\mathrm{s}=20$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Doubling the rotation frequency exactly doubles the number of complete cycles in any fixed time interval, since each cycle takes half as long to complete.

mcq.stem: A strong bar magnet sits completely motionless, fully inside a coil of wire connected to a sensitive meter. What does the meter read?

options.text: Zero, because nothing about the coil's exposure to the field is changing.
A small but steady nonzero reading, because the field is strong.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes a strong but unchanging field can induce a steady e.m.f.; induction needs a changing exposure to the field, not merely a strong one.

options.text: A reading that slowly decreases to zero over several seconds.
options.why_wrong: invents a gradual decay with no physical basis; with nothing changing, the reading is zero immediately, not after a delay.

options.text: A reading equal to the field strength of the magnet.
options.why_wrong: confuses the meter's reading (induced e.m.f.) with the magnet's field strength, which are different physical quantities, and ignores that no change means no induced e.m.f. at all.

mcq.explanation: With the magnet motionless, nothing about the coil's exposure to the field is changing, so no e.m.f. is induced and the meter reads zero, regardless of how strong the magnet's field is.

mcq.stem: A coil of $50$ turns and an otherwise identical coil of $150$ turns each have the same magnet pushed in at the same speed. Which coil has the larger induced e.m.f.?

options.text: The $50$-turn coil, because fewer turns means less resistance to oppose the induced e.m.f.
options.why_wrong: introduces resistance, which is not one of the factors that sets the size of the induced e.m.f. in this lesson, and reaches the wrong coil as a result.

options.text: The $150$-turn coil, because each turn's induced e.m.f. adds to the total.
Both coils have the same induced e.m.f., because the magnet and its speed are identical.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the number of turns is itself one of the three factors that affects the size of the induced e.m.f., independently of the magnet and its speed.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the coils' resistance.
options.why_wrong: is unnecessary information; the number of turns alone is enough to compare the induced e.m.f.s here, with speed and field strength held equal.

mcq.explanation: With speed and field strength the same in both cases, more turns means a larger total induced e.m.f., since each turn's own induced e.m.f. adds to the others.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly describes a generator's e.m.f.-time graph over one complete rotation of its coil?

options.text: It rises to a positive peak, falls to zero, and stays at zero for the rest of the rotation.
options.why_wrong: stops the graph partway through the rotation; the full rotation continues into a negative half, not a flat zero section.

options.text: It rises to a positive peak and stays there for the whole rotation.
options.why_wrong: describes a constant, d.c.-like output, which contradicts the coil's motion relative to the field reversing every half turn.

options.text: It rises to a positive peak, falls back through zero to a negative trough, and returns to zero.
It is a straight line that increases steadily throughout the rotation.
options.why_wrong: describes a steadily increasing quantity with no physical basis here; the induced e.m.f. depends on the coil's changing orientation, which repeats, not accumulates.

mcq.explanation: The coil's motion relative to the field reverses every half turn, so the induced e.m.f. itself reverses sign, giving a graph that alternates between a positive peak and a negative trough every complete rotation.

mcq.stem: A generator lights a bulb when its coil is turned by hand. Which statement correctly describes the energy involved?

options.text: The generator creates the electrical energy from nothing; no other energy input is needed.
options.why_wrong: contradicts conservation of energy; a generator transforms an existing energy input, it does not create energy from nothing.

options.text: The bulb's light energy is transformed back into mechanical energy at the coil.
options.why_wrong: reverses the actual direction of the energy transformation, which goes from mechanical energy at the coil to electrical energy, and then to light at the bulb.

options.text: The magnet inside the generator provides all the energy, and turning the coil has no effect on the energy output.
options.why_wrong: ignores that turning the coil is precisely the mechanical energy input the generator transforms; without it, no e.m.f. is induced at all, however strong the magnet is.

options.text: Mechanical energy from turning the coil is transformed into electrical energy.

mcq.explanation: A generator transforms the mechanical energy supplied by whatever turns its coil into electrical energy, consistent with conservation of energy; it cannot produce electrical energy without that mechanical input.

flashcards.front: What two situations induce an e.m.f. in a conductor?
flashcards.back: A conductor moving relative to a magnetic field (cutting field lines), or a magnetic field linking a stationary conductor that is itself changing in strength.

flashcards.front: Name the three factors that increase the size of an induced e.m.f.
flashcards.back: Faster relative motion (or a faster-changing field), a stronger magnetic field, and more turns on the coil.

flashcards.front: Does a steady, unchanging magnetic field linking a stationary coil induce a current?
flashcards.back: No. Induction needs a change in the conductor's exposure to the field; a steady field linking a stationary conductor induces nothing, however strong it is.

flashcards.front: Compare slip rings (generator) with a split-ring commutator (motor, covered later).
flashcards.back: A generator's slip rings are two separate, continuous rings that simply maintain contact with the rotating coil, without reversing anything themselves. A motor's split-ring commutator is specifically designed to reverse a connection every half turn.

flashcards.front: A generator's coil rotates at $50$ turns per second. What is the period of its e.m.f.-time graph, and what happens to that period if the rotation speed doubles?
flashcards.back: $T=1/50\,\mathrm{Hz}=0.02\,\mathrm{s}$; doubling the rotation speed halves the period to $0.01\,\mathrm{s}$.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A magnetic field, as long as it is present, always induces a current in a nearby conductor.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A magnetic field and an induced current are introduced together, so it is easy to associate the mere presence of a field with the effect, rather than a change in it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a continuing induced current while a magnet sits motionless inside a coil, or while a steady field simply surrounds a stationary conductor.
misconceptions.correct_model: Induction needs change: either the conductor must move relative to the field (cutting field lines), or the field linking a stationary conductor must itself be changing in strength. A steady field linking a stationary conductor induces nothing at all, however strong that field is.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two cases explicitly: a magnet moving into a coil (e.m.f. induced while moving) and the same magnet held still inside the coil (no e.m.f., however strong the field).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A generator creates electrical energy on its own, without needing any energy input.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A generator is often first met simply as 'a source of electricity', in the same breath as a cell, without emphasising that something must be turning it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a generator's electrical output without mentioning any mechanical input turning its coil.
misconceptions.correct_model: A generator transforms mechanical energy, supplied by whatever is turning its coil (for example, a hand crank, a turbine driven by steam, water or wind), into electrical energy; it cannot output more electrical energy than the mechanical energy put in, consistent with conservation of energy.
misconceptions.remediation: Name the mechanical energy input explicitly for a real example (a wind turbine's rotating blades, a hand-cranked torch) before describing the generator's electrical output.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The e.m.f.-time graph of a generator's output stays positive throughout, like a rising and falling but never-negative wave.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A d.c. source's voltage-time graph (a constant positive line) is the most familiar reference graph, so a new graph is assumed to share that same 'always positive' feature.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner sketches a generator's e.m.f.-time graph entirely above the time axis, with troughs that return to zero rather than crossing below it.
misconceptions.correct_model: An a.c. generator's e.m.f. alternates: it rises to a positive peak, falls back through zero, continues to a negative trough, and rises back through zero again, repeating this pattern every full turn of the coil.
misconceptions.remediation: Connect the direction of the induced e.m.f. to the coil's motion relative to the field at each quarter-turn, and show that this motion itself reverses every half turn, which is exactly why the graph must cross below zero.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting a magnetic field to induce a current simply because it is present, even when nothing about the conductor's exposure to it is changing.
common_mistakes.why: A magnetic field and induction are introduced together, so the field's mere presence is easy to associate with the effect.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask explicitly what is changing (position or field strength) before predicting any induced e.m.f.; no change, no induced e.m.f.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a generator as producing electrical energy without any mechanical energy input.
common_mistakes.why: A generator is often first met simply as 'a source of electricity', without emphasising what is turning its coil.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Name the mechanical energy input explicitly (what is turning the coil, and where that motion comes from) before describing the electrical output.

common_mistakes.mistake: Sketching a generator's e.m.f.-time graph as staying at or above zero throughout.
common_mistakes.why: A constant, always-positive d.c. graph is the most familiar reference, so a new graph is assumed to share that feature.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Link the graph's shape directly to the coil's motion reversing every half turn, and draw the negative half explicitly, not just the positive half repeated.

exam_notes: A factors-affecting-induced-e.m.f. answer needs a reason attached to each factor named, not just a bare list; 'faster' or 'more turns' alone, without saying why that increases the e.m.f., typically loses marks.
Always draw or describe the generator's e.m.f.-time graph with an explicit negative half, not only a positive peak; an all-positive sketch is a common way to lose marks on this topic.
Keep 'slip rings' (generator) and 'split-ring commutator' (motor) as two separate terms for two separate components with two separate jobs; do not use them interchangeably.

summary.big_idea: An e.m.f. is induced only by a change in a conductor's exposure to a magnetic field, and a generator turns this effect into a continuous, naturally alternating electrical output by rotating a coil whose motion relative to the field reverses every half turn.
key_points: Induction needs change: relative motion between conductor and field, or a changing field strength; a steady field linking a stationary conductor induces nothing.
Induced e.m.f. increases with faster relative motion, a stronger field, and more turns on the coil.
A rotating-coil generator uses slip rings and brushes to maintain contact with the turning coil without twisting the leads.
The coil's motion relative to the field reverses every half turn, so the output alternates, giving an e.m.f.-time graph with a positive and a negative half each cycle, with period $T=1/f$.
A generator transforms mechanical energy input into electrical energy output; it cannot create electrical energy from nothing.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: No change, no induced e.m.f.; a rotating coil's motion relative to the field reverses every half turn, which is exactly why a generator's output alternates rather than staying constant.

11_Current_makes_fields_and_motor_forces.title: Current makes fields and motor forces
11_Current_makes_fields_and_motor_forces.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe the magnetic field pattern around a straight current-carrying wire and around a solenoid, and state how the field responds to a change in the current.

Predict the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field from the relative directions of force, field and current, state the effect of reversing the current or the field, and explain how a d.c. motor's coil, split-ring commutator and brushes keep it turning in one direction.

prerequisites.statement: Describe a magnetic field as a region where a pole experiences force, and sketch field lines showing direction.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Describing the field a current produces, and the force a field produces on a current, both reuse the same field-line picture built earlier in the unit.

prerequisites.statement: State that conventional current flows from positive to negative, opposite to electron drift in a metal.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Both the field pattern around a wire and the direction of the motor-effect force are stated in terms of conventional current direction; using electron flow instead would reverse every prediction.

prerequisites.statement: State that a generator's slip rings are separate, continuous rings that do not reverse any connection, unlike a split-ring commutator.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson introduces the split-ring commutator; keeping it clearly distinct from the generator's slip rings from the previous lesson avoids the two components, which look superficially similar, being confused.

diagnostic_items.question: A bar magnet is drawn on a page with its N pole on the left and its S pole on the right, and a field line is drawn looping from one pole round to the other outside the magnet. Which way does the arrow on that field line point, and what does a plotting compass placed on the line do?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The arrow points away from the N pole and towards the S pole, i.e. from left to right outside the magnet. A plotting compass placed on the line settles along the line, with its N-seeking end pointing the same way as the arrow.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The arrow points from the S pole to the N pole outside the magnet.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has reversed the convention (that is the direction inside the magnet), so every field direction in this lesson, including the right-hand grip rule and the left-hand rule, will come out backwards.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The arrows point straight out from the magnet in all directions, like spokes.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is picturing a field of force lines radiating from a source rather than the closed loops of a magnetic field, and will not recognise the circular pattern around a current-carrying wire.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This lesson asks the learner to read and draw field directions for a wire, a solenoid and the motor effect; all of it rests on the convention that a field line points from N to S outside the magnet and shows which way a compass settles.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Re-plot a bar magnet's field with a plotting compass before starting the lesson, marking each arrow in the direction the compass's N-seeking end points, and state the N-to-S convention out loud.

diagnostic_items.question: A copper wire is connected across a cell. In which direction does the conventional current in the wire flow, in terms of the cell's terminals, and which way do the electrons in the wire actually drift?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The conventional current flows round the circuit from the positive terminal of the cell to the negative terminal; the electrons drift the opposite way, from negative to positive.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The current flows from negative to positive, because that is the way the electrons go.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has replaced the conventional current direction with electron flow, which reverses every prediction made with the right-hand grip rule and with Fleming's left-hand rule.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The electrons and the current both flow from positive to negative.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner knows the convention but has not separated it from what the charge carriers do, so cannot explain why the two directions are opposite.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Both the field pattern around a wire and the direction of the motor-effect force are stated in terms of conventional current, so a learner who uses electron flow will get every direction in this lesson exactly reversed.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Redraw a simple circuit, marking the conventional current arrow from + to - and the electron drift arrow underneath it in the opposite direction, and agree that every rule in this unit uses the conventional arrow.

diagnostic_items.question: A rotating coil is connected to an external circuit by two separate, continuous metal rings on its shaft. Do these rings ever swap which end of the coil is joined to which brush as the coil turns?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. Slip rings are complete, separate rings, so each end of the coil stays joined to the same brush all the way round; they do not reverse any connection.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, they swap the connections every half turn.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has attributed the split-ring commutator's job to slip rings, and will not be able to explain what is special about a d.c. motor's commutator later in this lesson.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: The split-ring commutator introduced in this lesson is defined by contrast with the generator's slip rings; a learner who thinks slip rings already reverse connections sees no reason for the split ring to exist.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch the two contacts side by side, a pair of complete rings and a single ring cut into two halves, and say what each one does to the connection as the shaft turns.

theory_blocks.title: A current is a magnet too
theory_blocks.body:
Every one of this unit's magnetic fields so far has come from a permanent magnet. But a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field of its own, with no permanent magnet involved at all: [[blue:the moving charge itself produces the field]]. A compass needle placed near a current-carrying wire deflects, exactly as it would near a bar magnet, and the deflection reverses if the current's direction is reversed.

This single fact, that current itself creates a field, is what makes an electromagnet and a solenoid's bar-magnet-like field possible. It is also the key to the motor effect later in this lesson: a current-carrying wire placed in a second, external field (from a permanent magnet or an electromagnet) feels a force, because its own field interacts with that external field.

theory_blocks.title: The field around a straight wire, and around a solenoid
theory_blocks.body:
The magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire forms **concentric circles** centred on the wire, in a plane perpendicular to it. The field's direction follows the **right-hand grip rule**: point the right thumb in the direction of conventional current, and the curled fingers show the field's direction around the wire.

A **solenoid** (a coil of wire wound into a tube shape) produces a field that, outside the coil, looks just like a bar magnet's field, with a N pole at one end and a S pole at the other; inside the coil, the field runs nearly straight along the solenoid's axis. The same right-hand grip rule gives the solenoid's polarity: curl the right-hand fingers in the direction conventional current flows around each turn, and the thumb points out of the N pole end.

In both cases, reversing the current's direction reverses the field's direction at every point; increasing the current's size increases the field's strength without changing its pattern.

assets.caption: Left: the concentric field circles around a straight wire carrying current out of the page, running anticlockwise as the right-hand grip rule predicts. Right: a solenoid's field, running from right to left inside the coil, out of the N end, round the outside and back into the S end, exactly like a bar magnet's field. The red arrows show the current flowing up the near side of each turn, which is what fixes the N pole at the left-hand end.
assets.purpose: Make both required field patterns (straight wire, solenoid) visible and comparable in one figure, with the current direction shown so that the solenoid's polarity can be checked with the right-hand grip rule.

theory_blocks.title: The motor effect: force on a current in a field
theory_blocks.body:
A current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field experiences a force, called the **motor effect**. The force is always perpendicular to both the current's direction and the field's direction, and it is largest when the current flows at right angles to the field; a conductor lying along the field direction feels no force at all.

The force's direction is predicted using **Fleming's left-hand rule**: holding the left thumb, first finger and second finger all mutually at right angles, the First finger points along the Field (from N to S), the seCond finger points along the Current (conventional current, from + to -), and the thuMb then points along the direction of the resulting Force.

[[blue:Reversing either the current or the field reverses the direction of the force]]; reversing both leaves the force in its original direction. The size of the force is increased by using a larger current or a stronger field.

**Extension (beyond this course).** For a straight conductor of length $L$ carrying a current $I$ at right angles to a uniform field of magnetic flux density $B$, the size of the force is $F=BIL$; for example, a wire of length $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ carrying $4.0\,\mathrm{A}$ at right angles to a field of $0.50\,\mathrm{T}$ feels a force $F=0.50\,\mathrm{T}\times4.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.20\,\mathrm{m}=0.40\,\mathrm{N}$. This equation is **not examinable** in GCSE, where you are asked only for the direction of the force and for the effect of reversing the current or the field, but it does show why a larger current or a stronger field gives a bigger force.

assets.caption: Left: a wire carrying current out of the page, in a field pointing to the right, is pushed upwards, as Fleming's left-hand rule predicts. Right: the same effect on a coil seen end-on between the poles; its two sides carry current in opposite directions, so one is pushed up and the other down, and this pair of forces turns the coil about its axle (shown here in the position of greatest turning effect).
assets.purpose: Show the relative directions of force, field and current for a single wire, and the couple that the same effect produces on a coil.

theory_blocks.title: Why a coil turns, and what the split-ring commutator does
theory_blocks.body:
A rectangular coil placed between magnetic poles has two sides running parallel to the poles' faces. Current flows one way along one side and, because it is the same single loop, the opposite way back along the other side. With both sides in the same external field, the motor effect pushes one side one way and the other side the opposite way: this pair of opposite forces on opposite sides of the coil forms a **couple**, which turns the coil. The turning effect is increased by increasing the number of turns on the coil, the current, or the strength of the magnetic field.

As the coil turns past the vertical position (its plane at right angles to the field), each side moves across to the other side of the axle, so without anything else changing, the forces would now push the coil back the way it came, and it would simply rock back and forth rather than turn continuously. The **split-ring commutator**, two half-ring contacts that rotate with the coil, fixes this. Current is fed in and out through two fixed **brushes** (usually carbon blocks) that press against the rotating split ring. Just as the coil passes the vertical position, the gaps in the split ring pass the brushes and the split ring reverses which side of the coil is connected to which brush. This reverses the current in the coil at exactly the moment the geometry would otherwise reverse the turning direction. The two reversals cancel, so the turning effect keeps pushing the same way, every half turn, and the coil rotates continuously in one direction (its momentum carries it through the vertical position, where the turning effect is momentarily zero).

assets.caption: The split-ring commutator seen end-on, with the two fixed brushes pressing on it. Each half-ring is joined to one side of the coil. After half a turn the halves have changed places, so each coil side is now connected to the other brush: the current through the coil has been reversed at exactly the moment the coil passed the vertical position.
assets.purpose: Make the action of the split-ring commutator and brushes (0654 P4.5.5.2) visible: the halves swap brushes every half turn.

keywords.definition: A rule giving the magnetic field's direction around a current-carrying wire: the right thumb points along the current, and the curled fingers show the field's direction.
The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field.
A rule giving the direction of the motor-effect force: with thumb, first finger and second finger mutually at right angles, thuMb = Force, First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current.
A two-part ring contact on a d.c. motor's coil that reverses the coil's connection every half turn, keeping it turning in one direction.

worked_examples.statement: **Field direction around a wire.** A long straight wire carries current out of the page. Using the right-hand grip rule, state the direction of the magnetic field circles around the wire: clockwise or anticlockwise, as seen by someone looking at the page.
knowns: current direction: out of the page, towards the viewer
reasoning: Point the right thumb out of the page, towards the viewer, matching the current's direction.
The curled fingers show the field's direction around the wire.
worked_examples.solution: With the thumb pointing out of the page, the fingers curl anticlockwise as seen by the viewer, so the field circles the wire anticlockwise.
worked_examples.interpretation: Reversing the current (into the page instead) would reverse this to clockwise; the field's direction always follows the current's direction through the same rule.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Guessing the field direction from the field lines of a bar magnet instead of applying the right-hand grip rule to the current's actual direction.

worked_examples.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** **Calculating a motor-effect force.** A straight wire of length $0.20\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a current of $4.0\,\mathrm{A}$, perpendicular to a magnetic field of $0.50\,\mathrm{T}$. Calculate the force on the wire.
reasoning: Apply $F=BIL$ directly, since the wire is perpendicular to the field.
worked_examples.solution: $F=0.50\,\mathrm{T}\times4.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.20\,\mathrm{m}=0.40\,\mathrm{N}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: dividing back, $0.40\,\mathrm{N}\div(4.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.20\,\mathrm{m})=0.50\,\mathrm{T}$, recovering the original field strength.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Multiplying only two of the three quantities (for example, $B\times I$ alone), instead of all three, $B$, $I$ and $L$, together.

worked_examples.statement: **Reversing the current.** A wire of length $0.40\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a current of $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$, perpendicular to a field of $0.25\,\mathrm{T}$, and experiences an upward force. The current is then reversed, with the field unchanged. State the new force's size and direction, and explain your reasoning. (The direction part is examinable; the calculation of the size uses $F=BIL$, which is beyond this course.)
reasoning: Calculate the size using $F=BIL$; this does not depend on which way the current points, only on its magnitude.
Apply Fleming's left-hand rule again with the current arrow reversed to find the new direction.
worked_examples.solution: Size: $F=0.25\,\mathrm{T}\times2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.40\,\mathrm{m}=0.20\,\mathrm{N}$, the same as before. Direction: reversing the current reverses the left-hand rule's result, so the new force points downward, the exact opposite of the original upward force.
worked_examples.interpretation: The force's size depends only on the current's magnitude; its direction depends on the current's direction, so reversing the current reverses the force's direction while leaving its size unchanged.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming reversing the current has no effect at all, since the field and the wire itself have not changed.

worked_examples.statement: **Motor or generator?** A device has a coil that rotates between magnetic poles, connected to the outside world through a ring-shaped contact on its shaft. (a) Explain how you would decide, from its energy input and output alone, whether this device is a motor or a generator. (b) State which type of ring-shaped contact (slip rings or a split-ring commutator) each type of device needs, and explain why they are different.
knowns: a rotating coil between poles, connected through a ring-shaped contact
unknowns: how to tell motor from generator
which ring-shaped contact each needs, and why
reasoning: A motor and a generator transform energy in opposite directions, even though they share a similar construction.
A generator's output alternates naturally as the coil turns; a motor needs its rotation to continue the same way, not alternate.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Check which way the energy flows: if electrical energy is supplied and mechanical (turning) energy comes out, it is a motor; if mechanical energy is supplied (something turns the coil) and electrical energy comes out, it is a generator. (b) A generator uses slip rings, two separate, continuous rings that preserve its naturally alternating output unchanged. A motor uses a split-ring commutator, which deliberately reverses the coil's connection every half turn, cancelling the force's natural reversal so the coil keeps turning the same way instead of oscillating.
worked_examples.interpretation: The two devices need opposite-behaving contacts precisely because they need opposite outcomes: a generator's alternation is wanted and left alone; a motor's would-be alternation is unwanted and is cancelled out.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the ring-shaped contact itself is what makes one device a motor and the other a generator, rather than the direction of energy transformation, which is the real distinguishing feature.

guided_exercises.statement: A solenoid is wound so that, viewed from its right-hand end, conventional current flows clockwise around each turn. Use the right-hand grip rule to state which end (left or right) is the N pole.
hints: Curl the right-hand fingers in the direction the current flows around the turns, as seen from the right-hand end.
The thumb then points out of the N pole end.
Check your answer is a single, definite end, not a direction along the axis only.
guided_exercises.answer: Curling the right-hand fingers clockwise as seen from the right-hand end points the thumb into the solenoid, towards the left-hand end, so the left-hand end is the N pole.
common_errors: Applying the rule as if viewed from the opposite end, which reverses the apparent sense of the current and gives the wrong pole.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Curl the right-hand fingers in the direction the current flows around the turns, as seen from the right-hand end.

**Step 2 — Method:** The thumb then points out of the N pole end.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Curling the right-hand fingers clockwise as seen from the right-hand end points the thumb into the solenoid, towards the left-hand end, so the left-hand end is the N pole.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer is a single, definite end, not a direction along the axis only.

guided_exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** A wire of length $0.10\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a current of $5.0\,\mathrm{A}$, perpendicular to a field of $0.40\,\mathrm{T}$. Calculate the force on the wire.
hints: Identify $B$, $I$ and $L$ from the question.
Apply $F=BIL$ directly.
Check your answer has units of newtons.
guided_exercises.answer: $F=0.40\,\mathrm{T}\times5.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.10\,\mathrm{m}=0.20\,\mathrm{N}$.
common_errors: Leaving out one of the three quantities, most often the length, when multiplying.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify $B$, $I$ and $L$ from the question.

**Step 2 — Method:** Apply $F=BIL$ directly.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $F=0.40\,\mathrm{T}\times5.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.10\,\mathrm{m}=0.20\,\mathrm{N}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer has units of newtons.

exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** A wire of length $0.30\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a current of $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$, perpendicular to a field of $0.80\,\mathrm{T}$. Calculate the force on the wire.
exercises.answer: $F=0.80\,\mathrm{T}\times2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.30\,\mathrm{m}=0.48\,\mathrm{N}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $0.48\,\mathrm{N}\div(2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.30\,\mathrm{m})=0.80\,\mathrm{T}$, recovering the stated field strength.

exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** A wire carrying $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$, perpendicular to a field of $0.60\,\mathrm{T}$, experiences a force of $0.90\,\mathrm{N}$. Calculate the length of wire in the field.
exercises.answer: Rearranging $F=BIL$: $L=F\div(B\times I)=0.90\,\mathrm{N}\div(0.60\,\mathrm{T}\times3.0\,\mathrm{A})=0.50\,\mathrm{m}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $0.60\,\mathrm{T}\times3.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.50\,\mathrm{m}=0.90\,\mathrm{N}$, recovering the stated force.

exercises.statement: **Extension (beyond this course).** A wire in a magnetic field carries a current of $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ and experiences a motor-effect force. The current is then increased to $6.0\,\mathrm{A}$, with the field and the wire's length unchanged. State what happens to the force, using $F=BIL$ to justify your answer. (For GCSE you only need to know that a larger current gives a larger force.)
exercises.answer: The force becomes three times as large as before.
exercises.full_solution: Since $B$ and $L$ are unchanged, $F=BIL$ is directly proportional to $I$ alone; tripling the current from $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ to $6.0\,\mathrm{A}$ triples the force.

exercises.statement: A loudspeaker contains a coil attached to a paper cone, placed in a magnetic field. An alternating current, from an amplifier, is passed through the coil. Using the motor effect and what reversing a current does to a force, explain why the cone vibrates back and forth rather than moving steadily in one direction.
exercises.answer: The alternating current repeatedly reverses direction through the coil, so by the motor effect, the force on the coil (and so the cone) also repeatedly reverses direction, pushing the cone first one way, then the other, in time with the alternating current; this back-and-forth motion of the cone is what produces sound.
exercises.full_solution: The alternating current repeatedly reverses direction through the coil, so by the motor effect, the force on the coil (and so the cone) also repeatedly reverses direction, pushing the cone first one way, then the other, in time with the alternating current; this back-and-forth motion of the cone is what produces sound.

exercises.statement: The diagram shows a straight wire passing at right angles through the page, between the poles of a magnet. The magnetic field points from the N pole on the left to the S pole on the right, and the current in the wire flows into the page. (a) State the direction of the force on the wire. (b) The magnet is now turned round, so that the S pole is on the left and the N pole on the right, with the current unchanged. State the direction of the force now. (c) State one other single change that would reverse the force's direction.
exercises.answer: (a) The force is directed downwards, in the plane of the page. (b) Upwards. (c) Reversing the current in the wire, so that it flows out of the page instead.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Use Fleming's left-hand rule: the First finger points along the Field, from N to S, so to the right; the seCond finger points along the Current, into the page; the thuMb then points downwards, so the force on the wire is downwards. (b) Turning the magnet round reverses the field, and reversing the field reverses the force, so the force is now upwards; its size is unchanged. (c) Reversing the current reverses the force in exactly the same way. (Reversing both the current and the field together would leave the force pointing downwards again, as the two reversals cancel.)

assets.caption: A straight wire between the poles of a magnet, seen end-on: the field runs from the N pole on the left to the S pole on the right, and the current in the wire flows into the page.
assets.purpose: Give the student a field-and-current diagram to apply Fleming's left-hand rule to.

exam_questions.statement: (a) Describe the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire. (b) A solenoid's field outside the coil is described as being 'like a bar magnet's field'. Explain what this means. (c) A solenoid has its current direction reversed. State what happens to its N and S poles.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Concentric circles centred on the wire, in a plane perpendicular to the wire. (b) Outside the coil, the solenoid's field lines emerge from one end (its N pole), curve round, and re-enter at the other end (its S pole), in the same pattern as a bar magnet's field lines; inside the solenoid, the field runs nearly straight along its axis, unlike a bar magnet's interior. (c) The N and S poles swap ends: the end that was N becomes S, and the end that was S becomes N.
exam_questions.full_solution: Both the straight wire's and the solenoid's field patterns, and their response to a reversed current, follow directly from the right-hand grip rule applied to the (now reversed) current direction.
mark_scheme: Describes the straight wire's field as concentric circles around the wire.
Describes the solenoid's external field as matching a bar magnet's pattern.
Contrasts this with the nearly straight field inside the solenoid's core.
States that reversing the current swaps the N and S poles.
(a) Adds that the circles are centred on the wire and lie in a plane perpendicular to it (or that they are further apart, i.e. the field is weaker, further from the wire).
common_errors: Describing the straight wire's field as pointing radially outward from the wire, rather than circling around it.

exam_questions.statement: A simple d.c. motor has a rectangular coil between two magnetic poles. One side of the coil has length $0.080\,\mathrm{m}$, carries a current of $4.0\,\mathrm{A}$, and lies perpendicular to a field of $0.30\,\mathrm{T}$. (a) **Extension (beyond this course):** calculate the force on this side of the coil, using $F=BIL$. (b) Explain why the opposite side of the coil experiences a force in the opposite direction. (c) Explain what would happen to the coil's rotation if the split-ring commutator were removed and replaced with two slip rings instead.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $F=0.30\,\mathrm{T}\times4.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.080\,\mathrm{m}=0.096\,\mathrm{N}$. (b) The current flows in the opposite direction along the opposite side (since it is the same single loop), so by Fleming's left-hand rule with the current reversed and the field the same, the force on that side points the opposite way. (c) With slip rings instead of a split-ring commutator, the coil's connection would never reverse, so once the coil passed the halfway point, the force on each side would reverse along with the coil's geometry, and the coil would rock back and forth about the position where its plane is perpendicular to the field, soon coming to rest there, rather than turning continuously in one direction.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $F=0.30\,\mathrm{T}\times4.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.080\,\mathrm{m}=0.096\,\mathrm{N}$. (b) The current flows in the opposite direction along the opposite side (since it is the same single loop), so by Fleming's left-hand rule with the current reversed and the field the same, the force on that side points the opposite way. (c) With slip rings instead of a split-ring commutator, the coil's connection would never reverse, so once the coil passed the halfway point, the force on each side would reverse along with the coil's geometry, and the coil would rock back and forth about the position where its plane is perpendicular to the field, soon coming to rest there, rather than turning continuously in one direction.
mark_scheme: Calculates the force correctly: $0.096\,\mathrm{N}$.
States that the opposite side carries current in the opposite direction.
Applies the left-hand rule correctly to explain the opposite force direction.
States that slip rings would not reverse the coil's connection.
Explains that the coil would no longer turn continuously: it would rock back and forth about, and come to rest at, the position where its plane is perpendicular to the field.
(a) Uses $F=BIL$ with the correct values substituted (method mark).
common_errors: Saying the coil would keep turning continuously, or would spin the other way, without a split-ring commutator; in fact it only turns until its plane is perpendicular to the field, rocks back and forth about that position and then comes to rest there.

exam_questions.statement: The coil of a simple d.c. motor turns, but too slowly for the job it has to do. State three changes that would increase the turning effect on the coil.
exam_questions.answer: Increase the number of turns on the coil; increase the current in the coil; use a stronger magnetic field (for example, stronger magnets).
exam_questions.full_solution: Each side of the coil carries a current across the field, so each feels a motor-effect force, and the pair of forces forms the couple that turns the coil. Anything that makes those forces larger, or that applies them more times, makes the turning effect larger: more turns means more current-carrying sides being pushed, a larger current means a larger force on each side, and a stronger field means a larger force on each side as well. Note that reversing the current or the field changes the direction the coil turns, not the size of the turning effect.
mark_scheme: Increases the number of turns on the coil.
Increases the current (in the coil).
Uses a stronger magnetic field / stronger magnets.
common_errors: Offering changes that alter the direction of rotation rather than the size of the turning effect, such as reversing the current or swapping the magnets round.
Repeating the same idea twice in different words (for example 'more current' and 'bigger battery') instead of giving three different changes.

challenge_questions.statement: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** A rectangular coil has two sides, each of length $0.080\,\mathrm{m}$, carrying a current of $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ in a field of $0.50\,\mathrm{T}$, perpendicular to both sides. The current flows in opposite directions along the two sides. Calculate the force on each side, and explain, using the directions of these two forces, why the coil turns rather than simply moving sideways. (The explanation of the couple is examinable; the calculation is not.)
hints: Apply $F=BIL$ to one side first; the other side has the same $B$, $I$ and $L$, so the same size of force.
Use the fact that the current direction is opposite on the two sides to find the force directions with the left-hand rule.
A pair of equal, opposite forces acting on opposite sides of an object produces a turning effect, not a sideways push.
challenge_questions.answer: Each side experiences a force of $F=0.50\,\mathrm{T}\times2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.080\,\mathrm{m}=0.080\,\mathrm{N}$. Because the current flows in opposite directions on the two sides, the left-hand rule gives forces in opposite directions on the two sides, for example one side pushed upward and the other pushed downward.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Two equal-sized forces acting in opposite directions on opposite sides of the coil do not cancel to give a net sideways push; instead, because they act at different points on the coil, they form a couple, which is exactly what turns the coil rather than translating it.

mcq.stem: An electric fan has a motor that spins its blades when plugged in. Which statement correctly describes its energy transformation?

options.text: Electrical energy is transformed into mechanical (kinetic) energy.
Mechanical energy is transformed into electrical energy, which is then transformed back into mechanical energy.
options.why_wrong: adds an unnecessary and incorrect extra step; a motor transforms electrical energy directly into mechanical energy, with no intermediate stage.

options.text: The fan is a generator, so it produces electrical energy as the blades spin.
options.why_wrong: confuses a motor with a generator; the fan is supplied with electrical energy and outputs mechanical energy, the reverse of a generator.

options.text: No energy transformation occurs; the blades simply spin because current is present.
options.why_wrong: ignores that a transformation must occur for the blades to gain kinetic energy at all, which cannot appear from nowhere.

mcq.explanation: A motor is supplied with electrical energy and transforms it into mechanical (kinetic) energy, turning its shaft and the attached blades.

mcq.stem: A long straight wire carries current into the page. Using the right-hand grip rule, what is the direction of the magnetic field circles around the wire, as seen by someone looking at the page?

options.text: Anticlockwise
options.why_wrong: is the result for current coming out of the page towards the viewer, not into the page as stated here.

options.text: Clockwise
Radially outward from the wire, like spokes on a wheel.
options.why_wrong: describes a pattern the field does not actually have; the field forms closed circles around the wire, not radial lines.

options.text: There is no field, since the wire is straight.
options.why_wrong: is incorrect: any current-carrying wire, straight or not, produces a magnetic field around it.

mcq.explanation: Pointing the right thumb into the page, matching the current's direction, curls the fingers clockwise as seen by the viewer, so the field circles the wire clockwise.

mcq.stem: A wire carrying current in a magnetic field experiences an upward force. The current is then reversed, with the field unchanged. What happens to the force?

options.text: It stays the same size and the same upward direction.
options.why_wrong: ignores that reversing the current direction reverses the left-hand rule's result, so the direction cannot stay the same.

options.text: It becomes zero, since the current and field now oppose each other.
options.why_wrong: misapplies the idea of opposition; the force does not become zero simply because the current's direction has been reversed.

options.text: It stays the same size but now points downward.
It becomes twice as large, in the same upward direction.
options.why_wrong: invents a doubling with no basis; reversing a current's direction does not change the size of the force, only its direction.

mcq.explanation: The size of the force depends on the size of the current, the strength of the field and the length of wire in the field, and none of these has changed, so the force's size is unchanged; applying Fleming's left-hand rule with the current reversed gives a force in the opposite direction, downward instead of upward.

mcq.stem: What is the split-ring commutator's role in a d.c. motor?

options.text: It produces the motor's alternating output, in the same way as a generator's slip rings.
options.why_wrong: confuses the split-ring commutator's job with a generator's slip rings; a motor's output is not alternating current, and the split ring's job is to prevent oscillation, not to produce alternation.

options.text: It increases the current in the coil every half turn to keep it turning.
options.why_wrong: invents a current-boosting function the split ring does not have; it reverses a connection, it does not increase current.

options.text: It has no electrical function; it is only a mechanical support for the coil.
options.why_wrong: ignores the split ring's actual electrical role, which is to reverse which side of the coil each brush connects to.

options.text: It reverses the coil's connection every half turn, keeping the turning effect pushing the same way.

mcq.explanation: The split-ring commutator reverses the coil's connection every half turn, exactly cancelling the force's natural reversal from the coil's changing geometry, so the coil keeps turning the same way rather than oscillating.

mcq.stem: A wire carries a current at right angles to a magnetic field and is pushed to the left. The magnets are then turned round, so that the field points the opposite way; the current is unchanged. What happens to the force on the wire?

options.text: It stays the same size but now pushes the wire to the right.
It stays the same size and still pushes the wire to the left.
options.why_wrong: ignores that reversing the field reverses the result of Fleming's left-hand rule, so the direction cannot stay the same.

options.text: It becomes zero, because the field now opposes the current.
options.why_wrong: misreads 'reversed' as 'cancelled'; the field is just as strong as before, so a force of the same size still acts.

options.text: It stays to the left but becomes smaller.
options.why_wrong: invents a change of size; turning the magnets round changes only the field's direction, not its strength.

mcq.explanation: Reversing the field reverses the direction of the force while leaving its size unchanged: with the first finger of the left hand now pointing the opposite way, and the second finger (current) unchanged, the thumb points the opposite way, so the wire is pushed to the right.

flashcards.front: What rule gives the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire?
flashcards.back: The right-hand grip rule: point the right thumb along the current's direction, and the curled fingers show the field's direction around the wire.

flashcards.front: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** What is the formula for the motor-effect force on a current-carrying conductor perpendicular to a magnetic field, and what does each symbol mean?
flashcards.back: $F=BIL$, where $B$ is the magnetic flux density, $I$ is the current, and $L$ is the length of conductor in the field; the force is perpendicular to both the current and the field. The 0654 syllabus asks only for the force's direction, not for this calculation.

flashcards.front: Does reversing the current in a wire change the size of the motor-effect force it experiences, the direction, both, or neither (field unchanged)?
flashcards.back: Only the direction. The size of the force depends on the size of the current, the field strength and the length of conductor in the field, none of which changes when the current is reversed; the left-hand rule gives a reversed force direction.

flashcards.front: Compare a generator's slip rings with a motor's split-ring commutator.
flashcards.back: Slip rings are two separate, continuous rings that preserve a generator's naturally alternating connection unchanged. A split-ring commutator deliberately reverses a motor's coil connection every half turn, cancelling the force's natural reversal so the coil keeps turning one way.

flashcards.front: **Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** A wire of length $0.50\,\mathrm{m}$ carries a current of $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$, perpendicular to a field of $0.20\,\mathrm{T}$. What force does it experience?
flashcards.back: $F=0.20\,\mathrm{T}\times3.0\,\mathrm{A}\times0.50\,\mathrm{m}=0.30\,\mathrm{N}$.

flashcards.front: State three ways of increasing the turning effect on the coil of a d.c. motor.
flashcards.back: Increase the number of turns on the coil; increase the current; use a stronger magnetic field.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A motor and a generator perform the identical energy function; the two names are just alternative labels for the same device.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A motor and a generator look similar (a coil, magnets, a rotating shaft) and are studied back to back, so the superficial similarity is mistaken for an identical function.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a motor as 'generating electricity' or a generator as something that 'makes things spin', interchanging the two devices' roles.
misconceptions.correct_model: A motor transforms electrical energy into mechanical (kinetic) energy: you supply current, and it turns. A generator does the reverse: you supply mechanical energy by turning it, and it produces electrical energy. They are built from similar parts, but their energy input and output are opposite.
misconceptions.remediation: For a named example of each (an electric fan motor; a wind-turbine generator), state explicitly which energy goes in and which comes out, and show the two are reversed.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Reversing the current in a wire within a magnetic field has no effect on the force it experiences.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The field and the wire both look unchanged after reversing the current, so it is easy to assume the force on the wire is unchanged as well.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts the same force direction (or no force at all) after being told the current in a wire has been reversed, with the field unchanged.
misconceptions.correct_model: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force, while leaving its size the same (the size depends on how big the current is, not on which way it flows): applying Fleming's left-hand rule with the current arrow reversed gives a force arrow pointing the opposite way.
misconceptions.remediation: Apply Fleming's left-hand rule twice to the same wire and field, once with the original current direction and once with it reversed, and compare the two resulting force directions explicitly.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A motor's split-ring commutator is what produces the alternating output of an a.c. generator.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both devices have a ring-shaped contact mounted on a rotating shaft, so the split ring of one is easily confused with the slip rings of the other.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner attributes a generator's alternating output to a split ring, or describes a motor's split ring as making its output alternate.
misconceptions.correct_model: A generator's output alternates because the coil's motion relative to the field reverses every half turn; its slip rings are two separate, continuous rings that do not reverse anything. A motor's split-ring commutator does the opposite job: it deliberately reverses the connection to the coil every half turn, which cancels out the force's natural reversal and keeps the coil turning the same way instead of alternating.
misconceptions.remediation: State the two components' jobs side by side: slip rings preserve a naturally alternating connection unchanged; a split-ring commutator deliberately reverses a connection to prevent alternation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a motor and a generator as the same device with two names, rather than opposite energy transformations.
common_mistakes.why: The two devices share a similar construction (coil, magnets, a rotating shaft), so the superficial similarity is mistaken for an identical function.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: For any named device, state explicitly which energy goes in and which comes out before deciding whether it is a motor or a generator.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming reversing a current has no effect on the motor-effect force, since the wire and the field both look unchanged.
common_mistakes.why: Nothing about the wire or the magnet themselves has visibly changed, so it is tempting to assume nothing about the force has either.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Apply Fleming's left-hand rule explicitly with the new current direction, rather than assuming the previous answer still applies.

common_mistakes.mistake: Attributing a generator's alternating output to a split-ring commutator, or a motor's continuous turning to slip rings.
common_mistakes.why: Both components are ring-shaped contacts on a rotating shaft, so they are easy to confuse with each other.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State each device's needed outcome first (alternation wanted for a generator; alternation unwanted for a motor), then match it to the contact that produces that outcome.

exam_notes: State Fleming's left-hand rule using all three mutually perpendicular directions (thuMb = Force, First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current); naming only one or two of the three rarely earns full marks.

The 0654 syllabus does not ask you to calculate this force: the marks come from the force's direction, from the effect of reversing the current or the field, and from the three ways of increasing a motor's turning effect (more turns on the coil, a larger current, a stronger field).
A split-ring commutator question almost always expects the word 'reverses' (the connection, every half turn) rather than a vaguer description like 'switches' or 'changes'.

summary.big_idea: A current creates its own magnetic field, and a current placed in an external magnetic field experiences a force; applying this force to both sides of a coil, with a split-ring commutator to keep reversing the connection at the right moment, is what turns a d.c. motor continuously in one direction.
key_points: A straight current-carrying wire has a field of concentric circles around it; a solenoid's external field matches a bar magnet's pattern; both follow the right-hand grip rule.
A current-carrying conductor at right angles to a magnetic field experiences a force at right angles to both the field and the current, in a direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule.
Reversing the current reverses the force's direction but not its size; reversing the field does the same.

A coil's two sides carry current in opposite directions, so the motor effect pushes them opposite ways, forming a turning couple; the turning effect is increased by more turns on the coil, a larger current or a stronger field.
A split-ring commutator reverses the coil's connection every half turn, cancelling the force's natural reversal so the coil turns continuously instead of oscillating.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Current creates its own field (right-hand grip rule); a current in an external field feels a force whose direction comes from Fleming's left-hand rule, and reversing the current or the field reverses that force; and a split-ring commutator reverses a motor's coil connection every half turn to keep it turning one way.

12_Transformers_and_efficient_transmissi.title: Transformers and efficient transmission
12_Transformers_and_efficient_transmissi.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe a transformer's construction (primary coil, secondary coil, soft-iron core), distinguish step-up from step-down, and calculate an unknown voltage, current or number of turns using $V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ and the ideal power relation $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$.
Explain, using $P=I^2R$, why transmitting electrical power at a high voltage reduces the current in the cables and so reduces the power lost to cable heating.

prerequisites.statement: Describe how a changing magnetic field linking a coil induces an e.m.f. in it, and state that an a.c. generator's coil produces a continuously alternating output.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A transformer induces its secondary e.m.f. purely by a changing field linking the secondary coil; this only makes sense once induction by a changing field, from the previous lesson, is already familiar.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate electrical power using $P=IV$, and recall that resistive heating in a cable depends on the current through it.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Explaining the advantage of high-voltage transmission depends on combining power, current and resistance correctly; without a secure $P=IV$ and a sense of current-driven heating, the argument for $P=I^2R$ has nothing to build on.

diagnostic_items.question: A coil of wire is connected to a sensitive centre-zero meter. A bar magnet is pushed into the coil, then held still inside it, then pulled out again. During which of these three stages is an e.m.f. induced across the coil?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: While the magnet is being pushed in and while it is being pulled out, because the magnetic field linking the coil is changing; while the magnet is held still inside the coil nothing changes, so no e.m.f. is induced. The two deflections are in opposite directions.

common_wrong_answers.answer: All the time the magnet is inside the coil, because the field is strong there.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner links the induced e.m.f. to the presence of a field rather than to a change in it, and will not see why a transformer needs an alternating current in its primary coil.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Only while the magnet is pushed in; pulling it out does nothing.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has not connected a decreasing field with induction either, so will miss that the e.m.f. induced in a transformer's secondary coil alternates.
