diagnostic_items.interpretation: A transformer's secondary e.m.f. is induced purely by the changing field in the core; a learner who thinks a steady field induces an e.m.f. will not understand why a transformer works on a.c. and not on d.c.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Repeat the magnet-and-coil demonstration (or its description) and write beside each stage whether the field linking the coil is changing, then state the rule: an e.m.f. is induced only while the field linking the coil changes.

diagnostic_items.question: An electric heater takes a current of $8.0\,\mathrm{A}$ from a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ mains supply. Calculate the power it transfers.

common_wrong_answers.answer: $230\,\mathrm{V}\div8.0\,\mathrm{A}=28.75$, giving an answer in ohms.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has reached for $V=IR$ instead of $P=IV$, so cannot yet move between power, current and voltage, which every transformer and transmission calculation in this lesson requires.
The learner is combining the quantities without a relationship in mind, which signals that $P=IV$ is not available for use at all.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Both the ideal transformer equation $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$ and the argument for high-voltage transmission start from $P=IV$; without it, neither can be followed.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Rehearse two or three one-step $P=IV$ calculations, including one rearranged to find the current from a given power and voltage, before starting this lesson.

diagnostic_items.question: A long cable warms up as it carries a current. If the current in that same cable is made larger, does the rate at which the cable heats up increase, decrease or stay the same? What property of the cable itself does this heating also depend on?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The heating increases when the current increases. It also depends on the cable's resistance: the greater the cable's resistance, the more power is wasted heating it for the same current.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The heating depends only on the supply voltage, not on the current.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner cannot yet attribute cable losses to the current, so the whole argument for transmitting at high voltage (high voltage gives a smaller current, so less heating) will not make sense.

common_wrong_answers.answer: A good conductor such as copper has no resistance, so it does not heat up at all.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats a cable as a perfect conductor and will see no reason why power is lost in transmission lines in the first place.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This lesson explains high-voltage transmission by showing that a smaller current wastes much less power in the cables; that argument is only meaningful if the learner already accepts that cable heating grows with the current and depends on the cable's resistance.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Recall a familiar example (a thin extension lead getting warm under a heavy load) and state the rule that the power wasted in a cable depends on the current in it and on its resistance, before meeting $P=I^2R$.

theory_blocks.title: Two coils, linked only by a changing field
theory_blocks.body:
A transformer has two separate coils, the **primary** and the **secondary**, wound around a shared **soft-iron core**; [[blue:the two coils are not electrically connected to each other at all]]. The core is made of soft iron because it is very easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it can follow a rapidly changing field; its job is to carry the magnetic field efficiently from one coil to the other, so that almost all of the field produced by the primary coil also links the secondary coil.

An alternating current in the primary coil produces a continuously changing field in the core; since that same changing field links the secondary coil, it induces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary coil too, by exactly the induction rule met in the previous lesson. No charge ever actually crosses from the primary coil to the secondary: the energy is carried entirely by the changing magnetic field in the core.

assets.caption: A transformer: the primary coil (left) and secondary coil (right) are wound on the same soft-iron core but never touch each other electrically; the primary's alternating current produces a changing field in the core, which induces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary.
assets.purpose: Show the primary coil, secondary coil and shared core as physically separate windings linked only through the core, as required by 's assets_summary.

theory_blocks.title: The turns ratio: step-up and step-down
theory_blocks.body:
For an ideal transformer, the ratio of the primary and secondary voltages equals the ratio of the number of turns on each coil:
$$\frac{V_p}{V_s}=\frac{N_p}{N_s}.$$
A **step-down** transformer has fewer secondary turns than primary turns ($N_s<N_p$), so $V_s<V_p$: for example, $240\,\mathrm{V}$ on a primary coil of $600$ turns, with a secondary coil of $100$ turns, gives $V_s=240\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{100}{600}=40\,\mathrm{V}$.

A **step-up** transformer has more secondary turns than primary turns ($N_s>N_p$), so $V_s>V_p$: for example, $12\,\mathrm{V}$ on a primary coil of $50$ turns, with a secondary coil of $1000$ turns, gives $V_s=12\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{1000}{50}=240\,\mathrm{V}$. The same equation works in both directions: it is the ratio of turns, not any fixed rule about which coil is 'first', that decides whether a transformer steps voltage up or down.

theory_blocks.title: Conservation of power: the ideal transformer equation
theory_blocks.body:
An ideal transformer, with no losses, conserves power: the power delivered to the primary coil equals the power delivered by the secondary coil,
$$I_pV_p=I_sV_s.$$
This is a direct consequence of energy conservation applied to the transformer, not a separate assumption: whatever power goes in at the primary must come out at the secondary, with nowhere else for it to go in the ideal case.

For the step-down example above ($V_p=240\,\mathrm{V}$, $V_s=40\,\mathrm{V}$), if the secondary supplies a current of $I_s=3\,\mathrm{A}$, the primary current is $I_p=\dfrac{I_sV_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{3\,\mathrm{A}\times40\,\mathrm{V}}{240\,\mathrm{V}}=0.5\,\mathrm{A}$. Check: primary power $=0.5\,\mathrm{A}\times240\,\mathrm{V}=120\,\mathrm{W}$, and secondary power $=3\,\mathrm{A}\times40\,\mathrm{V}=120\,\mathrm{W}$, exactly equal, as required. Notice that the step-down transformer's smaller output voltage comes with a correspondingly larger output current, not a loss of power: a real transformer has small losses, so $100\%$ power conservation is always an idealisation, but a very good one for the transformers met at this level.

theory_blocks.title: Why high-voltage transmission wastes less power
theory_blocks.body:
Electricity is transmitted across the country at very high voltage, then stepped down close to where it is used. The reason follows a short, fixed chain of reasoning: for a fixed amount of power $P$ being transmitted, $P=IV$ means **a higher transmission voltage requires a correspondingly lower current**, since $I=P/V$. The cables themselves have some resistance $R$, and the power wasted heating them is $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$: because this loss depends on the *square* of the current, even a modest reduction in current gives a much larger reduction in wasted power.

For example, transmitting $5000\,\mathrm{W}$ through a cable of resistance $10\,\Omega$ at $250\,\mathrm{V}$ needs a current of $I=5000\,\mathrm{W}\div250\,\mathrm{V}=20\,\mathrm{A}$, wasting $P_{\text{loss}}=(20\,\mathrm{A})^2\times10\,\Omega=4000\,\mathrm{W}$, most of the power. Transmitting the same $5000\,\mathrm{W}$ through the same cable at $2500\,\mathrm{V}$ instead needs only $I=5000\,\mathrm{W}\div2500\,\mathrm{V}=2\,\mathrm{A}$, wasting just $P_{\text{loss}}=(2\,\mathrm{A})^2\times10\,\Omega=40\,\mathrm{W}$: a hundred times less, for ten times the voltage. Step-up transformers raise the voltage for this efficient transmission, and step-down transformers lower it again to a safe, usable voltage before it reaches homes and other buildings.

keywords.definition: The transformer coil connected to the input (supply) voltage.
The transformer coil connected to the output (load) voltage, linked to the primary only through the shared core's changing field.
The shared core that carries the magnetic field efficiently between a transformer's primary and secondary coils.
The power wasted as heat in a cable or conductor due to its resistance, equal to the square of the current times the resistance.

worked_examples.statement: **A step-down transformer.** A transformer's primary coil has $600$ turns and is connected to a $240\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Its secondary coil has $100$ turns. Calculate the secondary voltage, and state whether this is a step-up or a step-down transformer.
reasoning: Rearrange $V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ to make $V_s$ the subject: $V_s=V_p\times N_s/N_p$.
worked_examples.solution: $V_s=240\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{100}{600}=40\,\mathrm{V}$. Since $N_s<N_p$ and $V_s<V_p$, this is a step-down transformer.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $V_p/V_s=240/40=6$ and $N_p/N_s=600/100=6$, the same ratio, confirming the calculation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing by the wrong ratio, for example calculating $V_s=V_p\times N_p/N_s$ instead, which would give a voltage larger than $V_p$ for what is actually a step-down transformer.

worked_examples.statement: **A step-up transformer, with current.** A transformer's primary coil has $50$ turns and is connected to a $12\,\mathrm{V}$ supply, drawing a primary current of $5.0\,\mathrm{A}$. Its secondary coil has $1000$ turns. Calculate (a) the secondary voltage, and (b) the secondary current, assuming an ideal transformer.
reasoning: Find $V_s$ from the turns ratio first.
Use $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$ (power conservation) to find $I_s$.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $V_s=12\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{1000}{50}=240\,\mathrm{V}$. (b) $I_s=\dfrac{I_pV_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{5.0\,\mathrm{A}\times12\,\mathrm{V}}{240\,\mathrm{V}}=0.25\,\mathrm{A}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: primary power $=5.0\,\mathrm{A}\times12\,\mathrm{V}=60\,\mathrm{W}$; secondary power $=0.25\,\mathrm{A}\times240\,\mathrm{V}=60\,\mathrm{W}$, equal, as power conservation requires. Notice the secondary current is much smaller than the primary current, even though the secondary voltage is much larger: the step-up in voltage is exactly matched by a step-down in current.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming a step-up transformer increases both voltage and current, which would make the secondary power larger than the primary power, violating power conservation.

worked_examples.statement: **Two transmission voltages compared.** A power station transmits $5000\,\mathrm{W}$ along a cable of resistance $10\,\Omega$. Compare the power wasted as heat when this is transmitted at $250\,\mathrm{V}$ with when it is transmitted at $2500\,\mathrm{V}$ instead.
reasoning: Find the transmission current at each voltage using $I=P/V$.
Find the power wasted at each current using $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$.
worked_examples.solution: At $250\,\mathrm{V}$: $I=5000\,\mathrm{W}\div250\,\mathrm{V}=20\,\mathrm{A}$, so $P_{\text{loss}}=(20\,\mathrm{A})^2\times10\,\Omega=4000\,\mathrm{W}$. At $2500\,\mathrm{V}$: $I=5000\,\mathrm{W}\div2500\,\mathrm{V}=2\,\mathrm{A}$, so $P_{\text{loss}}=(2\,\mathrm{A})^2\times10\,\Omega=40\,\mathrm{W}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Raising the voltage by a factor of $10$ lowers the current by a factor of $10$, which, because the loss depends on current *squared*, lowers the wasted power by a factor of $10^2=100$: from $4000\,\mathrm{W}$ down to just $40\,\mathrm{W}$, for the same $5000\,\mathrm{W}$ being usefully transmitted.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the wasted power falls by the same factor as the voltage rises (a factor of $10$), rather than by the square of that factor (a factor of $100$), because $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$ depends on current squared.

worked_examples.statement: **A realistic distribution transformer.** A local substation transformer has a primary coil of $2000$ turns connected to an $11\,000\,\mathrm{V}$ supply cable, and a secondary coil of $40$ turns. (a) Calculate the secondary (output) voltage. (b) If the secondary supplies a current of $10\,\mathrm{A}$, calculate the primary current, assuming an ideal transformer. (c) Confirm that primary and secondary power are equal.
reasoning: Find $V_s$ from the turns ratio.
Use $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$ to find $I_p$.
Calculate both powers and compare.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $V_s=11\,000\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{40}{2000}=220\,\mathrm{V}$. (b) $I_p=\dfrac{I_sV_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{10\,\mathrm{A}\times220\,\mathrm{V}}{11\,000\,\mathrm{V}}=0.20\,\mathrm{A}$. (c) Primary power $=0.20\,\mathrm{A}\times11\,000\,\mathrm{V}=2200\,\mathrm{W}$; secondary power $=10\,\mathrm{A}\times220\,\mathrm{V}=2200\,\mathrm{W}$: equal, as required.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is a realistic local distribution transformer ($11\,000\,\mathrm{V}$ is a common local distribution voltage), stepping the high transmission voltage down to a safer, usable level; the same two equations used throughout this lesson handle a genuinely large voltage exactly as easily as a small laboratory example.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Losing track of which quantity ($V_p$, $N_p$, $N_s$) belongs in the numerator versus the denominator when the numbers involved are large, rather than carefully substituting into $V_s=V_pN_s/N_p$ as written.

guided_exercises.statement: A transformer's primary coil has $200$ turns connected to a $100\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Its secondary coil has $20$ turns. Calculate the secondary voltage.
hints: Write down $V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ and identify each known value.
Rearrange to make $V_s$ the subject.
Check your answer is smaller than $V_p$, consistent with $N_s<N_p$.
guided_exercises.answer: $V_s=100\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{20}{200}=10\,\mathrm{V}$.
common_errors: Using the turns ratio upside down, giving a secondary voltage larger than the primary voltage despite the secondary having fewer turns.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Write down $V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ and identify each known value.

**Step 2 — Method:** Rearrange to make $V_s$ the subject.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $V_s=100\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{20}{200}=10\,\mathrm{V}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer is smaller than $V_p$, consistent with $N_s<N_p$.

guided_exercises.statement: A transformer has a secondary coil of $50$ turns and produces $12\,\mathrm{V}$ from a $240\,\mathrm{V}$ primary supply. Calculate the number of turns on the primary coil.
hints: Write down $V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ and identify each known value.
Rearrange to make $N_p$ the subject this time.
Check your answer is larger than $N_s$, consistent with this being a step-down transformer.
guided_exercises.answer: $N_p=N_s\times\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=50\times\dfrac{240}{12}=1000$ turns.
common_errors: Substituting the known turns value, $50$, in place of $N_p$ instead of $N_s$, which inverts the whole calculation.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Write down $V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ and identify each known value.

**Step 2 — Method:** Rearrange to make $N_p$ the subject this time.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $N_p=N_s\times\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=50\times\dfrac{240}{12}=1000$ turns.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer is larger than $N_s$, consistent with this being a step-down transformer.

exercises.statement: A transformer's primary coil has $100$ turns connected to a $9.0\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Its secondary coil has $400$ turns. Calculate the secondary voltage, and state whether this is step-up or step-down.
exercises.answer: $V_s=9.0\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{400}{100}=36\,\mathrm{V}$; this is a step-up transformer, since $V_s>V_p$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $V_p/V_s=9.0/36=0.25$ and $N_p/N_s=100/400=0.25$, the same ratio.

exercises.statement: A transformer's primary coil draws a current of $4.0\,\mathrm{A}$ from a $120\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Its secondary voltage is $24\,\mathrm{V}$. Calculate the secondary current, assuming an ideal transformer.
exercises.answer: Primary power $=4.0\,\mathrm{A}\times120\,\mathrm{V}=480\,\mathrm{W}$; secondary current $=480\,\mathrm{W}\div24\,\mathrm{V}=20\,\mathrm{A}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $20\,\mathrm{A}\times24\,\mathrm{V}=480\,\mathrm{W}$, equal to the primary power, as power conservation requires.

exercises.statement: A student connects a transformer's primary coil to a steady $12\,\mathrm{V}$ battery instead of an a.c. supply. Explain what the secondary coil's voltmeter reads once the current has settled, and why.
exercises.answer: Once the current has settled to a steady value, the secondary voltmeter reads (close to) zero.
exercises.full_solution: A steady direct current produces a steady, unchanging field in the core once it has settled; with nothing left changing, no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil. Only the brief moments when the current is changing, right as the battery is connected or disconnected, induce any secondary e.m.f. at all.

exercises.statement: Using the current-and-$I^2R$ reasoning from this lesson, explain why the National Grid uses a step-up transformer near a power station and a step-down transformer near the homes and buildings that use the electricity, rather than transmitting electricity at the voltage it is generated or used at throughout.
exercises.answer: Stepping the voltage up near the power station allows the same power to be transmitted at a much lower current, which greatly reduces the $I^2R$ heating loss in the long transmission cables; stepping the voltage back down near homes and buildings then brings it to a lower, safer voltage suitable for ordinary use, after the efficient high-voltage transmission is complete.
exercises.full_solution: Stepping the voltage up near the power station allows the same power to be transmitted at a much lower current, which greatly reduces the $I^2R$ heating loss in the long transmission cables; stepping the voltage back down near homes and buildings then brings it to a lower, safer voltage suitable for ordinary use, after the efficient high-voltage transmission is complete.

exam_questions.statement: A transformer's primary coil has $1150$ turns connected to a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. Its secondary coil has $50$ turns. (a) Calculate the secondary voltage. (b) State whether this is a step-up or step-down transformer, with a reason.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $V_s=230\,\mathrm{V}\times\dfrac{50}{1150}=10\,\mathrm{V}$. (b) Step-down, because the secondary coil has fewer turns than the primary ($50<1150$), and the secondary voltage is smaller than the primary voltage ($10\,\mathrm{V}<230\,\mathrm{V}$).
exam_questions.full_solution: Check: $230/10=23$ and $1150/50=23$, the same ratio, confirming the calculation.
mark_scheme: Rearranges $V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ correctly.
Calculates the secondary voltage correctly: $10\,\mathrm{V}$.
States step-down correctly.
Gives a reason referring to both the turns and the voltage comparison.
common_errors: Inverting the turns ratio and calculating a secondary voltage larger than $230\,\mathrm{V}$.

exam_questions.statement: A transformer's primary coil has $2000$ turns connected to a $230\,\mathrm{V}$ supply; its secondary voltage is $11.5\,\mathrm{V}$. (a) Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil. (b) The primary current is $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate the secondary current, assuming an ideal transformer. (c) Explain, using $P=I^2R$, why a real transmission cable carrying the larger of these two currents (rather than the smaller one) would need to have a low resistance to avoid significant power loss.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $N_s=N_p\times\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=2000\times\dfrac{11.5}{230}=100$. (b) $I_s=\dfrac{I_pV_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times230\,\mathrm{V}}{11.5\,\mathrm{V}}=40\,\mathrm{A}$. (c) The $40\,\mathrm{A}$ secondary current is much larger than the $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ primary current; since $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$ depends on current squared, carrying this larger current through any resistance at all would waste far more power as heat than the smaller primary current would, so a cable expected to carry it needs a correspondingly low resistance to keep that loss acceptable.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $N_s=N_p\times\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=2000\times\dfrac{11.5}{230}=100$. (b) $I_s=\dfrac{I_pV_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{2.0\,\mathrm{A}\times230\,\mathrm{V}}{11.5\,\mathrm{V}}=40\,\mathrm{A}$. (c) The $40\,\mathrm{A}$ secondary current is much larger than the $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ primary current; since $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$ depends on current squared, carrying this larger current through any resistance at all would waste far more power as heat than the smaller primary current would, so a cable expected to carry it needs a correspondingly low resistance to keep that loss acceptable.
mark_scheme: Calculates the secondary turns correctly: $100$.
Calculates the secondary current correctly: $40\,\mathrm{A}$.
Identifies that the secondary current is larger than the primary current.
States that $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$ depends on current squared.
Links the larger current to a greater risk of power loss, requiring low cable resistance.
(b) Uses $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$ with the correct values substituted (method mark).
common_errors: Calculating the secondary current correctly but then not connecting it back to the $I^2R$ reasoning required in part (c).

challenge_questions.statement: A power station transmits $10\,000\,000\,\mathrm{W}$ ($10\,\mathrm{MW}$) of power along a cable of resistance $5.0\,\Omega$. Compare the power wasted as heat, both in watts and as a percentage of the transmitted power, when this is transmitted at $400\,000\,\mathrm{V}$ (a realistic high-voltage transmission line) with when it is transmitted at $25\,000\,\mathrm{V}$ instead.
hints: Find the transmission current at each voltage using $I=P/V$.
Find the power wasted at each current using $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$.
Express each loss as a percentage of the $10\,000\,000\,\mathrm{W}$ transmitted, by dividing and multiplying by $100$.
challenge_questions.answer: At $400\,000\,\mathrm{V}$: $I=10\,000\,000\,\mathrm{W}\div400\,000\,\mathrm{V}=25\,\mathrm{A}$, so $P_{\text{loss}}=(25\,\mathrm{A})^2\times5.0\,\Omega=3125\,\mathrm{W}$, about $0.03\%$ of the transmitted power. At $25\,000\,\mathrm{V}$: $I=10\,000\,000\,\mathrm{W}\div25\,000\,\mathrm{V}=400\,\mathrm{A}$, so $P_{\text{loss}}=(400\,\mathrm{A})^2\times5.0\,\Omega=800\,000\,\mathrm{W}$, about $8.0\%$ of the transmitted power.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The $16$-fold increase in voltage (from $25\,000\,\mathrm{V}$ to $400\,000\,\mathrm{V}$) gives a $16$-fold decrease in current, and because $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$ depends on current squared, this is a $16^2=256$-fold decrease in wasted power ($800\,000\,\mathrm{W}\div3125\,\mathrm{W}=256$), which is why real transmission lines operate at several hundred thousand volts rather than tens of thousands.

mcq.stem: A transformer's primary coil is connected to a steady direct current from a battery, instead of an a.c. supply. What does the secondary coil's voltmeter read once the current has settled to a steady value?

options.text: The same steady voltage the turns ratio would predict for an a.c. supply.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the turns-ratio equation assumes a continuously changing field; a steady direct current, once settled, produces no changing field at all.

options.text: Zero, because a steady current produces no changing field to induce a secondary e.m.f.
A steady voltage, but smaller than the turns ratio would predict.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes some reduced but still steady secondary voltage; with no changing field once the current has settled, the induced e.m.f. is zero, not merely reduced.

options.text: An alternating voltage, generated by the transformer itself.
options.why_wrong: invents an alternating output a transformer cannot produce from a steady input; a transformer cannot create alternation that is not present in its primary current.

mcq.explanation: A transformer works by electromagnetic induction, which needs a continuously changing field; once a direct current has settled to a steady value, the field in the core stops changing, and no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil.

mcq.stem: A fixed amount of power is transmitted along a cable. If the transmission voltage is increased, what happens to the transmission current?

options.text: It increases, in proportion to the voltage.
options.why_wrong: has the relationship backwards; for a fixed power, $P=IV$ means current and voltage vary inversely, not together.

options.text: It stays the same, since the power is fixed.
options.why_wrong: ignores that current must adjust for a fixed power to be maintained at a different voltage; both cannot stay fixed if the other changes, by $P=IV$.

options.text: It decreases.
It cannot be determined without knowing the cable's resistance.
options.why_wrong: is unnecessary information; $I=P/V$ gives the transmission current directly from the fixed power and the voltage, without needing the cable's resistance.

mcq.explanation: For a fixed transmitted power, $P=IV$ means a higher voltage requires a correspondingly lower current, since $I=P/V$.

mcq.stem: An ideal step-up transformer increases the voltage from $10\,\mathrm{V}$ to $100\,\mathrm{V}$. What happens to the power delivered?

options.text: It increases by the same factor as the voltage, becoming $10$ times larger.
options.why_wrong: contradicts power conservation; an ideal transformer's output power equals its input power, it is never multiplied by the voltage step-up factor.

options.text: It decreases, since increasing voltage always comes at the cost of some power.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes a cost with no basis in an ideal transformer, where power is conserved exactly, not reduced simply because the voltage has changed.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the number of turns on each coil.
options.why_wrong: is unnecessary information; power conservation ($I_pV_p=I_sV_s$) holds for an ideal transformer regardless of the specific turns numbers.

options.text: It stays the same; the larger output voltage is accompanied by a correspondingly smaller output current.

mcq.explanation: An ideal transformer conserves power ($I_pV_p=I_sV_s$): a step-up in voltage is always matched by a step-down in current, so the delivered power is unchanged.

mcq.stem: Why does the National Grid transmit electricity at a very high voltage rather than at the voltage used in homes?

options.text: A high voltage lowers the transmission current, which greatly reduces $I^2R$ heating loss in the cables.
A high voltage makes the electrons move faster, delivering the power sooner.
options.why_wrong: misidentifies the mechanism; the advantage of high-voltage transmission is a reduced $I^2R$ heating loss from a lower current, not a change in delivery speed.

options.text: A high voltage reduces the total power that needs to be generated.
options.why_wrong: confuses the transmission voltage with the amount of power generated; the same useful power is transmitted either way, only the current (and so the loss) changes with voltage.

options.text: A high voltage is simply the standard the generators happen to produce.
options.why_wrong: misses the actual reason; generators do not naturally produce transmission-level voltages, step-up transformers raise the voltage specifically for efficient transmission.

mcq.explanation: For a fixed transmitted power, a higher voltage means a lower current, and since cable heating loss is $I^2R$, this lower current gives a much smaller power loss, which is the entire reason for transmitting at high voltage.

flashcards.front: Name the three main parts of a transformer.
flashcards.back: A primary coil, a secondary coil, and a shared soft-iron core that carries the magnetic field between them.

flashcards.front: State the turns-ratio equation and the ideal power equation for a transformer.
flashcards.back: $V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ (turns ratio) and $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$ (ideal power conservation).

flashcards.front: Does a transformer work with a steady direct current, once the current has settled?
flashcards.back: No. A transformer needs a continuously changing field to induce a secondary e.m.f.; a steady, settled direct current produces no changing field and induces nothing.

flashcards.front: Compare what happens to current when voltage is stepped up by a transformer, versus what happens to power.
flashcards.back: Stepping voltage up steps current down by the same factor (power conserved, $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$); it does not increase the power delivered.

flashcards.front: Why does raising the transmission voltage reduce power lost in cables, even though the cables' resistance has not changed?
flashcards.back: A higher voltage means a lower current for the same transmitted power ($I=P/V$); since cable loss is $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$, a lower current gives a much smaller loss, even with the same resistance.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A transformer works just as well with a steady direct current as with an alternating current.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A transformer is often first pictured simply as 'a device that changes voltage', without emphasising that the mechanism inside it depends specifically on a changing field.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a transformer will produce a steady, correctly scaled secondary voltage when its primary coil is connected to a steady battery instead of an a.c. supply.
misconceptions.correct_model: A transformer works by electromagnetic induction: the primary coil's current must be continuously changing (as it is with a.c.) to produce a continuously changing field in the core, which is what induces an e.m.f. in the secondary coil. A steady direct current produces a steady, unchanging field, which induces nothing in the secondary coil at all, except for a brief pulse at the instant the direct current is switched on or off.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace the full causal chain explicitly: changing primary current, changing field in the core, changing field linking the secondary, induced secondary e.m.f.; show that a steady current breaks this chain at the very first step.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Raising the voltage for transmission also raises the current, for the same transmitted power.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Voltage and current are often remembered as varying together (for example, in a fixed resistor, both might be adjusted together), so it is tempting to assume they always increase or decrease together.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states that a higher transmission voltage means a higher transmission current, while describing this as an advantage.
misconceptions.correct_model: For a fixed amount of power being transmitted, $P=IV$ means current and voltage vary inversely: raising the voltage lowers the current needed to transmit the same power, it does not raise it. This falling current, not a falling voltage, is exactly what reduces the $I^2R$ heating loss in the cables.
misconceptions.remediation: Hold the transmitted power fixed and calculate the current at two different voltages explicitly, showing the higher voltage gives the lower current.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A step-up transformer creates extra electrical power, since its output voltage is larger than its input voltage.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A larger output number (voltage) is easy to read as 'more', without checking what happens to the matching current at the same time.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a step-up transformer as increasing the total power available, rather than only redistributing the same power between voltage and current.
misconceptions.correct_model: An ideal transformer conserves power: $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$. A step-up transformer's larger output voltage is always accompanied by a correspondingly smaller output current, so the output power equals the input power, not more than it.
misconceptions.remediation: Calculate both the primary and secondary power for a step-up example explicitly and show the two values are equal, not different.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a transformer works the same way with a steady direct current as with an alternating current.
common_mistakes.why: A transformer is often first pictured simply as 'a device that changes voltage', without emphasising that its mechanism depends on a changing field.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Trace the full chain explicitly: changing current, changing field, induced secondary e.m.f.; check that each step actually requires change.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a higher transmission voltage means a higher transmission current, for the same transmitted power.
common_mistakes.why: Voltage and current are sometimes remembered as varying together, rather than checking the specific relationship $P=IV$ for a fixed power.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate the current at two different voltages explicitly, using $I=P/V$ with the power held fixed, rather than guessing the direction of the relationship.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a step-up transformer as creating extra electrical power.
common_mistakes.why: A larger output voltage number is easy to read as simply 'more', without checking what has happened to the matching current.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate both the primary and secondary power explicitly and confirm they are equal, using $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$.

exam_notes: Always state explicitly which transformer equation you are using ($V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ for voltages and turns, or $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$ for power conservation); mixing the two up part-way through a calculation is a common source of lost marks.
A transmission-loss question almost always expects $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$ with the transmission current found first from $I=P/V$, not a resistance calculation done directly on the transmitted power.
State explicitly that $100\%$ power conservation ($I_pV_p=I_sV_s$) is an idealisation for a real transformer, if a question asks about efficiency or losses in a real device.

summary.big_idea: A transformer links two separate coils only through a changing magnetic field in a shared core, so it needs alternating current to work at all; its turns ratio sets the output voltage, power is conserved between primary and secondary, and transmitting power at high voltage sharply cuts the $I^2R$ heating loss in cables.
key_points: A transformer's primary and secondary coils are not electrically connected; energy crosses between them only through a changing field in the shared soft-iron core.
A steady direct current produces no changing field once settled, so a transformer induces nothing from a steady d.c. supply.
$V_p/V_s=N_p/N_s$ relates voltage to turns; $I_pV_p=I_sV_s$ expresses ideal power conservation.
For a fixed transmitted power, a higher voltage means a lower current; since $P_{\text{loss}}=I^2R$ depends on current squared, this sharply reduces cable heating loss.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A transformer needs a changing field to work at all, so it needs a.c.; its turns ratio sets the voltage, power is conserved (not created), and high-voltage transmission wins because $I^2R$ loss falls with the square of the (now smaller) current.

summary.big_idea: Use the key physics ideas and methods from electricity and magnetism accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: Which one of these statements is true? A magnet attracts: (A) plastics, (B) any metal, (C) iron and steel, (D) aluminium, (E) carbon.
exercises.answer: C — iron and steel.
exercises.full_solution: A magnet only attracts 'magnetic' materials: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt (and their alloys). It does NOT attract all metals — aluminium, copper, brass, gold and most other metals are non-magnetic, and plastics and carbon are not metals at all and are not attracted either. So option C (iron and steel) is the only correct choice; B is a common wrong answer because people assume 'metal' automatically means 'magnetic', which is false.

exercises.statement: the supplied diagram shows a plotting compass placed near one end of an unlabelled bar magnet, with the compass needle already deflected away from the magnet. Label the N pole of the magnet and draw the field line on which the compass lies.
exercises.answer: The end of the magnet nearer the compass (the end the needle points away from) is the N pole; the field line is the smooth curve that starts at this N pole, passes through the compass in the same direction as the needle, and curves round to end at the S pole.
exercises.full_solution: A plotting-compass needle always settles so that it lies along the magnetic field line at its position, with its N-seeking (pointer) end pointing in the direction of the field there. Magnetic field lines, by convention, leave a magnet at its N pole, curve round through the space outside the magnet, and re-enter at its S pole. So, to label the poles: look at the direction the needle points. The needle points AWAY from the N pole and curves around towards the S pole. In the supplied diagram the needle deflects away from the end of the bar nearest the compass, so that nearby end must be the magnet's N pole (field lines diverge outward from it), and the far end is the S pole. The field line through the compass position is then drawn as a single smooth curve: starting at the N pole, passing through the compass position pointing in the same direction as the needle arrow, and curving round to terminate at the S pole — exactly as the other field lines already drawn around a bar magnet would look. (This is a drawing/labelling exercise, so the 'answer' here is the reasoning used to decide which end is N and how the line must be drawn, rather than a single numeric result.)

assets.caption: the supplied diagram, redrawn: a plotting compass placed just beyond one end of a bar magnet whose poles are not labelled. The red tip is the needle's N-seeking end, and it points away from the nearer end of the magnet.
assets.purpose: Show the geometry the question depends on: which end of the magnet the compass is near, and which way its N-seeking end points.

exercises.statement: Two identical conducting balls, suspended on nylon threads from the same point, come to rest with the threads making equal angles with the vertical (the supplied diagram). Which of these statements is true? (A) the balls are equally and oppositely charged; (B) the balls are oppositely charged but not necessarily equally charged; (C) one ball is charged and the other is uncharged; (D) the balls both carry the same type of charge; (E) one is charged and the other may or may not be charged.
exercises.answer: D — the balls both carry the same type (sign) of charge.
exercises.full_solution: For the two threads to spread apart into equal angles, the balls must be pushing each other apart, i.e. the force between them must be repulsive — and repulsion between charged objects only happens when both charges have the SAME sign (both positive or both negative). If the charges were opposite (as in A or B) the balls would attract and swing together, not apart. By Newton's third law the force each ball exerts on the other is always equal and opposite, regardless of how the charge happens to be shared between them, so the two (identical-mass, identical-length-thread) balls must hang at the same angle whenever they repel — this is true whether the charges are equal or very different in size. So the angles being equal tells us only that the charges are of the same sign (repulsion), not that they are equal in amount; that matches option D exactly and rules out A, B, C and E.

exercises.statement: Explain in terms of electron movement what happens when a polythene rod becomes charged negatively by being rubbed with a cloth.
exercises.answer: Friction strips electrons off the cloth and transfers them onto the rod; the rod ends up with a surplus of electrons (net negative charge) and the cloth with a deficit of electrons (net positive charge).
exercises.full_solution: Rubbing two insulators together transfers electrons from one surface to the other (it does not create or destroy charge — the total charge is conserved). Polythene holds onto its electrons more strongly than the cloth does, so when the two are rubbed together, electrons are pulled from the cloth's atoms and deposited on the polythene's surface. The polythene rod therefore ends up with more electrons than protons overall, i.e. a net negative charge, while the cloth — having lost those electrons — is left with more protons than electrons, i.e. a net positive charge equal in size to the rod's negative charge.

exercises.statement: Which of statements A to E is true? In the process of electrostatic induction: (A) a conductor is rubbed with an insulator; (B) a charge is produced by friction; (C) negative and positive charges are separated; (D) a positive charge induces a positive charge; (E) electrons are 'sprayed' into an object.
exercises.answer: C — negative and positive charges are separated.
exercises.full_solution: Electrostatic induction is the redistribution of charge that already exists within a conductor when a charged object is brought near it (no contact and no friction are needed, so A, B and E, which describe charging by friction/contact, do not describe induction). The free electrons in the conductor are repelled or attracted by the nearby charge, so they redistribute: the end nearer an external positive charge becomes negatively charged (electrons are attracted there) while the far end becomes positively charged (depleted of electrons) — i.e. the induced charge nearest the inducing charge is always OPPOSITE in sign to it, never the same sign, which rules out D. This separation of the conductor's own negative and positive charge to opposite ends is exactly what option C describes, with no net charge created on the conductor overall.

exercises.statement: If the current in a floodlamp is 5 A, what charge passes in (a) 1 s, (b) 10 s, (c) 5 minutes?
exercises.full_solution: Charge and current are related by Q = I × t (charge = current × time, with time in seconds). Here I = 5 A throughout, so: (a) t = 1 s → Q = 5 × 1 = 5 C. (b) t = 10 s → Q = 5 × 10 = 50 C. (c) t = 5 minutes = 5 × 60 = 300 s → Q = 5 × 300 = 1500 C.

exercises.statement: What is the current in a circuit if the charge passing each point is (a) 10 C in 2 s, (b) 20 C in 40 s, (c) 240 C in 2 minutes?
exercises.full_solution: Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t (with t in seconds). (a) I = 10/2 = 5 A. (b) I = 20/40 = 0.5 A. (c) t = 2 minutes = 120 s, so I = 240/120 = 2 A.

exercises.statement: The p.d. across the lamp in the supplied diagram is 12 V. How many joules of electrical energy are changed into light and heat when (a) a charge of 1 C passes through it, (b) a charge of 5 C passes through it, (c) a current of 2 A flows in it for 10 s?
exercises.full_solution: The energy transferred when charge Q passes through a p.d. of V is W = Q × V (this follows directly from the definition of the volt: 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb). Here V = 12 V. (a) Q = 1 C → W = 1 × 12 = 12 J. (b) Q = 5 C → W = 5 × 12 = 60 J. (c) First find the charge: Q = I × t = 2 A × 10 s = 20 C, then W = Q × V = 20 × 12 = 240 J.

exercises.statement: What is the resistance of a lamp when a voltage of 12 V across it causes a current of 4 A?
exercises.full_solution: By Ohm's law, resistance R = V/I. Substituting the given values: R = 12 V ÷ 4 A = 3 Ω.

exercises.statement: Calculate the p.d. across a 10 Ω resistor carrying a current of 2 A.
exercises.full_solution: By Ohm's law, V = I × R. Substituting: V = 2 A × 10 Ω = 20 V.

exercises.statement: The p.d. across a 3 Ω resistor is 6 V. What is the current flowing (in ampere)? (A) 1/2, (B) 1, (C) 2, (D) 6, (E) 8.
exercises.answer: C — 2 A.
exercises.full_solution: By Ohm's law, I = V/R = 6 V ÷ 3 Ω = 2 A, which is option C.

exercises.statement: (a) The graph in the supplied diagram shows how the p.d. across the ends of a conductor varies with the current in it. (i) What law may be deduced from the graph? (ii) What is the resistance of the conductor? (b) Draw diagrams to show how six 2 V lamps could be lit to normal brightness when using (i) a 2 V supply, (ii) a 6 V supply, (iii) a 12 V supply.
exercises.answer: (a)(i) Ohm's law (V is directly proportional to I for this conductor at constant temperature); (ii) R ≈ 2 Ω. (b)(i) all six lamps in parallel across the 2 V supply; (ii) two parallel branches, each of three lamps in series, across the 6 V supply; (iii) all six lamps in a single series loop across the 12 V supply.
exercises.full_solution: (a)(i) The graph is a straight line through the origin, showing that p.d. is directly proportional to current — this is Ohm's law. (ii) Resistance is the gradient of the V–I graph (R = V/I). Reading a convenient point on the line, e.g. I = 3 A gives V = 6 V, so R = 6/3 = 2 Ω (any other point on the same straight line through the origin gives the same gradient). (b) Each lamp needs exactly 2 V across it (and its rated current) for normal brightness, so the arrangement must give every lamp 2 V: (i) On a 2 V supply, each lamp must be connected directly across the full supply, so all six lamps must be wired in PARALLEL with each other (each branch then has the full 2 V across it). (ii) On a 6 V supply, 3 lamps in series share the 6 V equally (3 × 2 V = 6 V), so each lamp again gets 2 V; to use all six lamps, make two such series strings of 3 lamps and connect the two strings in parallel with each other across the 6 V supply. (iii) On a 12 V supply, 6 lamps in series share the 12 V equally (6 × 2 V = 12 V), so simply wire all six lamps in a single series loop across the 12 V supply.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P5 Questions, Q12 and Figure P5.30

exercises.statement: Study the five circuits A-E in the supplied diagram. Each is a single loop containing the same battery and the same three lamps P, Q and R, and in each the switch S is open (there is a break in the circuit at that point). In circuits B, C and E there is also an extra plain connecting wire, with no component in it, joining a point on the top wire to the return wire at the bottom. In which circuit would lamps Q and R light but not lamp P?
exercises.answer: Circuit B.
exercises.full_solution: In circuit B there is a connecting wire linking the junction just after switch S (between P and Q) straight down to the return wire that goes back to the battery. Because this link is a plain wire (no component in it), it ties that junction directly to the battery's other terminal. This means lamps Q and R are connected directly across the battery through this link, completely independently of switch S and lamp P — so Q and R light up (indeed they would light with S either open or closed). Lamp P, on the other hand, has both of its terminals effectively tied to the same node once the link is taken into account (one side through the plain return wire, the other side through S when closed), so no p.d. ever appears across P and it never lights; with S open, P's only possible path is broken anyway. Checking the others: in A and D, P, Q, R and S are all in one series loop with no extra link, so opening S breaks the only path and none of the lamps light. In C the link joins the point between P and Q to the return wire, but S sits between Q and R, so the open switch is in the only path through R (and Q) back to the battery — nothing lights. In E the link is again between P and Q, but S is next to the battery, so opening S cuts the battery off from every lamp — nothing lights. Only circuit B gives exactly 'Q and R lit, P not lit'.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P6 Questions, Q1 and Figure P6.2

assets.caption: the supplied diagram, redrawn: the five circuits A to E. The switch S is open in every circuit, and the red wire in B, C and E is a plain connecting wire with no component in it, joining a point on the top wire to the return wire at the bottom.
assets.purpose: Show where the switch and the extra link wire sit in each of the five circuits, which is the whole of this question.

exercises.statement: Using the circuit in the supplied diagram (lamps A and B in series, with switch S1 in the main supply line and switch S2 connected in parallel with lamp A only), which of the following statements is correct? (A) When S1 and S2 are closed, lamps A and B are lit. (B) With S1 open and S2 closed, A is lit and B is not lit. (C) With S2 open and S1 closed, A and B are lit.
exercises.answer: C.
exercises.full_solution: S1 is in series with the whole circuit, so if S1 is open nothing can light at all (ruling out any reading of B that implies current flows with S1 open). S2 is wired in parallel with lamp A only, so S2 acts as a short-circuit switch for A: when S2 is closed, it provides a zero-resistance bypass around A, so essentially all the current takes that path and A does not light (it is shorted out), while B — in series with the rest of the circuit — still lights normally. That makes statement A false ('A and B are lit' when both switches closed — in fact A is shorted and stays dark). When S2 is open instead (and S1 closed), there is no bypass, so the current is forced to flow through lamp A as well as lamp B, completing a normal series circuit through both lamps — so both A and B light. That is exactly statement C, which is therefore the correct one.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P6 Questions, Q2 and Figure P6.3

exercises.statement: A p.d. of 24 V from a battery is applied to a network in which a 6 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel with each other, and this parallel combination is connected in series with an 8 Ω resistor across the 24 V supply. Find: (a) the combined resistance of the 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors in parallel; (b) the current in the 8 Ω resistor; (c) the voltage across the parallel network; (d) the current in the 6 Ω resistor.
exercises.full_solution: (a) For two resistors in parallel, 1/R₁ = 1/6 + 1/12 = 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4, so R₁ = 4 Ω (equivalently, product/sum = (6×12)/(6+12) = 72/18 = 4 Ω). (b) The 4 Ω parallel combination is in series with the 8 Ω resistor, so the total circuit resistance is R = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω. By Ohm's law the total (supply) current is I = V/R = 24/12 = 2 A; since the 8 Ω resistor carries the whole supply current (it's the only path before the circuit splits), the current in the 8 Ω resistor is 2 A. (c) The voltage across the parallel network equals this current times the parallel network's resistance: V₁ = I × R₁ = 2 A × 4 Ω = 8 V (check: the remaining 24 − 8 = 16 V must be across the 8 Ω resistor, and indeed I×8 = 2×8 = 16 V ✓, 8+16=24 V ✓). (d) The 6 Ω resistor has the full 8 V of the parallel network across it, so its current is I₆ = V₁/R₆ = 8/6 = 4/3 A ≈ 1.33 A. As a check, the 12 Ω branch current is 8/12 = 2/3 A, and 4/3 + 2/3 = 2 A, which correctly matches the total current found in part (b).

exercises.statement: The lamps and the cells in all six circuits of the supplied diagram are identical. If the lamp in circuit (a) [one cell, one lamp] has its full, normal brightness, what can you say about the brightness of the lamps in (b) [two cells in series, both facing the same way, one lamp], (c) [two cells facing the same way with a lamp between them in the loop, plus a second lamp in the return wire — i.e. two cells and two lamps all in series], (d) [two cells in series but connected in opposition, with their positive terminals facing each other, and two lamps in series], (e) [three cells in series, all facing the same way, two lamps in series] and (f) [three cells in series, two facing one way and the third reversed, one lamp]? (Look carefully at which way round each cell is: the long line is the positive terminal.)
exercises.answer: Taking the current in (a) as 1 unit (normal brightness): (b) 2 units — brighter than normal (the brightest of the six). (c) 1 unit — normal brightness, the same as (a). (d) The two cells oppose each other, so the net e.m.f. is zero: no current, the lamps do not light. (e) 1.5 units — brighter than normal, but dimmer than (b). (f) Two cells aid and one opposes, so the net e.m.f. is that of one cell: 1 unit — normal brightness, the same as (a).
exercises.full_solution: Let one cell have e.m.f. E and one lamp have resistance R, and treat the lamp as behaving like a fixed resistor (an approximation the question intends). In a single series loop the current is I = (net e.m.f.)/(total resistance). Cells in series facing the same way add their e.m.f.s; a cell connected the opposite way round (its + terminal facing the + terminal of its neighbour) subtracts its e.m.f. (a) 1 cell, 1 lamp: I = E/R — the reference current, 'normal brightness'. (b) 2 cells aiding, 1 lamp: I = 2E/R = 2 × (a) — double the current, so the lamp is much brighter than normal (and may blow). (c) 2 cells aiding, 2 lamps, all in one loop (the position of a lamp in the loop makes no difference): I = 2E/2R = E/R — the same as (a), so both lamps have normal brightness. (d) The two cells face each other (+ to +), so their e.m.f.s cancel: net e.m.f. = E − E = 0, so I = 0 and neither lamp lights. (e) 3 cells aiding, 2 lamps in series: I = 3E/2R = 1.5 × (a) — both lamps are brighter than normal, but not as bright as the lamp in (b). (f) Two cells aid and the third is reversed, so the net e.m.f. = E + E − E = E; with one lamp, I = E/R — the same as (a), so normal brightness. Summary: (b) brightest; (e) brighter than normal; (c) and (f) normal; (d) not lit.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P6 Questions, Q3 and Figure P6.16

assets.caption: the supplied diagram, redrawn: the six circuits (a) to (f). All six use identical cells and identical lamps; the long line of each cell symbol is its positive terminal, so look carefully at which way round each cell is connected.
assets.purpose: Show the six circuits, and in particular which way round each cell is connected, which is what the question turns on.

exercises.statement: If the lamps are both the same in the supplied diagram (a single ammeter A1 in the main supply line, which then splits into two identical parallel branches, each containing a lamp between a pair of ammeters A2–A3 and A4–A5) and ammeter A1 reads 0.50 A, what do ammeters A2, A3, A4 and A5 read?
exercises.answer: A2 = A3 = A4 = A5 = 0.25 A each.
exercises.full_solution: A1 measures the total current leaving the battery, 0.50 A, before it splits at the junction into the two parallel branches. Since the two branches are identical (same lamp in each, and presumably the same connecting-wire resistance), the total current divides equally between them, so each branch carries 0.50/2 = 0.25 A. Within a single branch, an ammeter and a lamp in series must read the same current (current is unchanged along any single series path), so A2 and A3 (in one branch) both read 0.25 A, and A4 and A5 (in the other branch) both read 0.25 A as well.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P6 Questions, Q4 and Figure P6.17

exercises.statement: Three 2 V cells are connected in series and used as the supply for a circuit. (a) What is the p.d. at the terminals of the supply? (b) How many joules of electrical energy does 1 C of charge gain on passing through (i) one cell, (ii) all three cells?
exercises.full_solution: (a) Cells connected in series add their e.m.f.s, so three 2 V cells in series give a total terminal p.d. of 3 × 2 V = 6 V (assuming negligible internal resistance / ideal cells, as is standard at this level). (b) By the definition of the volt (1 V = 1 J per coulomb), 1 coulomb passing through a 2 V cell gains 2 J of electrical energy, so (i) through one cell it gains 2 J. (ii) Passing through all three cells in series, it gains energy from each one in turn, so the total is 3 × 2 J = 6 J — consistent with the 6 V combined terminal voltage found in part (a).

exercises.statement: Three voltmeters V, V1 and V2 are connected as in the supplied diagram, with V1 across lamp L1, V2 across lamp L2 (L1 and L2 in series with each other), and V across the whole series combination of L1 and L2 (and an ammeter A in the main line). (a) If V reads 18 V and V1 reads 12 V, what does V2 read? (b) If the ammeter A reads 0.5 A, how much electrical energy is changed to heat and light in lamp L1 in one minute? (c) Copy the supplied diagram and mark with a + the positive terminals of the ammeter and voltmeters for correct connection.
exercises.answer: (a) V2 = 6 V. (b) 360 J. (c) Each meter's + terminal must be on the side nearer the battery's + terminal (i.e. the side the conventional current enters from).
exercises.full_solution: (a) V1 and V2 measure the p.d.s across L1 and L2 individually, while V measures the p.d. across the two lamps together (L1+L2 in series), so V = V1 + V2. Rearranging, V2 = V − V1 = 18 − 12 = 6 V. (b) The power dissipated in L1 is P = V1 × I = 12 V × 0.5 A = 6 W (6 joules every second). Over one minute (60 s), the energy transferred is W = P × t = 6 × 60 = 360 J. (c) An ammeter is always connected in series, with its + terminal on the side the conventional current flows IN from (i.e. nearer the battery's + terminal), so that current enters at + and leaves at −; a voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component being measured, and its + terminal must likewise be connected to the end of that component that is nearer the battery's + terminal, to avoid reverse-deflecting (damaging) the meter. So on the diagram: A's + faces the battery's + side; V1's + is on the L1 terminal nearer the battery's +; V2's + is on the L2 terminal nearer the battery's +; and V's + is on the end of the whole L1–L2 combination nearer the battery's +.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P6 Questions, Q6 and Figure P6.18

exercises.statement: Three voltmeters V, V1 and V2 are connected as in the supplied diagram (V1 across one lamp, V2 across a second lamp in series with the first, and V across both lamps together), and readings were obtained with three different batteries, giving the table: when V1 = 12 V and V2 = 6 V, V = x; when V = 6 V and V1 = 4 V, V2 = y; when V = 12 V and V2 = 4 V, V1 = z. Find x, y and z.
exercises.full_solution: As in the similar circuit of Q6, because V measures the p.d. across the two lamps together while V1 and V2 measure the p.d.s across each lamp separately, V = V1 + V2 in every row of the table. Row 1: x = V1 + V2 = 12 + 6 = 18 V. Row 2: V2 = y = V − V1 = 6 − 4 = 2 V. Row 3: V1 = z = V − V2 = 12 − 4 = 8 V.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P6 Questions, Q7 and Figure P6.19

exercises.statement: Calculate the effective resistance between A and B in the supplied diagram, where two 4 Ω resistors are connected in parallel between A and B.
exercises.full_solution: For two equal resistors R in parallel, the combined resistance is R/2 (or use the product-over-sum rule: (4×4)/(4+4) = 16/8 = 2 Ω). So the effective resistance between A and B is 2 Ω.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P6 Questions, Q8 and Figure P6.20

exercises.statement: What steps should be taken before replacing a blown fuse in a plug?
exercises.answer: Switch off and unplug the appliance from the mains first; find and fix whatever fault caused the fuse to blow (e.g. a short circuit or overloaded circuit); then fit a new fuse of the same current rating recommended by the appliance's manufacturer (never a higher-rated one).
exercises.full_solution: A blown fuse is a safety device that has done its job by breaking the circuit when the current became too large — simply replacing it without care could be dangerous or could blow it again immediately. Standard safe practice is: (1) switch off the supply and unplug the appliance before touching the plug, so there is no danger of shock while the fuse is out; (2) try to identify why the fuse blew (a short circuit from damaged insulation, or too many appliances/an overloaded circuit) and fix that fault if possible, since otherwise the new fuse will simply blow again (or worse, overheat the wiring if a too-high-rated fuse were fitted); (3) replace the fuse with one of exactly the same current rating recommended by the appliance's manufacturer — using a higher-rated fuse would fail to protect the appliance and its cable from an excessive current in future.

exercises.statement: What size fuse (3 A or 13 A) should be used in a plug connected to (a) a 150 W television, (b) a 900 W iron, (c) a 2 kW kettle, if the supply is 230 V?
exercises.full_solution: The normal operating current is I = P/V, and the fuse fitted must have a rating that safely exceeds this normal current (otherwise it would blow under ordinary use), while still being as low as practical for good protection; only the two standard sizes 3 A and 13 A are offered here. (a) TV: I = 150/230 ≈ 0.65 A — well below 3 A, so a 3 A fuse is appropriate (and gives the better protection of the two options). (b) Iron: I = 900/230 ≈ 3.91 A — this exceeds 3 A, so a 3 A fuse would blow in normal use; a 13 A fuse is required. (c) Kettle: I = 2000/230 ≈ 8.70 A — again above 3 A, so a 13 A fuse is required.

exercises.statement: How much electrical energy in joules does a 100 watt lamp transfer in (a) 1 second, (b) 5 seconds, (c) 1 minute?
exercises.full_solution: Energy transferred is W = P × t (power in watts, time in seconds). (a) t = 1 s → W = 100 × 1 = 100 J. (b) t = 5 s → W = 100 × 5 = 500 J. (c) t = 1 minute = 60 s → W = 100 × 60 = 6000 J.

exercises.statement: (a) What is the power of a lamp rated at 12 V 2 A? (b) How many joules of electrical energy are transferred per second by a 6 V 0.5 A lamp?
exercises.answer: (a) 24 W. (b) 3 J per second (i.e. 3 W).
exercises.full_solution: Electrical power is P = V × I. (a) P = 12 V × 2 A = 24 W. (b) P = 6 V × 0.5 A = 3 W, and since 1 watt = 1 joule per second by definition, this lamp transfers 3 J of electrical energy every second.

exercises.statement: The largest number of 100 W lamps connected in parallel which can safely be run from a 230 V supply with a 5 A fuse is: (A) 2, (B) 5, (C) 11, (D) 12, (E) 0.
exercises.full_solution: The total current drawn must not exceed the 5 A fuse rating. With n identical 100 W lamps in parallel across 230 V, the total current is I = n×100/230. Setting this just below 5 A: n×100/230 ≤ 5 → n ≤ 5×230/100 = 11.5. Checking: 11 lamps draw 11×100/230 ≈ 4.78 A (safely under 5 A, fuse stays intact), but 12 lamps draw 12×100/230 ≈ 5.22 A, which exceeds 5 A and would blow the fuse. So the largest safe number is 11, option C.

exercises.statement: What is the maximum power in kilowatts of the appliance(s) that can be connected safely to a 13 A 230 V mains socket?
exercises.full_solution: Maximum safe power is limited by the fuse/socket current rating: P = V × I = 230 V × 13 A = 2990 W = 2.99 kW.

exercises.statement: (a) Below is a list of wattages of various appliances: 60 W, 250 W, 850 W, 2 kW, 3.5 kW. State which is most likely to be the correct one for each of the appliances named: (i) kettle, (ii) table lamp, (iii) iron. (b) What will be the current in a 920 W appliance if the supply voltage is 230 V?
exercises.answer: (a) (i) kettle ≈ 2 kW, (ii) table lamp ≈ 60 W, (iii) iron ≈ 850 W. (b) 4 A.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Of the appliances listed, a table lamp (an incandescent bulb) draws only a small power, so the smallest wattage, 60 W, fits it; a kettle needs to boil water quickly and so is a high-power appliance, matching the 2 kW rating; a small domestic iron typically sits in between, matching 850 W (the remaining values, 250 W and 3.5 kW, are not needed for these three appliances and are included as distractors/for other appliances not asked about here). (b) Current I = P/V = 920/230 = 4 A.

exercises.statement: The vertical wire in the supplied diagram passes at right angles through a horizontal card. Point A is on the card just in front of the wire (on its south side, as the perspective drawing shows), and a plotting compass placed at A initially points towards geographic N, as marked. In what direction will the compass at A point when (a) there is no current in the wire, (b) the current direction is upwards?
exercises.answer: (a) It still points N (there is no field from the wire, only the Earth's field). (b) It swings round to point (roughly) east, at right angles to its original direction: the wire's field at A is along the circular field line, not towards or away from the wire. (If the wire's field is not much stronger than the Earth's field, the needle settles between N and E.)
exercises.full_solution: (a) With no current flowing, the wire produces no magnetic field of its own, so the only field acting on the compass is the Earth's, and the needle stays pointing towards geographic N, as shown in the figure. (b) A current in a straight wire produces a magnetic field whose lines are concentric circles around the wire, in the plane of the card. The right-hand grip rule gives the direction: grip the wire with the right hand, thumb pointing upwards (the current direction); the fingers curl round the wire anticlockwise as seen from above. At any point the field is along the circle through that point, i.e. at right angles to the line from the wire to the point. A lies on the south side of the wire, so the circle through A runs east–west there, and for an anticlockwise circulation (seen from above) the field at a point south of the wire points east. If the current is large enough for the wire's field to be much stronger than the Earth's field at A, the compass needle turns through about 90° to point east; if the two fields are comparable, it settles somewhere between N and E (along their resultant).
exercises.source_label: Chapter P7 Questions, Q1 and Figure P7.5

assets.caption: the supplied diagram, redrawn: a vertical wire passing at right angles through a horizontal card. The plotting compass at A lies on the card, just in front of (south of) the wire, and its needle starts off pointing towards geographic N.
assets.purpose: Show where A lies relative to the wire and which way the compass points to begin with, which the question's answer depends on.

exercises.statement: the supplied diagram shows a solenoid wound on a core of soft iron. End A is on the left. The arrow on the lead at the far (right-hand) end shows that the current enters the winding there; it flows round the turns towards A and leaves by the lead near end A. On the front of the core each turn of wire runs from the top of the core down to the bottom as it goes towards A. Will end A be a N pole or S pole when the current is in the direction shown?
exercises.answer: End A is a S pole (the far end, where the current enters, is the N pole).
exercises.full_solution: A solenoid behaves like a bar magnet whose polarity can be found with the right-hand grip rule: curl the fingers of the right hand round the coil in the direction of the current in the turns, and the thumb points along the field inside the coil, towards the N pole. In the supplied diagram the current enters at the right-hand lead and travels round the turns towards A. On the front (visible) face of the core it flows downwards in every turn. Hold your right hand with the fingers curling the same way (down the front, back up behind the core): your thumb points to the right, away from A. So the field inside the core points from A towards the far end, which means the far (right-hand) end is the N pole and end A is the S pole. Check with the 'clock' rule: looking at end A, the current goes round clockwise, and a clockwise current seen from an end makes that end a S pole.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P7 Questions, Q2 and Figure P7.6

assets.caption: the supplied diagram, redrawn: a solenoid wound on a soft-iron core, with end A on the left. The current enters by the lead at the far right and flows round the turns towards A; the solid red segments are the turns on the front of the core and the dashed segments are the parts hidden behind it.
assets.purpose: Show the winding sense the answer depends on: on the front of the core each turn runs downwards as it goes towards A.

exercises.statement: In the simple electric motor of the supplied diagram, the coil rotates anticlockwise as seen by the eye from position X (looking along the coil's axis of rotation, with the N pole on one side and the S pole on the other) when current flows in the coil. Is the current flowing clockwise or anticlockwise around the coil when viewed from above?
exercises.answer: Clockwise (when viewed from directly above).
exercises.full_solution: Set up the directions from the supplied diagram: the field runs horizontally from the N pole to the S pole, at right angles to the axis of rotation; the coil lies horizontally between the poles with one long side near the N pole and the other near the S pole, both parallel to the axis. Seen from X (looking along the axis, with N on the left and S on the right), 'anticlockwise' means the side near the S pole is pushed UP and the side near the N pole is pushed DOWN. Apply Fleming's left-hand rule to the side near S: First finger (field) points from N to S, i.e. to the right as seen from X; thuMb (force) points up; then the seCond finger (current) points towards the eye at X. So in the side near S the current flows towards X, and in the side near N (the other half of the same loop) it flows away from X. Now look down on the coil from above, with X at the bottom of your view: the right-hand side (near S) carries current towards the bottom of the view and the left-hand side (near N) carries current towards the top. Going right side down, bottom side to the left, left side up, top side to the right is a clockwise circulation. So the current flows clockwise round the coil when viewed from above.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P7 Questions, Q3 and Figure P7.13

assets.caption: the supplied diagram, redrawn as two views of the same motor. Left: looking along the axle from X, with the N pole on the left and the S pole on the right; the coil, seen edge-on, turns anticlockwise. Right: the same coil seen from above, with the eye at X at the bottom of the view. The current direction is what the question asks you to work out.
assets.purpose: Fix the geometry (which pole is on which side, where the eye at X is, how the view from above relates to the view from X) that the answer depends on.

exercises.statement: An electric motor is a device which transfers: (A) mechanical energy to electrical energy; (B) heat energy to electrical energy; (C) electrical energy to heat only; (D) heat to mechanical energy; (E) electrical energy to mechanical energy and heat.
exercises.answer: E.
exercises.full_solution: An electric motor's intended job is to convert electrical energy into mechanical (kinetic) energy — ruling out A, B and D, which all have the energy flow backwards or involve the wrong forms. It is not perfectly efficient, though: resistance in the coil wires and friction in the bearings mean some of the electrical energy input is always wasted as heat as well. So the full, correct description is that a motor transfers electrical energy into BOTH mechanical energy and (some) heat — exactly option E, not C (which wrongly says only heat, ignoring the whole point of a motor, which is to do mechanical work).

exercises.statement: (a) Draw a labelled diagram of the essential components of a simple d.c. motor. Explain how continuous rotation is produced and show how the direction of rotation is related to the direction of the current. (b) State what would happen to the direction of rotation of the motor you have described if (i) the current was reversed, (ii) the magnetic field was reversed, (iii) both current and field were reversed simultaneously.
exercises.answer: (b)(i) rotation reverses; (ii) rotation reverses; (iii) rotation stays the same (unchanged) as originally, because reversing both the current and the field cancels out.
exercises.full_solution: (a) The essential parts of a simple d.c. motor are: a rectangular coil of wire mounted on an axle so it can spin freely between the curved pole pieces (N and S) of a permanent magnet or electromagnet, with each end of the coil connected to one half of a split-ring commutator fixed to the axle, and two fixed carbon brushes pressing against the commutator to carry current in from the battery. When current flows, the two long sides of the coil (each carrying current along the axis, in opposite directions on each side because it is one continuous loop) sit in the magnetic field between N and S and experience forces given by Fleming's left-hand rule (First finger = Field, from N to S; se-Cond finger = Current; thuMb = Motion/force); because the current in the two sides is in opposite directions, the forces on them are in opposite directions too, and — since the sides are on opposite sides of the axle — this pair of opposite forces produces a turning effect (a couple) that spins the coil. The split-ring commutator is the key to making the rotation continuous rather than just a quarter-turn oscillation: every half-turn, as the coil passes through the vertical (plane perpendicular to the field, where the turning effect would otherwise reverse and the coil would simply oscillate back and forth), the two halves of the split ring swap which brush each is touching, which automatically reverses the current direction in the coil at exactly the right moment to keep the force on each side acting in the same rotational sense as before — so the coil keeps turning the same way, continuously. (b)(i) Reversing the current alone reverses the force direction on each side (Fleming's left-hand rule with Field unchanged but Current reversed gives the opposite force), so the whole motor turns the other way. (ii) Reversing the magnetic field alone (keeping the current direction the same) likewise reverses the force direction, so again the motor turns the other way. (iii) If BOTH the current and the field are reversed together, Fleming's left-hand rule is applied with both of its first two 'inputs' flipped, which leaves the resulting force (and hence rotation) direction unchanged — the two reversals cancel out, so the motor keeps turning the same way as originally.

exercises.statement: (a) The south pole of a bar magnet is moved steadily into a coil of wire which is connected to a centre-zero ammeter. What happens to the pointer on the meter? (b) The magnet is then withdrawn quickly from the coil. What happens to the pointer on the meter now?
exercises.answer: (a) The pointer deflects to one side (away from zero) while the magnet is moving in, and returns to zero once the magnet is held still inside the coil. (b) When withdrawn, the pointer deflects to the OPPOSITE side from before, and — because the withdrawal is quick — by a LARGER amount than during the slower insertion.
exercises.full_solution: Moving a magnet in or out of a coil changes the magnetic flux linking the coil, which (by Faraday's/Lenz's law of electromagnetic induction) induces an e.m.f., and hence a current, in the coil for as long as there is relative motion between magnet and coil; there is no induced current when the magnet is stationary, however close it is. (a) As the S pole moves steadily into the coil, flux through the coil is increasing, inducing a current in one particular direction, so the centre-zero ammeter pointer deflects away from zero to one side; once the magnet is held still inside, the flux stops changing, no e.m.f. is induced, and the pointer returns to zero. (b) Withdrawing the magnet reduces the flux through the coil (the opposite change to insertion), so by Lenz's law the induced current flows in the OPPOSITE direction to before, deflecting the pointer to the opposite side. Because the withdrawal is done quickly (a faster rate of change of flux than the earlier steady insertion), the induced e.m.f. — and hence the deflection — is also larger in size than it was during insertion.

exercises.statement: A simple generator is shown in the supplied diagram, where the rotating coil's two ends are each connected to a continuous metal ring (labelled A and B) mounted on the axle, against which fixed brushes press to connect the coil to the external circuit. (a) What are A and B called and what is their purpose? (b) What changes can be made to increase the p.d. generated?
exercises.answer: (a) A and B are the slip rings; their purpose is to maintain continuous electrical contact between the rotating coil and the stationary external circuit (via the fixed brushes) as the coil spins, without reversing the connections — this is what allows the generator's alternating output to reach the external circuit unchanged (unlike the split-ring commutator of a d.c. motor/dynamo, which DOES reverse the connections every half turn). (b) The p.d. generated can be increased by: spinning the coil faster; using a coil with more turns; using a stronger magnetic field (stronger magnets); and/or using a soft iron core inside the coil to concentrate the magnetic field.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Unlike the SPLIT-ring commutator used in a d.c. motor (or dynamo), which is deliberately broken into two halves so the connections swap every half-turn, A and B here are plain, unbroken 'slip rings' — continuous conducting rings fixed to the rotating axle, each permanently connected to one end of the coil. Fixed carbon brushes press against these rings and stay in electrical contact with them throughout the rotation, carrying the current out to the external circuit without ever reversing the connection. Because the connection is never swapped, whatever alternating e.m.f. the spinning coil generates (reversing direction every half-turn, as explained for the supplied diagram) is passed straight through to the external circuit unchanged — which is exactly why this arrangement is used to generate a.c., not d.c. (b) The size of the induced e.m.f. depends (from Faraday's law) on how quickly the flux linking the coil changes, so anything that increases the rate of flux change increases the generated p.d.: turning the coil faster (more rotations per second), increasing the number of turns N on the coil (each turn contributes its own induced e.m.f., and they add up in series), using stronger magnets (greater flux density B), and/or placing a soft iron core inside the coil to concentrate/strengthen the magnetic field through it.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P7 Questions, Q7 and Figure P7.20

exercises.statement: Describe the deflections observed on the sensitive, centre-zero galvanometer G (the supplied diagram) when the copper rod XY is connected to its terminals and is made to vibrate up and down (as shown by the arrows), between the poles of a U-shaped magnet, at right angles to the magnetic field. Explain what is happening.
exercises.answer: The galvanometer pointer swings alternately to one side and then the other, in time with the rod's vibration, momentarily passing through zero each time the rod reverses direction (at the top and bottom of each swing) — i.e. it oscillates back and forth, generating a small alternating current.
exercises.full_solution: As rod XY moves through the magnetic field at right angles to it, it 'cuts' field lines and an e.m.f. is induced across its ends (electromagnetic induction, exactly as for the single straight wire investigated earlier with the supplied diagram): this is only produced while the rod is actually moving, and its direction depends on the direction of motion. As the rod vibrates up and down, it moves upward for half of each cycle and downward for the other half; by Lenz's law, these two opposite directions of motion induce currents in opposite directions, so the galvanometer deflects one way while the rod moves up and the opposite way while it moves down. Since the rod is vibrating continuously, this means the pointer swings back and forth repeatedly, in step with the vibration — passing through zero deflection at the instants the rod is momentarily at rest at the top or bottom of its swing (where its speed, and hence the induced e.m.f., is zero) and reaching maximum deflection when the rod is moving fastest (in the middle of its swing). This oscillating back-and-forth deflection is in effect a small alternating current being generated by the vibrating rod — the same basic principle used (with a continuously rotating coil instead of a vibrating rod) in an a.c. generator.

exercises.statement: A transformer steps down the mains supply from 230 V to 10 V to operate an answering machine. (a) What is the turns ratio of the transformer windings? (b) How many turns are on the primary if the secondary has 100 turns? (c) What is the current in the primary if the transformer is 100% efficient and the current in the answering machine is 2 A?
exercises.full_solution: (a) For a transformer, the turns ratio equals the voltage ratio: Ns/Np = Vs/Vp = 10/230 = 1/23, so the secondary has 1 turn for every 23 turns on the primary. (b) Rearranging Ns/Np = 1/23 with Ns = 100 gives Np = 23 × Ns = 23 × 100 = 2300 turns. (c) For an ideal (100%-efficient) transformer, power in the primary equals power in the secondary: Vp×Ip = Vs×Is, so Ip = (Vs/Vp) × Is = (10/230) × 2 = 20/230 = 2/23 ≈ 0.087 A. (As expected for a step-down transformer, the current is stepped UP by the same factor — 23× — that the voltage is stepped down, consistent with power being conserved.)

exercises.statement: The main function of a step-down transformer is to: (A) decrease current; (B) decrease voltage; (C) change a.c. to d.c.; (D) change d.c. to a.c.; (E) decrease the resistance of a circuit.
exercises.answer: B — decrease voltage.
exercises.full_solution: A step-down transformer's defining job is to reduce (step down) an alternating voltage to a lower alternating voltage — that's what 'step-down' refers to. It does not decrease the current: for an ideal step-down transformer the output (secondary) current is LARGER than the primary current, because power is conserved (Vp×Ip = Vs×Is), so A is wrong. A transformer only works with alternating current in the first place (it needs a changing flux to induce an e.m.f.), so it can't 'change a.c. to d.c.' or vice versa (ruling out C and D), and it doesn't directly change any circuit's resistance (E). So the correct description is B: it decreases the voltage.

exercises.statement: (a) Calculate the number of turns on the secondary of a step-down transformer which would enable a 12 V lamp to be used with a 230 V a.c. mains supply, if there are 460 turns on the primary. (b) What current will flow in the secondary when the primary current is 0.10 A? Assume there are no energy losses.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Using Ns/Np = Vs/Vp: Ns = Np × (Vs/Vp) = 460 × (12/230) = 5520/230 = 24 turns. (b) For an ideal (no-loss) transformer, Vp×Ip = Vs×Is, so Is = Ip × (Vp/Vs) = 0.10 × (230/12) = 23/12 ≈ 1.92 A. (This makes sense: stepping the voltage DOWN by a factor of 230/12 ≈ 19.2 steps the current UP by that same factor, from 0.10 A to about 1.92 A, keeping input and output power equal.)

exercises.statement: A transformer has 1000 turns on the primary coil. The voltage applied to the primary coil is 230 V a.c. How many turns are on the secondary coil if the output voltage is 46 V a.c.? (A) 20, (B) 200, (C) 2000, (D) 4000, (E) 8000.
exercises.answer: B — 200 turns.
exercises.full_solution: Using Ns/Np = Vs/Vp: Ns = Np × (Vs/Vp) = 1000 × (46/230) = 1000 × 0.2 = 200 turns, which is option B.
